title: Texans Can't Ignore What Rookie TE Marlin Klein Showed vs. Colts
full_text:
The Houston Texans saw several names stand out en route to their dominant 26-3 win over the Indianapolis Colts .
However, it's hard to say anyone around the roster had a more unexpectedly impressive night than the Texans' second-round rookie tight end Marlin Klein, who turned in some of his best overall production of his first-year campaign thus far.
Klein, in just 16 total offensive snaps, made an unmissable impact for the Texans’ scoring attack. He saw four targets from C.J. Stroud, in which he turned in for four receptions, 24 receiving yards, and his first career touchdown from a 13-yard catch in the red zone in the third quarter.
Stroud finds German TE Marlin Klein for six! @nfldeutschland INDvsHOU on Prime Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/fS7L7wS8O3
Klein, despite seeing the third-most snaps for the Texans at the tight end position, was their most impactful pass-catcher of the night.
But on top of that production as a vertical threat, he also stood out noticeably as a blocker.
Klein was on the field as a run-blocker for just eight snaps–– half of his total playing time–– and turned in an impressive three pancake blocks in the process. Pro Football Focus had him at a 65.3 run blocking grade for the night , along with a rather impressive 87.0 overall grade.
I gotta stop watching Marlin Klein tape. I'm sick. Three pancakes in 8 run block snaps.. pic.twitter.com/dvt4sTGiIF
This type of impact is exactly what the Texans drafted Klein to be : a physical, versatile threat at the tight end position with strong size and physical traits who can be a strong blocker, but also an underrated receiver; something that he didn't get to showcase much of during his time in college with Michigan.
This week against the Colts, Klein finally got a chance to show off that appealing skillset with a much larger share of opportunities compared to what he had been accustomed to throughout the first half of the regular season.
Klein has been active for the Texans in six of their 10 games this season. He was a healthy scratch in four of them, and in four of the games that Klein actually was activated in, he never saw more than 10 offensive snaps. He failed to see any targets come his way from Weeks 2 through 10.
Why has it taken the Texans so long to get Klein involved in the game plan? It's a bit head-scratching.
Perhaps it's because Houston's staff felt he was a bit too unpolished to play over the other four tight ends on the roster until now. Maybe it truly is because the Texans felt he needed to improve on special teams, as coordinator Frank Ross mentioned after Week 4 against the Dallas Cowboys.
Regardless of why Klein hasn't been truly deployed until now, it's going to be extremely hard for the Texans to keep him off the field moving forward after the events of Thursday night.
While the Texans did give Klein an increased workload in Week 11, there's still much more room for Houston to expand his opportunities over the next few weeks.
Keep in mind, Klein has still yet to see 20 or more offensive snaps in a single game this year.
For perspective, Houston's current TE2 on the depth chart, Foster Moreau, has done that in all but one game this season: Week 9 against the LA Chargers, where he saw 19 total snaps offensively . Dalton Schultz has seen at least 25 snaps in every game so far this season.
But after Klein's latest performance, he's got a great case to eat into the snaps of both Moreau and Schultz.
His versatility as a pass-catcher and blocker gives him great reason to be on the field more consistently, adding even more incentive for the Texans to get their high investment of a second-round pick involved for the second half of the regular season.
Of course, we've only seen a small sample size out of what Klein is capable of, but it's an encouraging one. The Texans need to keep increasing his involvement until he gives them a clear reason not to. And to this point, he hasn't shown any cause to believe he's not deserving.

title: Texans Have No Excuse Not to Sign Justin Reid After Saints Release
full_text:
In a bit of surprising news that surfaced ahead of the NFL's Week 11 action, the New Orleans Saints are expected to release two-time Super Bowl champion safety Justin Reid, according to NFL insider Jordan Schultz.
Sources: The #Saints are planning to grant the release requested by safety Justin Reid, as both sides agreed this would be mutually beneficial. Reid, a 2x Super Bowl champion, is just 29 years old and has 698 total tackles, 11 INTs, 52 pass deflections, 6.5 sacks, 3 forced… pic.twitter.com/vahHoVZRZ6
Reid, who has been with the Saints for the past two seasons as a solid starting safety and team captain, seemingly didn't have a long-term role in New Orleans moving forward.
His snap share had dipped over the last three weeks. The Saints as a whole were struggling, and as a result, the two sides have parted ways despite Reid having one year left on his existing contract.
So now, the door becomes wide open for Reid to look around the market for a new team to call home for the second half of the 2026 season. Schultz reports that Reid is looking to sign with a contender, thus shrinking the pool of candidates to sign him to those with a realistic route for a playoff appearance.
Immediately, one team that sticks out as a strong suitor–– even with a 4-6 record–– is Reid's former team, the Houston Texans; a team that's building momentum at the right time for a late-season run to the playoffs , but could also use the extra help at safety with an experienced veteran like Reid.
Throughout the first half of the Texans' season, their defense has lacked the true elite production that they had proven to be capable of over the course of last year. Their consistency within the back-end of their secondary has been a big component of those struggles.
While Calen Bullock has held his own, it's been that second safety spot that's been an issue for the Texans across most of the season.
Reed Blankenship has seemingly regressed from his time with the Philadelphia Eagles and has struggled to adjust in his new situation, while his backup, M.J. Stewart, hasn't been much of an upgrade himself when he's been elevated as a starter.
Those back-end woes became so much of a concern for the Texans that rumors surfaced at the trade deasdline linking the team to interest in acquiring a safety.
That move ultimately didn't happen, yet it did show that Houston might've been interested in adding another contributor to the position to  help raise their floor from where things have stood through the first half of the regular season.
However, only a few weeks after the deadline has passed, and a starting-level safety in Justin Reid has now emerged on the market that the Texans could sign as a low-risk, high-reward addition to their secondary.
Now, throughout the first half of the season, Reid has not played particularly well compared to some of his prior years.
Pro Football Focus puts him at an overall grade of 49.1 that nearly ranks in the bottom 10 of eligible safeties. He's allowed 24 receptions with 12.5 yards per catch, has 11 missed tackles, and a not-so-great 141.7 passer rating when targeted.
At the same time, he is an experienced, veteran safety who the Texans could simply roll into the mix as a rotational piece in their secondary. He's a physical presence who can support the run rather well, and he was a former team captain from his time in New Orleans; all of which are traits that Houston values in any defensive back.
For a team that has struggled at the safety position like the Texans have this year, adding Reid is a risk worth taking.
Houston has over $8 million in available salary cap spending and could add on the nine-year veteran to a rest-of-season deal in an attempt that he can, at the very least, add depth and run support to a position that has been underwhelming for most of the season.
Worst case scenario: the Texans add Reid, realize he's not a great fit or the player he once was, turn back to either Blankenship or Stewart , and revert back to the status quo.
Best case scenario: he adds security to the back-end of Houston's secondary, becomes a weekly starter next to Bullock, and helps patch a hole that has consistently plagued this defense over the course of the season.
Regardless, a signing of the former Texans safety is a clear aggressive push from this front office that shows they still have belief in what this team could do in the second half of the season.
For a team that had real Super Bowl expectations heading into Week 1, at the very least, it's a move to seriously consider to try and keep building momentum to close out the year on a high note.

title: Texans' TNF Snap Counts Show Big Changes for Nico Collins, 2 Rookies
full_text:
The Houston Texans claimed a much-needed victory over the Indianapolis Colts on Thursday Night Football that might end up as the necessary spark to help this Texans team rattle off a few wins in a row over the coming weeks.
And in the aftermath of the Texans' win over their division rival Colts, we're now able to take a glance at the snap counts for both sides in the midst of Thursday night's action, and pick apart a few aspects that stand out from Houston's side of the equation.
Let's take a look at how those snap counts unraveled, then break down five key notes from how the Texans' lineup decisions panned out.
It may not seem like much, but Nico Collins seeing around 90% of the Texans' offensive snaps is something we haven't seen much of this season. The number actually sets his season-high in snaps through his eight appearances on the year.
Normally, Collins is on the field for a little under 75% of the Texans' total offensive looks. But over the past two weeks, Houston's star wideout has seen over 85%. Before Week 10, his highest on the season was 73% against the Jacksonville Jaguars.
Perhaps it's because of the multiple injuries to the wide receiver position, or simply because the coaching staff wants to feature Collins more than he has been this season. Whatever the reason is, it's resulted in back-to-back weeks of over 50 yards and a touchdown.
The Texans have been forced to make a change in their linebacker unit over the past two weeks due to Azeez Al-Shaair's injured reserve placement. And at first, it seemed as if Jake Hansen was in line to claim most of his snaps to start next to Henry To'oTo'o.
And Hansen did see over 60% of the defensive snaps in this game. However, fourth-round rookie linebacker Wade Woodaz also stepped up for a 32% snap share on the defensive side, his highest on the season so far.
Maybe that increased involvement from Woodaz is a sign of things to come after the Texans come off their mini-bye. Woodaz finished those 16 snaps with two solo tackles.
Another rookie who stepped up and saw some of his highest share of opportunities for the season: second round tight end Marlin Klein, who finally became a more featured component of the Texans' offense with a 24% snap share.
And the Texans made sure to give Klein his fair share of targets when he was on the field. Klein converted on all four of his targets for four catches, 24 yards, and his first-career touchdown thanks to a 13-yard red-zone reception sent in by C.J. Stroud.
Klein still found himself as third in the pecking order at tight end behind Dalton Schultz and Foster Moreau. But considering Klein was a weekly healthy scratch only a few weeks ago, this is certainly a step in the right direction for his development.
DeMeco Ryans explained after the win that the Texans had planned to rotate their right tackle spot between Braden Smith and Trent Brown before Brown would go down with a back injury early in the game.
That back injury left Brown to just seven snaps. As for Smith, though, he saw a season-high 59 offensive snaps and played pretty well in the process. He came out to an 88.1 overall grade via Pro Football Focus, excelling as a run blocker while also allowing just two pressures and zero sacks in pass protection.
Considering how well David Montgomery was running the ball, paired with his production as a pass-blocker, it might be hard to pull Smith out of the mix as a starter now. We'll see how the Texans approach things upfront once Week 12 arrives.
After M.J. Stewart had stepped up as the Texans' starting safety next to Calen Bullock over the last three weeks, the Texans made a pivot in their secondary against the Colts ; Reed Blankenship would fill back into his starting spot after seemingly being benched in Week 10 after recovering from his hand injury.
As for Stewart, he saw zero defensive snaps, instead filling into a more frequent part of the special teams unit with over 80% of Houston's total special teams snaps.

title: Texans Have Two Offensive Injuries to Monitor After TNF Win
full_text:
The Houston Texans put together a commanding win over the Indianapolis Colts on Thursday night en route to a 26-3 victory that might just be the spark needed to help this team rattle off a few wins in a row through the second half of their season.
However, in the midst of the Texans winning effort over the Colts, the team also saw their offense suffer a pair of injuries that will be worth keeping an eye on as they approach their next matchup.
According to an update from the Texans during Thursday night's game, wide receiver Kayshon Boutte (hip) and offensive lineman Keylan Rutledge (stinger) would be deemed questionable for a return in the fourth quarter.
. @ShariffLawFirm Texans Injury Update: #14 WR Kayshon Boutte is questionable with a hip injury. #66 C/G Keylan Rutledge is questionable with a stinger.
We ultimately wound up seeing neither return to the action. But given that the Texans were so close to ending the game, it's unclear as to whether or not either player was dealing with a serious injury issue, or were simply being held out for precautionary reasons as the result of the game had already been decided.
However, seeing both Boutte and Rutledge go down with an injury––each of whom has their respective key roles on the Texans' offense––is less than an ideal end to an overall successful night for Houston altogether.
One of these injuries has been an issue the Texans have already seen surface earlier in the month, and that's the stinger that Rutledge suffered that makes for his second stinger in the past two weeks.
The first stinger for Rutledge was bad enough that it led to him being sidelined for an entire week of the Texans' team practice , along with missing Week 10's game against the Cleveland Browns, forcing fourth-round rookie Febechi Nwaiwu into his first-ever start.
Rutledge was cleared to return on a short week against the Colts, but now after the same injury has surfaced once again, there might be a slim chance that Houston's first-round rookie is set to miss a little more time moving forward.
As for Boutte, his hip injury seems to be a new issue to surface throughout Thursday night, which turned out to be a pretty successful night on his behalf.
Boutte converted on both of his targets against the Colts for two catches, 40 yards, and an aggressive touchdown reception in the second quarter for C.J. Stroud's second of three touchdown passes on the night––making for his second game on the season where he's seen over 40 yards in a single game.
If Boutte is forced to miss any time, it'd mark yet another injury to the Texans’ wide receiver room following up on Jaylin Noel's injured reserve designation before Week 8 , along with the recent absence of Marvin Harrison Jr., which has led to him missing the last two games against the Browns and the Colts.
The good news surrounding both of these injuries is that the Texans are able to get a mini-bye at their disposal before they're tasked with taking on their Week 13 matchup against the Baltimore Ravens.
That means, for both Boutte and Rutledge, they'll have a little over a week to rest and prepare for their next game on the schedule, which could be just what each needs to get back on the field in time for this coming Sunday.
But for now, Houston's stuck in a bit of wait-and-see mode on the status of both until they're back in the building later next week.

title: What C.J. Stroud's Recent Hot Streak Means for His Contract Extension
full_text:
The Houston Texans have been witnessing some stellar play from C.J. Stroud over the first half of the regular season.
Really, it's been the best we've seen from the Texans' signal-caller since he broke out onto the scene during his rookie season .
Through the first 10 games of the year, Stroud has been averaging over 265 yards per game, completing 64% of his passes, and perhaps most impressively, is on pace to shatter his career-best touchdown-to-interception ratio as he's recorded 22 touchdowns to just four total picks.
Coming off of his last two up-and-down seasons of production, it's certainly a breath of fresh air for both the Texans and Stroud to be taking in––and especially so for Stroud himself, who's all but certain to cash in on a lucrative contract extension after holding off on a new deal this past offseason.
When Stroud was in talks of getting a big-time contract extension earlier this offseason , the general consensus remained that the Texans quarterback was due to get a noteworthy bump in pay if he decided to sign a deal before the season started.
That expected bump in pay seemed pretty certain even after Stroud's abysmal playoff exit against the New England Patriots , in which he recorded a haunting four interceptions in the first half en route to a haunting 16-28 loss in the divisional round.
According to ESPN's Jeremy Fowler and D.J. Bien-Aime , the Texans offered Stroud a deal "well within the $50 million-per-year club" when negotiations were ongoing; an offer that was considered to be a pretty strong effort, but still left Houston's signal-caller holding off on signing, and betting on himself to boost that value even further.
Fast forward to Week 11 of the season, and it seems as if Stroud's managed to do just that, plus more––to the point where it's not hard to imagine the Texans quarterback's value shooting up past those prior projections in the range of $60 million annually.
Stroud's going to find himself as one of the NFL's highest paid players if he keeps up this level of production. When combining the nature of quarterback contracts, along with the ever-appreciating value of those deals, the stage is set for Stroud to cash in.
Right now, eight quarterbacks in the NFL have an average contract value of $55 million or higher. Only two have values that reach $60 million or higher: that's Kansas City Chiefs quarterback Patrick Mahomes, and Dallas Cowboys quarterback Dak Prescott.
If Stroud keeps up the same momentum he's on right now by performing as one of the best quarterbacks in the league, there's little reason to believe that he can't join that exclusive club of netting $60-plus million annually on his next deal.
And that's especially so when factoring in that Stroud won't be the only big-time quarterback negotiating for a new deal this summer. Many high-end starting signal-callers are up for a fresh context as well.
Caleb Williams, Drake Maye, Jayden Daniels, and Bo Nix will all be eligible for some pretty sizable deals themselves. And the larger their respective contracts get, the same will likely happen for the Texans' quarterback as well.
Now, the landscape of Stroud's value could certainly shift significantly from where things currently stand. There's still seven weeks to go before the regular season wraps up, and that doesn't even include the postseason.
It was less than 12 months ago when everybody witnessed Stroud implode in his and the Texans' infamous postseason collapse that made many question whether or not he was the long-term answer at quarterback for the Texans, let alone a massive contract extension like he's expected to see now.
Another similar collapse from Stroud this year–– if Houston makes a late run for the playoffs –– would only spark those conversations around his future and contract value once again, and make those discussions on a new deal even more complicated than they once were.
But as Stroud currently sits, thanks to some MVP-level production through 10 games of this season, all signs are pointing towards him seeing a nice raise come his way at some point over the course of next offseason.
And based on how the Texans have leaned on him and their offense through their turbulent first half of the season, there's little reason to think that Houston will have no choice but to open the checkbook and pay their quarterback what we want to keep him around for the long haul.

Jared Koch is the Publisher of Houston Texans On SI. He has covered the NFL and NBA with On SI since 2023, and is a graduate of Western Kentucky University.

title: Everything Texans QB C.J. Stroud Said After 3-TD Performance vs. Colts
full_text:
The Houston Texans took care of business in their Thursday Night Football showing over the Indianapolis Colts in a dominant 26-3 victory.
And in the process of the Texans' primetime win, we saw C.J. Stroud have a pretty impressive performance from start to finish: completing 21 of his 27 passes, throwing for 194 yards, three touchdowns, and one pick to make for only his fourth interception on the year thus far.
Let's take a look at six of the most notable quotes from Stroud's post-game presser after the win that now takes Houston to a 4-6 record with just seven games to go on the season:
While Stroud had an impressive game individually, he made sure to not go without highlighting how their Will Anderson performed in one of his best games of the season : coming away with a sack, a safety, and a season-high 37.5% pressure rate with seven pressures and four quick pressures.
"Will is a dog, man. He's the definition of what you want for a Texan. I know DeMeco loves him. I know the ownership loves him. He just works super hard. He doesn't complain. He gets put in tough spots," Stroud said of Anderson.
"Just his tenacity. I think he just brings a swag to this team that I'm just proud to call him my brother. A lot of time spent together, so just really proud of him and what he's been able to do, and his faith. And also his family, being able to be an anchor there. So, big fan of Will for life."
Texans' C.J. Stroud after Will Anderson's performance against the Colts: 🗣️ "Will is a dog, man. He's the definition of what you want for a Texan." "I know DeMeco loves him. I know the ownership loves him. He just works super hard... Big fan of Will for life." pic.twitter.com/8lUGJ9REFJ
During the first half, Stroud's most glaring error from the night would be inevitably followed by one of his best plays–– as the Texans quarterback would come off of his only interception on the night to send a bomb of a touchdown pass to Nico Collins in the first two drives of the game.
Stroud said after that interception on the first drive, he went to the sidelines, worked on his footwork, then came out a bit more recalibrated to go and allow Collins to make a big play.
"I think because on the last drive, I kind of had something similar. I didn't get touched, but I just didn't put enough on it, and then it ended up being an interception," Stroud said. "I know I can make that throw, but I think being Thursday night, I needed to get my juices going a little more. I think that was a perfect example of that."
"I went back to the sideline and started doing a little bit of footwork that I knew I needed to get more oomph on the ball, more power... That play was great. I thought Nico did a good job attacking the high point. He's a heck of a football player. So if you give him a shot, he's going to make a play."
C.J. Stroud breaking down his TD throw to Nico Collins last night vs. the Colts: 🗣️ "That play was great. I thought Nico did a good job attacking the high point." "He's a heck of a football player. So if you give him a shot, he's going to make a play." https://t.co/ffWIT8Njbn pic.twitter.com/aDLvKAS7gE
Stroud is now putting together one of the best stretches of games we've seen from him dating back to his rookie year. On his current pace, he's set to total over 4,500 passing yards on the season, with 37 passing touchdowns.
Especially after the ups and downs he's faced over the past two years, Stroud is grateful to be in the spot that he is now, not only performing as well as he has been, but also playing alongside this Texans team.
"Ever since I've been a rookie, honestly, when I started playing, I knew what type of player I could be in this league. Just to get on that groove and have a rhythm has been amazing. Honestly, I would be lying to you if I said it didn't feel good," Stroud said.
"I'm very grateful for this opportunity to even play in the NFL. People probably think I'm crazy for always saying that, but I really did not expect my life to be like this. It's nothing but the grace of God that I'm sitting up here and playing the way that I am."
"It's nothing but credit to the team. The way the defense prepared us in training camp, the way the O-linemen are blocking their tails off and giving me a shot, and the way the receivers have been running their routes and getting open. I'm just super grateful to play on a team like this. I don't take it for granted at all."
Along with a strong night from Stroud, the Texans' offense was also able to witness an impressive stat line from David Montgomery, who saw his first 100-yard game on the ground in over a year, which also came in his first appearance on the field for Houston since Week 5 because of a groin injury.
Stroud says he was talking to Montgomery all week, trying to get him fired up for a good showing on Thursday. Clearly, that strategy proved to be an effective one.
"He's a baller, bro," Stroud said of Montgomery. "I've been motivating him all week, just talking mess to him and trying to get him going. He responds in the best ways. He's been making plays since I've been in the league and even before that. I'm super proud of that guy, and I think he'll continue to do great things for us."
"We were definitely missing him, and hopefully we get Woody [Marks] back next week. That'll be great."
C.J. Stroud on David Montgomery's 100-plus rushing yards against the Colts: 🗣️ "I've been motivating him all week, just talking mess to him, just trying to get him going. He responds in the best ways." "Just to give him an opp tonight, man, I'm super proud of that guy." pic.twitter.com/YcSSO3cOBl
The Texans' defense turned things around in a big way against the Colts compared to their lowly performance from last weekend against the Cleveland Browns . Houston allowed just three points and less than 200 yards to Indianapolis on the night; their second time doing so this season.
Stroud––who faces off against the Texans' defense more than anyone in weekly practices––knew that Houston was more than capable of turning things around on that side of the ball. He also emphasized that this roster should carry themselves "as one" rather than dividing the credit or blame to one side of the football.
"If anybody has respect, hope and faith in our defense, it's me. I get to play against them on a day-to-day basis," Stroud said.
"I don't rock with the whole winning-waves thing and how people change their opinions because you can flip it on its head, have a great game and everybody flips their mindset. I'm all about the process. What is your process? I think their process has been great. I think it's getting better. I honestly think they're great, and I'm just super happy to have them."
"It's not always perfect. Last year, they held us down as an offense a lot. When it flip-flops, we're not complaining. We're a team. We're one. That's something I've been trying to preach. We're not defense and offense. I don't think that talk is good for our team. We're one."
C.J. Stroud on the Texans' defense allowing 3 points vs. the Colts: 🗣️ "If anybody has respect and hope and faith in our defense, it's me. I get to play against them on a day-to-day basis..." "I think they're great, and I'm just super happy to have them." pic.twitter.com/zMzjD8ReQY
Stroud also didn't leave his post-game presser without showing some support for the Texans' fanbase, who have stuck by him and the team throughout the ups and downs of the season, and finally saw that rewarded on Thursday in the form of their first home win since Week 18 of last season.
And while Stroud loves the support from the Texans' fans, he certainly believes that he and the rest of the team have more to show them over the course of their second-half stretch of the season:
"One thing I love about our fans, even though it might not be all of them, is that there are a select few people who are always encouraging me and telling me how much they have my back, no matter what I go through. I'm really appreciative of that."

title: 3 Free Agent Bridge Quarterback Options for the Colts in 2027
full_text:
The release of Daniel Jones has added a new layer of chaos into the Indianapolis Colts' 2027 plans.
The question that has haunted the franchise since Andrew Luck's retirement will once again echo throughout the halls of West 56th street when the Week 18 scoreboard mercifully hits triple zeroes.
Who's playing quarterback?
The dearth of options isn't going to inspire optimism for those hoping to find quality play in 2027. However, when a franchise is forced to dip into the free agency pool for sports most important position, the outcomes will rarely end favorably.
Case in point, Malik Willis was recognized as one of the better true free agent quarterback options in several years. Yet his primary job is seemingly to be the tank commander for a team competing for the first overall pick.
After that rousing introdution, or more accurately, an expectation setter, let's take a look at three potential free agent bridge quarterback options for the Colts in 2027.
I didn't want to start the list with the same names that have already begun to permeate the Colts' sphere.
The name will probably illicit several, vapid groans from readers.
I offer Pickett's name as a proverbial "Trojan Horse" to the idea that the goal of the 2027 season should be the following:
Be entertaining while bad.
Maybe Pickett's name isn't the best proxy for the idea, but then again he is on the younger and more mobile side of the names that will be available.
Feel free to insert Justin Fields, Zach Wilson, Sam Howell, or Sam Ehlinger, if so inclined. In this case, Pickett has at least shown a flicker of promise when he's been in a positive situation in Philadelphia.
Indianapolis won't be the most uplifting offensive environment in 2027, but it also shouldn't be a dumpster fire. If the new general manager were to actually make this move, it would probably be in conjunction with another free agent quarterback signing alongside the addition of a mid-round rookie at the position.
If the Colts wish to be competent in 2027, Mac Jones may offer the best chance at reaching that coveted level. Jones, like Pickett was a former first round pick. However, unlike Pickett, the former Alabama quarterback has had tangible success at the highest level.
Most recently in 2025 under the tutelage of Kyle Shanahan, Jones posted a career best QBR of 62.3, a number good enough to finish top 10 in the NFL. In 8 starts, he completed nearly 70% of his passes for over 2,100 yards, while also tossing 13 touchdowns.
The former first rounder could be one of the most sought after free agent quarterbacks on the market this offseason. If the Colts want to outbid the rest of the NFL for Jones' services, then they would be wise to hire someone from within the Shanahan tree to run the offense.
Captaining an offense in a scheme in which he has recently thrived, Jones would raise the floor for an offense that has been truly putrid in 2027.
Whether or not a floor raising quarterback should be on the shopping list this offseason will continue to be a hot topic of debate as the 2026 season winds down.
If you could designate a clubhouse leader to be the Colts starting quarterback in week 1 of 2027, Drew Lock might currently be in pole position.
It would settle some type of karmic balance for Lock to come start for the franchise that he effectively put in the dirt in 2024, when he manufactured one of the most inexplicable one off performances in NFL history.
Still, if Indianapolis wanted the best possible combination of entertaining, bad and floor raising, Drew Lock is their best shot at landing in the middle of that Venn diagram.
Since being drafted in 2019 by the Denver Broncos, Drew Lock's big arm and tantalizing tools have made him a polarizing player. After a litany of struggles in Denver however, Lock has thrived in Seattle in relief of Sam Darnold. He is in the midst of the best stretch of play in his pro career, albeit in only three starts.
The thirty-year old is now eight years into his pro career, and has seemingly left the brash, overly aggressive playstyle by the wayside, to the tune of a 73% completion percentage in 2026. While he still picks his spots to use the powerful right arm that once got him drafted in the second-round, his decisions more often align with those of a wily vet.
Maybe it's time for Drew Lock to get a second lease on starting.
All he may need is a runway and a clean slate. Much like what was afforded to the teammate he's currently filling in for.

title: 3 Reasons Why the Colts Shutting Down Alec Pierce is the Right Decision
full_text:
The Indianapolis Colts have officially reached the point where protecting their future takes priority over what remains of their 2026 season.
The Colts chose to shut down wide receiver Alec Pierce for the remainder of the year as Pierce hasn't played since Week 2.
The #Colts do the right thing, shutting WR Alec Pierce down for season, with all eyes on a fully healthy 2027. My story on Pierce: https://t.co/u5JVfH900r https://t.co/u5JVfH900r
It's another disappointing development for an offense that has struggled to find consistency, but it's also the right move for the organization. Indianapolis has little reason to rush one of its most expensive players back in a lost season.
There are several reasons why shutting down the star wide receiver is the best decision for the Colts moving forward. Here are the three main reasons why it’s the correct choice.
At 3-8, the Colts have very little left to play for this season. Their postseason hopes have effectively disappeared, and the organization has stripped the roster down to the studs between their fire sale at the trade deadline and the decision to release quarterback Daniel Jones.
That makes the potential reward of bringing Pierce back difficult to justify.
The fifth-year receiver has been sidelined since September after aggravating his surgically repaired left heel. Although he initially returned for the season opener, his comeback lasted just one game before the injury forced him back to the sidelines.
Considering how that initial return played out, there is little reason to take another chance on a premature comeback. Even if Pierce were able to get back on the field for the final few games, the potential consequences of another setback would far outweigh whatever short-term benefit his return might provide.
The Colts certainly want to finish the season competitively, but that shouldn't come at the expense of a player who remains such an important part of their plans. They need to weigh the risks against the potential reward, and there isn't a whole lot to gain by letting Pierce suit up for any of their remaining games.
Perhaps the biggest reason for Indianapolis to shut down Pierce is the importance of having him at his absolute best next season.
The Colts made a significant investment in the wide receiver this offseason, signing him to a four-year contract worth up to $114 million. That commitment came after Pierce established himself as one of the NFL's premier deep threats, leading the league in yards per reception in each of the previous two seasons. He also surpassed 1,000 receiving yards for the first time in 2025, further solidifying his place as a key piece of the Indianapolis offense.
Pierce's ability to stretch the field vertically provides the Colts with an element that is difficult to replace, as demonstrated by their passing game's struggles this season. His presence opens up opportunities for other receivers and creates more space for the offense to operate underneath.
That makes his long-term availability considerably more important than anything he could provide over the final few weeks of an otherwise lost season.
Indianapolis needs to prioritize getting Pierce through a full offseason of rehab and preparation without another setback. Having him healthy and ready for the start of the 2027 campaign should be the primary objective.
And by shutting him down, that appears to be the Colts' line of thinking as well.
While Pierce's absence is undoubtedly a negative for the Indianapolis offense, it also creates opportunities for other players to establish themselves over the final stretch of the season.
Younger receivers such as Deion Burks and Anthony Gould could benefit from expanded roles, giving the coaching staff a better opportunity to evaluate what they can contribute moving forward.
The Colts have several important decisions to make this offseason, and determining which players deserve a larger role should be among them. Improving at wide receiver will still be a primary offseason objective for Indianapolis, but the remaining games provide an opportunity to gather valuable information about the players the team has on their roster now and determine if those players have a role beyond 2026.
Obviously, none of those players can fully replicate what Pierce brings to the offense. However, the organization can still find value in giving them a chance to prove themselves.
Ultimately, shutting down Pierce is the right call for an organization that needs to start looking towards 2027. His return might have provided a temporary boost to a struggling offense, but the potential consequences of another injury setback simply aren't worth the risk.
The Colts have already invested heavily in Pierce. Now, they need to protect that investment until at least the start of next season.

title: What Anthony Richardson Must Do With Colts to Revive Career
full_text:
The Indianapolis Colts shocked the NFL world by releasing quarterback Daniel Jones after getting bludgeoned by the Houston Texans on Thursday Night Football, 26-3.
The Colts have released Daniel Jones. pic.twitter.com/GfU0H1TLic
With Jones out of the Circle City, it means one thing at the quarterback position for the Colts: it's now Anthony Richardson Sr.'s time to shine with six games remaining.
Richardson hasn't been the go-to option at QB for the Colts since his disastrous 2024 campaign, and while fans are happy to see him get another shot to start, the skepticism is alive and well regarding how this stretch will go.
This is Richardson's last chance to make something of his Colts tenure, and he'll need to accomplish these three goals to revive his incredibly shaky NFL career as the 2026 campaign winds down.
It's fair to say Jones was a disaster during his 11 games with the Colts this year. Jones threw a whopping 13 interceptions and fumbled five times.
This comes out to an average of 1.18 interceptions per game and 0.45 fumbles per game. However, if we examine Richardson's 2024 campaign, it's eerily similar to Jones' 2026.
That year, Richardson also played 11 games and threw 12 interceptions while fumbling nine times. This comes out to an average of 1.09 interceptions per game and 0.82 fumbles.
Richardson has had two seasons to adjust, improve, and develop. One of Richardson's biggest criticisms has been his inability to limit turnovers and play cleaner football.
Ahead of the Week 11 Sunday slate, the Colts are tied with the New England Patriots with 20 giveaways, the most in the NFL.
If Richardson can help Shane Steichen's offense take care of the football, it gives this team the best chance to win while showing everyone that he's no longer a turnover machine.
Right up there with the turnovers, Richardson has arguably been more criticized for his wild accuracy and difficulty with completing the easy passes.
Richardson was a curious quarterback to watch when he was on the field. He struggled with easy completions but thrived with highlight throws that most field generals can't put together.
No throw encapsulates this more than Richardson's Week 1 moon ball to Alec Pierce in 2024 against the Texans.
ANTHONY RICHARDSON 60-YARD DIME TO ALEC PIERCE. 📺: #HOUvsIND on CBS/Paramount+ 📱: https://t.co/waVpO909ge pic.twitter.com/p0xddm5Kl1
Richardson's accuracy wasn't too bad during his rookie year, considering his lack of college football experience. That season in 2023, he played four games and completed 50/84 passes for a passing percentage of 59.5.
The following year, Richardson fell off a cliff and looked like the most inaccurate QB in the league, posting a brutal 47.7 completion percentage.
It's worth noting that Richardson had the likes of Michael Pittman Jr., Pierce, Josh Downs, and Quenton Nelson on the offensive line when he posted that sub-50 completion percentage.
Now, Nelson, Pittman, and Downs are gone, and Pierce is injured. Not to mention, the Colts didn't have their offensive tackles, Bernhard Raimann and Jalen Travis, in the last game against Houston.
Richardson won't have it easy with arguably the NFL's worst wide receiver corps and a banged up offensive line.
Regardless, this is the situation Richardson's been handed, and he'll have to figure out a way to be more accurate with the pigskin.
It's of the highest importance that Richardson limits turnovers, is more accurate, and shows he can properly command the offense.
But nothing compares to Richardson showing the Colts and NFL that he can stave off injuries and simply stay on the field.
To say Richardson's NFL career has been marred by injuries is an understatement. Below is a brief breakdown of his injuries during his professional tenure.
As you can see, Richardson's worst quality has been his health, and even if he was an MVP-caliber talent, nothing matters if you can't play.
During his two years as the starter (2023 and 2024), Richardson only logged 15 out of 34 possible games due to injuries, and if he wants to make anything of these next six games, he has to stay on the field.
While Richardson is exciting and threatens a defense far more than Jones ever did, he's still facing a massive uphill battle.
This offense has little to no impact players outside of Jonathan Taylor, and even he's been bottled up badly over the past few weeks due to the lack of pass-catching talent.
On paper, Richardson isn't being done many favors by being thrown into this situation. However, if somehow the former fourth-overall pick can elevate Steichen's attack without much talent around him, it will clearly display he's improved and might be on a solid trajectory.
These last six games will be interesting for Richardson and are likely the last contests he'll play in a Colts uniform.
