title: Anthony Richardson Brings New Life to a Lifeless Colts Offense
full_text:
The Indianapolis Colts just managed 167 yards and three points on national television. At this point, a little excitement would go a long way.
And with Anthony Richardson Sr. taking over for Daniel Jones, we might finally get some.
At 3-8, Indianapolis has lost six of its last seven games, and watching this offense over the past month has been downright painful. Thursday's 26-3 embarrassment in Houston was the final straw, and the Colts made the right call by handing Richardson the keys.
The defense at least has a few young guys, including CJ Allen and Justin Walley, giving fans something to look forward to. Now, maybe Richardson can help uncover some of those same bright spots on offense.
It's been a long road back for the former No. 4 overall pick.
Richardson flashed serious potential as a rookie in 2023 before a shoulder injury ended his season. His 2024 campaign was a roller coaster, with injuries, a brief benching for Joe Flacco, and a brutal 47.7% completion rate.
Then came 2025. Richardson lost the starting job to Jones and later suffered a freak orbital fracture during pregame warmups that ended his season.
He spent most of 2026 watching from the sideline, seemingly out of favor with Shane Steichen. Now, with Jones released and free agency looming, he's getting another opportunity to prove he belongs.
And what a redemption story this could be if he actually pulls it off.
Let's not pretend Richardson is suddenly going to become an accurate passer. His career completion percentage sits at 50.6%, and unless something major has changed with his mechanics, timing, or decision-making, those struggles probably aren't disappearing overnight.
But accuracy isn't what makes Richardson special.
It's the elite arm strength, his ability to attack downfield, and his unreal ability to scramble with the football. The guy has 640 career rushing yards and 10 rushing touchdowns, and defenses have to account for that on every snap.
That mobility could be especially valuable behind an offensive line that's struggled with injuries and inconsistency. Richardson can escape pressure, extend plays, and potentially keep drives alive that would've otherwise ended in sacks.
And don't forget Jonathan Taylor. Making defenses respect the quarterback as a runner could open up some much-needed room for JT, who's had very little to work with recently.
Look, the Colts aren't winning the division or making a playoff run. But with their 2027 first-round pick belonging to the Jets, I'd rather not watch Indianapolis hand New York an incredible selection, either.
I just want to see points, competitive football, and young players getting meaningful experience as this rebuild gets underway.
If Richardson can deliver that, these final six games might actually be worth watching. And I'm genuinely excited to see how his redemption story plays out.
Michael Greene is a graduate of Indiana University and the Scouting Academy. He's in his first year covering the Indianapolis Colts and NFL, with a unique focus on fantasy football.

title: 3 Reasons to Believe in Colts Owner Carlie Irsay-Gordon
full_text:
Carlie Irsay-Gordon's life has been a constant whirlwind since she and her sisters, Kalen Jackson and Casey Foyt, became the newest ownership group of the Indianapolis Colts .
In a short time after taking the reins from their father, Jim Irsay, following his passing, Irsay-Gordon and Co. have seen the highest of highs and the lowest of lows.
In her first season as an NFL principal owner and CEO, Irsay-Gordon watched her Indianapolis Colts take the league by storm with a 7-1 start, greenlit a blockbuster trade at the trade deadline that mortgaged the future, and ended the season on a seven-game losing streak.
Yes, she ultimately decided to run it back with longtime general manager Chris Ballard, head coach Shane Steichen, and Daniel Jones for the 2026-27 season, but even though things have crashed and burned as expected, her willingness to strike while the iron is hot is a promising sign for things to come.
Irsay-Gordon and Co.'s decision to run it back was met with a ton of flak, given that her first order of business was eerily reminiscent of how the Colts got to this point in the first place, but her reasoning made sense, especially when you consider the state of the organization at the time.
"Chris [Ballard] was able to adapt and adjust his approach. I think we saw a lot of improvement there," Irsay-Gordon said in her post-season press conference following the 2025-26 season. "We believe that they can replicate what we started off doing, and the sense of urgency has never been higher."
Irsay-Gordon allowed Ballard and Co. to finish what they started, and although it's fair to say the experiment should've ended then and there, this process has allowed the Colts to kick off their rebuild early, and Irsay-Gordon's newfound conviction is something to be excited about.
It took just six weeks for Irsay-Gordon to fire Chris Ballard , and almost every passing week since has been followed up with more sweeping changes in the organization.
Since Ballard's mid-season firing, the Colts have parted ways with Quenton Nelson, DeForest Buckner, Josh Downs, Keenan Allen, and now Daniel Jones.
They've also extended their homegrown star on the defensive side of the ball, defensive tackle Adetomiwa Adebawore, which has strengthened their rebuild's early outlook.
Some of Irsay-Gordon and Co.'s trade deadline decisions, such as the retention of veterans Jonathan Taylor, Grover Stewart, and Daniel Jones, have been heavily criticized, but it's hard to be overly critical when you take into account the fact that every move has had the next general manager in mind.
The Colts' aforementioned trade deadline exodus exclusively featured players on expiring contracts who did not fit the rebuild's timeline, and their collective return was a great start to improving their 2027 draft capital.
Indianapolis' infamous blockbuster trade package of multiple first-round picks, as well as wide receiver Adonai Mitchell, for cornerback Sauce Gardner hurt the rebuild's outlook, so trying to replace that value via an aggregate of draft picks was a smart move.
Trading Jonathan Taylor at the deadline would've been the biggest needle-mover in this regard, and although I still disagree with the notion of declining a trade package that includes a second-round pick and additional late-round capital for his services, I both understand and applaud Irsay-Gordon and Co. for sticking to their guns when their demands weren't met.
Furthermore, Grover Stewart's reported trade interest suggested that an offer of a late-round pick swap was on the table, but given that he was one of the few veterans on an expiring deal who seemed like they wanted to stay in Indianapolis, keeping him around to potentially make a Colt for life is worth the non-move.
Finally, the decision not to trade Daniel Jones at the deadline, only to release him weeks later , has become the final nail in the coffin for some sports fans and analysts. The Minnesota Vikings and Baltimore Ravens were the teams interested in trading for Jones, but his market dried up after they pivoted to Jacoby Brissett and Kirk Cousins.
As interested as the reports claimed they were, we've yet to see an actual offer for Jones's services be reported. If the Colts indeed turned down even a seventh-round pick for Jones, then this will be an undeniable blemish on Irsay-Gordon's resume, but for now, that's pure speculation. If nothing else, like the Gardner trade, this could be a learning lesson for Irsay-Gordon and Co.
Every move that Carlie Irsay-Gordon has made since Chris Ballard's firing has been made to empower the next front office, and this forward-thinking should ultimately make the Colts' general manager opening all the more attractive.
Some may still be skeptical about the Colts' current outlook, which is fair, but I'm willing to explain why I feel that ownership no longer deserves grace, but rather a belief in what they're building with Carlie Irsay-Gordon leading the charge.
The biggest talking point that continues to surround Carlie Irsay-Gordon is not about what she's doing behind the scenes, but rather what she's doing on the field.
Irsay-Gordon is regularly positioned on the Colts' sidelines on gamedays, headset on with a pen and notepad in hand. Ever since she became the Colts' principal owner, Irsay-Gordon's involvement on the sidelines has been widely criticized for being nothing more than micromanagement.
This is incredibly unusual, given that NFL owners have historically kept to themselves in a suite somewhere in the stadium as the focus on the bigger picture, but it's also not new.
“It’s been going on for years..." longtime Colts' veteran tight end Mo Alie-Cox said about Irsay-Gordon's involvement on the sidelines. "It's not an issue because she doesn't bother us. But I think mainly she’s just trying to learn the game of football, learn what we’re doing. She owns the team, so she wants to know what's going on."
Irsay-Gordon has been on the Colts' sidelines for 10+ years at this point, so the recent outcry against her involvement is not only ignorant, but it also makes me believe that misogyny is playing a factor.
It's ironic, considering that you'd assume real fans of the sport would welcome the idea of owners getting more involved, as opposed to them remaining out of touch, but I digress.
All Irsay-Gordon is trying to do is learn the game from the inside out, and I simply cannot view this as being anything other than a net-positive.
And if you were to ask the players, both former and current, they would agree.
The Chris Ballard era was so dsyfunctional that mediocrity became the end goal, and Carlie Irsay-Gordon quickly became fed up with all of the half-measures that resulted in such complacency.
For years, the same players, coaches, and decision-makers that failed to meet expectations were brought back for second and third chances, and this delusional belief only dug the franchise in a deeper hole.
Now, with Carlie Irsay-Gordon leading the charge, the Colts are showcasing more accountability than the entirety of the Ballard era ever showed.
As I pointed out, Irsay-Gordon has had some big misses early on, but she's not wasted any time in trying to right her wrongs.
She's fired Chris Ballard mere months after giving him one last shot, parted ways with longtime contributors who weren't getting the job done, and most recently made a bold, abrupt move that will be criticized for the foreseeable future.
However, it's promising to see Irsay-Gordon strike while the iron is hot.
It's clear that Irsay-Gordon is doing everything in her power to set up the next regime with a fresh slate, and this concerted effort to empower potential candidates should be praised.
The only remaining decision to question is that of Shane Steichen's retention as the Indianapolis Colts' head coach. Perhaps a post-season firing is as inevitable as it was going into the season, though we'll have to see what Irsay-Gordon and Co. have in mind before we pick apart the…

title: Ranking 9 Mistakes That Defined Chris Ballard's Colts Tenure
full_text:
Chris Ballard's tenure as general manager of the Indianapolis Colts is over, leaving behind a complicated legacy.
There were successes along the way, but ultimately, his inability to build a consistent contender and address some of the franchise's most pressing needs proved too costly.
Evaluating Ballard's time in Indianapolis isn't as simple as pointing to a handful of bad trades, draft picks or free-agent signings. Some of his most consequential mistakes were part of larger patterns that repeatedly held the organization back. For that reason, several related decisions have been grouped together into broader themes rather than treated as isolated incidents.
With that in mind, here is a look at the nine biggest mistakes of the Ballard era and how they helped shape the direction of the franchise.
Chris Ballard has long valued accumulating draft capital, but his decision to trade out of the first round in 2019 is worth revisiting given the talent Indianapolis left on the board.
Holding the 26th overall pick, the Colts traded down with Washington, receiving the 46th selection and the Redskins' 2020 second-round pick. Ballard believed the depth of the draft class offered comparable value later in the draft, giving Indianapolis three second-round selections and another the following year.
However, several notable prospects remained available, including Mississippi State pass rusher Montez Sweat and Washington cornerback Byron Murphy. Both went on to become impact players, with Sweat recording 60 career sacks across his time in Washington and later Chicago. Murphy has also developed into one of the league's premier cornerbacks, recording 20 career interceptions and 75 passes defended.
Those positions were particularly relevant to Indianapolis, which entered the offseason needing to improve its pass rush and secondary. The Colts ultimately used some of their additional draft capital on Ben Banogu and Parris Campbell, neither of whom lived up to their second-round billing.
There's no guarantee Indianapolis would have selected Sweat or Murphy at No. 26, but passing on the opportunity to add a potential difference-maker at a position of need is worth questioning. Ballard gained valuable draft capital, but the eventual return wasn't enough to eliminate the opportunity cost of moving out of the first round.
Ballard's reluctance to spend aggressively in free agency made his decision to hand Matt Gay a record-setting contract in 2023 particularly surprising.
After two productive seasons with the Los Angeles Rams, Gay signed a four-year, $22.5 million deal with Indianapolis, making him the highest-paid free-agent kicker in NFL history at the time.
Given that Gay had converted 92.5% of his field-goal attempts over his previous two seasons with Los Angeles and helped the Rams win a Super Bowl, there was no reason to believe he wasn't deserving of his pay day.
Unfortunately, Gay never replicated that production in Indianapolis.
Gay converted just 64 of 78 field-goal attempts (82.1%) across two seasons, including an 11-of-22 mark from 50 yards or beyond. Simply put, he never lived up to his price tag. Indianapolis eventually released Gay in April 2025, just halfway through his four-year contract.
Paying a premium for an established kicker wasn't necessarily an unreasonable decision, particularly given Gay's previous production. However, committing that much guaranteed money to the position only to move on after two seasons represents another expensive miscalculation by Ballard.
One of the more frustrating aspects of Ballard's tenure was his inconsistent ability to identify talent in the second round of the NFL Draft.
While Indianapolis landed several foundational players in the round, including Shaq Leonard, Braden Smith, Jonathan Taylor and Alec Pierce, too many other selections failed to provide a meaningful return.
Quincy Wilson, selected 46th overall in 2017, appeared in just 29 games with Indianapolis before being traded to the New York Jets. Kemoko Turay and Ben Banogu, both selected to address the pass rush, combined for just 14.5 sacks during their Colts careers. Parris Campbell, meanwhile, was as injury-prone as they come, appearing in just 15 games through his first three seasons.
More recent selections haven't offered much encouragement, either. Cornerback JuJu Brents struggled to stay healthy and appeared in just 11 games across his first two seasons, while wide receiver Adonai Mitchell failed to establish himself in Indianapolis before being traded to the New York Jets after two seasons.
There were certainly successful picks mixed into the group, but the frequency of misses is difficult to overlook. For a team that consistently prioritized building through the draft, wasting so many valuable selections set the franchise back.
Ballard's inability to build a dependable pass rush was one of the most persistent weaknesses of his tenure, despite how much he harped on being dominant at the line of scrimmage. Indianapolis found productive pass rushers through free agency and trades, but rarely managed to retain them or develop their replacements.
Denico Autry led the Colts with nine sacks in 2018 before leaving for Tennessee. Justin Houston followed with 11 sacks in 2019 but spent just two seasons in Indianapolis. Yannick Ngakoue recorded 9.5 sacks after being acquired in 2022, only to depart after one season. Samson Ebukam also led the team with 9.5 sacks in 2023, but an Achilles injury limited him to two games the following year before he eventually left the building.
Several attempts to find replacements failed to provide a lasting solution. Kemoko Turay and Ben Banogu never developed into contributors. More recently, Arden Key has managed just half a sack in his first season with Indianapolis.
There were some bright spots, including a franchise-record 51 sacks in 2023, and DeForest Buckner provided a consistent interior presence. However, the Colts went years without developing a dominant edge rusher of their own. Kwity Paye never became the consistent difference-maker expected of a first-round pick, and Laiatu Latu has followed a similar path.
For a front office that invested considerable draft capital and resources into the defensive line, the lack of continuity and a true game-changing pass rusher stands out as a major failure.
Ballard's preference for building through the draft and retaining his own players wasn't inherently flawed. The problem was how often that philosophy prevented Indianapolis from making the kind of significant additions needed to address its roster deficiencies.
Ballard repeatedly emphasized his reluctance to overpay in free agency, famously saying he didn't want to give "B players A-plus player money." That discipline occasionally paid off, but it also left the Colts relying heavily on draft picks and internal development to fill important holes. Even when Indianapolis had ample salary cap space, Ballard was often unwilling to put it to use.
The result was a roster that frequently felt one or two pieces short of being a legitimate contender. Rather than consistently pursuing established difference-makers, Indianapolis often settled for short-term additions and hoped its draft picks would take the necessary steps forward. The team's repeated struggles to find a reliable pass rush and build a strong receiving corps were two examples of that approach's ineffectiveness.
Ballard wasn't opposed to making major moves, as the DeForest Buckner trade and extensions for players like Quenton Nelson demonstrated that to a degree.
But those exceptions didn't change the broader pattern. For much of his tenure, Ballard seemed more concerned with preserving future flexibility than aggressively addressing the weaknesses in front of him.
That cautious approach helped keep Indianapolis competitive at times, but it never produced a roster capable of getting over the hump.
Ballard's decision to trade for Sauce Gardner in November 2025 was an…

title: 3 Winners, 1 Loser From Colts' Decision to Release QB Daniel Jones
full_text:
After eleven weeks of near-disrespectful quarterback play, the Indianapolis Colts have turned from Daniel Jones to Anthony Richardson .
But the Colts didn't just bench Jones for the foreseeable future; they outright released him.
This abrupt move comes following an unacceptable stretch from Daniel Jones that painted him as being the league's worst starting quarterback, one that concluded with a 26-3 loss to the Houston Texans on primetime television .
Head coach Shane Steichen's offense is littered with unproven and subpar talent, so it's not shocking that Jones has been unable to find sustained success, but it got to a point that no amount of personnel acknowledgment could justify rolling with Jones as the team's starting quarterback.
The Colts' handling of Daniel Jones had come into question , given that Indianapolis ultimately decided to keep Jones rostered after teams came calling for the struggling quarterback's services ahead of the trade deadline.
However, despite how they got here, the Colts have moved one step closer to their full-fledged rebuild, and there's reason to believe they could benefit from such an unforeseen move.
There's certainly a strong chance that the Colts' offense will continue to struggle with Anthony Richardson leading the charge, given that he hasn't started a game since 2024, as well as what surrounds him, but Richardson's playstyle will provide a fresh look for the offense, and that's enough to be excited about.
So, which Colts are set to benefit most from Daniel Jones's release? I break it down below.
There's no greater winner from the Colts' decision to release Daniel Jones than Anthony Richardson.
The Indianapolis Colts ' former fourth overall pick from the 2023 NFL Draft had become a figment of our imagination after Jones was named the team's starting quarterback ahead of the 2025-26 regular season, and now he's been given one last chance to right his wrongs.
Richardson will need to quickly burst onto the scene in an unexpected fashion if he wants to remain an Indianapolis Colt beyond this year, given that his rookie contract runs out following the season and the Colts declined to exercise his fifth-year option earlier this past offseason, but more than anything, this is a chance for him to prove that he belongs in this league.
The fourth-year quarterback will not only need to prove that he can be a steady hand for the offense, but he'll also need to show that he can stay healthy down the stretch.
Richardson's on-field performance is enough to be skeptical of, given that he's thrown more interceptions than touchdowns (13:11) and has a 50.6% career completion rate to show for, but it's his overall health that we'll be monitoring closest.
Richardson's career thus far has been littered with injuries, and the season-ending orbital fracture that he suffered in 2025 , one that happened in pre-game warmups, is the most recent installment of such bad luck that suggests he is injury-prone.
Regardless of what history suggests, Anthony Richardson has been given one last shot to prove that the Colts gave up on him too early.
Some Indianapolis Colts fans may argue that they're bigger winners than Anthony Richardson is.
On one hand, some of these fans in question have been devout Richardson defenders since the jump, and they are now feeling vindicated that their chosen one has been given an opportunity to prove them right.
Others have fallen out of favor with Shane Steichen, citing the head coach's unjustified loyalty in Daniel Jones as being the patience and understanding that Richardson deserved to be given.
And when it comes to the biggest Anthony Richardson detractors, even they have since jumped on the train that has a destination of benching Daniel Jones.
No matter which side of the Anthony Richardson war you stand on, most everybody has come to the same conclusion: continuing to trot out Daniel Jones in a lost season was doing nobody any favors.
Now, with Anthony Richardson manning the charge, the Colts' fanbase at least has something to look forward to on gamedays for the rest of the season.
The Colts may very well lose every remaining game, and the offense is unlikely to turn into something worth betting on, but at least Richardson's missteps could be met with an exciting play.
The Jones-led offense from the past eleven weeks failed to establish any sort of consistency, but they also struggled to generate any explosive plays.
With Richardson leading the way, errant throws will almost certainly be on the menu, but at least he possesses the physical traits and playstyle to expect bigger and bolder shots downfield. It may not be a good product overall, but it should at least provide some fireworks in the meantime.
Not everyone will benefit from the move to Anthony Richardson's howitzer arm, but the Colts' downfield passing game certainly will.
The Colts' offense is devoid of serious playmakers outside of running back Jonathan Taylor, especially at wide receiver, but they still have a few speed options who, when paired with Richardson, could threaten as options in the deep passing game.
Wideouts Ashton Dulin, Deion Burks, and Anthony Gould all come to mind.
Dulin has always served as a sparkplug for the Colts' offense, and Gould has flashed from time to time throughout his career, but rookie Deion Burks may just be the biggest winner of the group.
Burks, the Colts' final pick of the 2026 NFL Draft, sports some serious speed (4.30 40-yard dash at the NFL Combine), and Richardson's strong arm could be what he needs to unlock it.
Furthermore, Richardson's legs should help open up the offense altogether.
The Colts don't have Alec Pierce to strike fear in opposing defensive backs on any given play, but they still have Jonathan Taylor. Forcing teams to respect Richardson's downfield ability will help the rushing attack, which should be even more dangerous as opposing defenses will have to worry about Richardson's legs on top of Taylor.
Perhaps the only definitive loser from the Colts' decision to release quarterback Daniel Jones is head coach Shane Steichen, more than the general manager who went all-in on Jones as a last-ditch effort to save his job, or even Jones himself.
Shane Steichen's aforementioned initial decision to make Daniel Jones his starting quarterback was the correct move for the 2025-26 season, but the way he's handled the position since then has been questionable.
The Colts re-signed Jones to a two-year, $88 million extension ahead of the 2026-27 season, so they were always going to roll with him as their starting quarterback for this season, or at least until the wheels fell off.
But that's the thing, the wheels fell off weeks ago, yet Steichen refused to bench Jones despite having ample evidence to suggest otherwise.
Steichen's steadfast and unwarranted belief in Jones has not only resulted in a 3-8 record after eleven weeks, but it's also crushed Steichen's outlook as a head coach candidate, whether that be for Indianapolis in 2027 or anywhere else.
Now, with Daniel Jones out of the building, Steichen has to reckon with the potential outcome that sees either Anthony Richardson or Riley Leonard perform better with the same offense.
Regardless of what happens down the stretch, Steichen's hypocrisy and uninspired leadership will stick with some fans for years to come.
Noah Compton is the Publisher of Indianapolis Colts On SI. Noah is from the Indy area and has been covering the Colts since 2022, including stops at FanSided, The Blue Stable, and SBNation.

title: Colts Trade Deadline Proves to Be Massive Disaster After Daniel Jones Release
full_text:
The Indianapolis Colts ' decision to release Daniel Jones has brought an abrupt end to one of the more disappointing quarterback investments in recent franchise history.
Jones' struggles made a benching the most likely outcome, especially following a putrid offensive performance on Thursday Night Football . An eventual departure in the offseason seemed like a more realistic outcome.
Now, Indianapolis finds itself facing questions about how it has handled its broader roster situation since the trade deadline.
The Colts had an opportunity to move on from Jones before the NFL trade deadline two weeks ago, with multiple teams reportedly contacting Indianapolis about the veteran quarterback.
The Baltimore Ravens were among the teams that expressed interest before eventually acquiring Jacoby Brissett from the Arizona Cardinals. The Minnesota Vikings were also mentioned as a potential landing spot for Jones, given their uncertainty at quarterback. They opted for a reunion with Kirk Cousins instead.
Despite the interest, Indianapolis ultimately informed Jones that he would not be traded before the deadline , believing they had already paid out too much in signing bonuses to Jones. They wanted to see their investment through and leave the decision on Jones’ future in the hands of their next general manager.
Sources: The #Colts opted not to trade QB Daniel Jones despite receiving interest, believing they had already paid too much in signing bonus money. But they continued stripping the rest of the roster. Now, shortly after, they release him and get nothing back. None of it made… https://t.co/Pwsih7pv41 pic.twitter.com/KBBtxWQRsC
At the time, that decision was understandable given the organization was entering a transitional period. Allowing the next person in charge to evaluate the roster and determine which players fit into the team's future was a reasonable approach.
But now, with the Colts choosing to release Jones so soon after receiving trade interest, their entire operation now looks completely dysfunctional. While there's no concrete evidence that the Colts rejected a specific trade proposal for Jones, multiple teams at least had interest.
Just 10 days after the trade deadline, rather than allowing the next general manager to determine whether Jones deserved another opportunity in 2027, the organization made the decision itself.
In a season that has seen the Colts move several significant pieces, including captains Quenton Nelson and DeForest Buckner, the decision to retain Jones only to release him shortly afterward is particularly difficult to overlook.
The decision to release Jones is even more significant when considering the financial commitment Indianapolis made to keep him around.
After joining the Colts last offseason, Jones enjoyed a career resurgence in Shane Steichen's offense---throwing for 3,101 yards, 19 touchdowns and eight interceptions in 13 games---helping Indianapolis get off to a 7-1 start before suffering a season-ending Achilles injury.
Despite the injury, the Colts believed enough in Jones to bring him back on a two-year, $88 million contract in March. The agreement included more than $60 million in reported guaranteed money and represented a significant investment in a quarterback who had experienced considerable ups and downs throughout his career.
The Colts made a hefty investment. But Jones was unable to live up to his end of the bargain .
Through 11 starts in 2026, Jones threw for 1,974 yards, seven touchdowns and 13 interceptions. He also lost three fumbles, bringing his total turnovers to 16, the most in the NFL this season.
The Colts entered 2026 believing they had found some stability at quarterback, at least for the next few years. Instead, they are now releasing Jones less than a year after making one of the most significant financial commitments in franchise history.
It is difficult to envision a much worse outcome for an organization that was hoping to build on its early success from last season.
Perhaps the biggest consequence of the decision is what it means for Indianapolis moving forward.
The Colts initially wanted to preserve the opportunity for their next general manager to decide what to do at the quarterback position. Now, that individual will inherit a franchise that's made no progress towards finding a franchise quarterback since Andrew Luck's retirement.
Anthony Richardson Sr. is expected to take over as the starter, giving the former fourth-overall pick an opportunity to redeem himself and show that he can be a long-term option.
But given that Richardson showed to be highly volatile and inconsistent during his first stint at the helm, plus the fact that he's a free agent at the end of the season, the Colts are no closer to finding an answer under center.
The next general manager will have to evaluate the existing quarterback options, determine whether Richardson deserves another opportunity and potentially explore the draft or free agency for a more permanent solution.
Ultimately, the Colts' decision to retain Jones at the trade deadline was intended to give their next general manager more control over the direction of the franchise. Instead, they have released him for nothing, and created another major question for the incoming front office to answer.

title: Colts Cut Daniel Jones, Hand Offense Back to Anthony Richardson
full_text:
Wow. The Indianapolis Colts actually did it.
Daniel Jones is gone. Following Thursday night's embarrassing 26-3 loss to the Houston Texans , Indianapolis released its starting quarterback and handed the offense back to Anthony Richardson Sr.
Per Shane Steichen, we have released QB Daniel Jones. pic.twitter.com/jdGAZqj9ZI
At 3-8, this season is a lost cause. The Colts just managed three points and 167 yards against Houston, and watching this offense has become borderline painful.
At least Richardson gives us something worth tuning in for.
Jones arrived in Indianapolis on a one-year, $14 million deal in 2025 and looked like he'd finally found his footing. He threw for 3,101 yards, 19 touchdowns and eight interceptions, earning himself a massive two-year, $88 million extension this offseason.
But 2026 has been a completely different story.
Through 11 games, Jones completed just 58.4% of his passes for 1,974 yards, seven touchdowns and a league-leading 13 interceptions. His 65.4 passer rating tells you just about everything you need to know.
After another miserable performance Thursday night , the Colts finally pulled the plug on their $88 million experiment.
Remember, this was supposed to be the future of the franchise. Indianapolis selected Richardson fourth overall in 2023 after the Florida product put on an absolute show at the NFL Combine, running a 4.43-second 40-yard dash.
His rookie season lasted just four games before a shoulder injury ended it. In 2024, he started 11 games, throwing for 1,814 yards, eight touchdowns and 12 interceptions while rushing for 499 yards and six scores.
The inconsistency was impossible to ignore, and Richardson ultimately lost the 2025 quarterback battle to Jones. Now, after spending most of the past two seasons watching from the sidelines, he's getting another opportunity.
Through 19 career appearances, Richardson has completed just 50.6% of his passes for 2,408 yards, 11 touchdowns and 13 interceptions. Not exactly the numbers you'd expect from a top-five pick.
But here's the part that still makes him so intriguing: 640 rushing yards and 10 rushing touchdowns in only 15 starts.
This guy is a freak athlete, and pairing his legs with Jonathan Taylor could completely change how defenses approach the Colts.
Instead of selling out to stop JT, opposing fronts have to account for Richardson keeping the football on read-options and taking off when a play breaks down.
Sure, he might sail a 10-yard pass into the third row. But after trading Josh Downs and Keenan Allen, with Alec Pierce still sidelined, who exactly are we expecting him to pick apart defenses with anyway?
Give me some explosive runs, deep shots and an offense that actually has a pulse.
Richardson requested a trade in February, and the Colts declined his fifth-year option for 2027. With the trade deadline already behind us, he can't be traded this season, but he can certainly audition for another team in free agency.
Or maybe, just maybe, he plays well enough to convince Indianapolis there is still something worth building around.
Either way, the Colts have nothing to gain from another month of lifeless offense.
Richardson might not be the answer. But at least we're finally going to find out, and for the first time in weeks, there's a reason to be excited about watching this team.
Michael Greene is a graduate of Indiana University and the Scouting Academy. He's in his first year covering the Indianapolis Colts and NFL, with a unique focus on fantasy football.

title: Colts Position Grades: Another Embarrassing Divisional Beatdown
full_text:
The Indianapolis Colts were embarrassed under the bright lights Thursday night, falling 26-3 to the Houston Texans in a game that somehow looked even worse than the scoreboard suggests.
Indianapolis (3-8) managed just eight first downs, 167 total yards, and went 1-for-11 on third down. Houston scored 26 unanswered after the Colts' opening field goal.
Everything about this team looks uninspired. And somehow, the defense is now giving us more hope than the offense, something you never would've guessed watching the first few weeks of this season.
It's the Colts' second straight road divisional beatdown. Here are my Week 11 position grades.
Daniel Jones has to go. I still think he's this team's best quarterback, and I don't dislike him, but 12-of-27 for 144 yards and an interception simply isn't getting it done.
To his credit, he pushed the ball downfield more than usual before Anthony Richardson entered late. At this point, Shane Steichen has to seriously consider making a change at quarterback, even if no one on this roster would look good behind this line.
Jonathan Taylor and Seth McGowan combined for just 28 rushing yards, with McGowan exiting due to a hamstring injury.
When the passing attack is this hopeless, you have to have success running the ball. This was a piss-poor performance.
Anthony Gould led the group with 48 receiving yards, and no other wideout topped 30.
Poor quarterback play doesn't help, but these guys aren't consistently creating separation, either.
Tyler Warren's lone catch for 22 yards accounted for the entire position group's receiving production.
Add in the horrible blocking, and there's not much positive to say here.
Both starting tackles were out, and boy, did it show.
Houston's front absolutely feasted all night, generating pressure on more than half of Indianapolis' dropbacks while the rushing attack managed just 38 yards.
Adetomiwa Adebawore remains the lone bright spot, recording seven pressures, seven tackles, and the Colts' only sack.
Adebawore entered Week 9 leading NFL defensive tackles with a 16.1% pressure rate, but the rest of this group got bullied, particularly against the run.
CJ Allen continues to look like a legitimate building block, finishing with a game-high 16 tackles.
Bryce Boettcher had his moments, but beyond Allen, this was a pretty average night.
Missing Sauce Gardner and Charvarius Ward certainly hurt, but the remaining corners were dismantled.
C.J. Stroud finished 21-of-27 with three touchdowns, and Houston found big plays whenever it needed them.
A.J. Haulcy grabbed his first career interception, while Cam Bynum nearly had another before replay overturned it.
The safeties weren't perfect, but they were probably the defense's best unit.
Spencer Shrader finished 1-for-3, missing from 56 yards before having a 62-yarder blocked.
Difficult kicks, sure, but execution from this unit was downright bad.
At 3-8, this team isn't just losing. It's getting embarrassed, and unless something changes quickly, things could get even uglier in Indianapolis.
Michael Greene is a graduate of Indiana University and the Scouting Academy. He's in his first year covering the Indianapolis Colts and NFL, with a unique focus on fantasy football.

title: The NFL Won't Admit It Got Parker Washington's Touchdown Wrong, and That's the Problem
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- The Jacksonville Jaguars lost to the New York Giants in Week 11 for a variety of reasons, but there is one play that has already struck the cord as the catalyst.
For the Jaguars, the Parker Washington non-touchdown call, both on the field and on review, was one of several key turning points of a tough, physical, and frankly weird game against the Giants. For most, it was the controversial call of the weekend.
But touchdown or not aside , there are bigger issues for the Jaguars after this loss. For the NFL, the issue has already become a moot point, which is the entire root of the problem.
When the officials first ruled Washington's catch incomplete, there was 12:26 left in the game and the Jaguars were trailing 20-6. Washington appeared to have gotten both feet down in bounds in the left corner of the end-zone before going out of the back of the end zone, but the play was ruled incomplete on the field after the officials discussed it on the field.
"I did not think he lost possession of the football... I think it's a touchdown, fellas." CBS rules analyst Gene Steratore disagreed with this being ruled incomplete after review on a potential Parker Washington TD for the Jaguars. 🏈🦓🎙️ pic.twitter.com/4RdlPYAYXQ
Jaguars head coach Liam Coen challenged the play, but the ruling was upheld on review and the Jaguars had to settle for a 31-yard Cam Little field goal and a 20-9 deficit. "I was told that the ball switched hands, so that was what it came down to," Coen said after the game.
NFL Vice President of Replay Mark Butterworth spoke to Pro Football Writers Association pool reporter Pat Leonard after the game, and here is what he had to say.
"The ruling on the field was an incomplete pass. First, to overturn a call, we need clear and obvious video evidence to overturn the on-field ruling. It was determined that the receiver did not gain full control of the ball until he was out of bounds. ... He needs to maintain control of the ball throughout the process of the catch."
It is clear when reviewing the play that, no matter how you slice it, Washington caught the pass. Just a few hours later there was a Mike Evans touchdown agains the Minnesota Vikings that defied everything Butterworth just said. There is no clear pattern on how the NFL rules catches, and it seems here they simply went with the original call on the field despite having the evidence to change it.
That is the NFL's motto when it comes to officiating issues, though. Catch or no catch has become as traditional in the NFL as tailgates and touchdown cellys. If the gut reaction to a clear catch is "let's see if they actually call it one," then the NFL has a problem with how they are ruling plays on a game-to-game basis.
But the NFL will not ever flat-out say they got it wrong. It is not the reason the Jaguars lost on Sunday; they have themselves to blame for that. And the NFL finally becoming accountable would not go back in time and give the Jaguars the points. But the fact they can not admit fault has become the biggest issue with such plays.
"Yeah, I mean, it's a close play, obviously. They called it and said it wasn't. I thought it was incredible that he gave us a shot there and he caught it. It looked like he had two feet down, but it was close, and you can't leave it in the ref's hands," Trevor Lawrence said post-game.
"I think it's a tough call for them. Even though that didn't go our way, we had so many opportunities that we just didn't capitalize on. So, we’ve got to keep playing the next play.
That wasn't the Jaguars' only odd sequence with the officials Sunday. There was also the replay assist debacle in the first-half, with the Jaguars having to use one of their challenges to overrule a Chris Rodriguez Jr. rush on third-down. Rodriguez was originally given the first down, but replay assist overruled it and changed it to fourth-and-short. Coen won the challenge, but the fact he had to use one of his limited challenges to correct a replay assist.
"For the first part, the ruling on the field was a first down. It was an improper replay assist to short of the line to gain. They thought the knee was down," Butterworth said. "The key here is even when we replay assist, that still allows teams to challenge in most circumstances if they don't agree with the replay assist. And when we went to challenge, it was clear and obvious that the runner's knee was up and he was, therefore, he made a first down and we awarded a successful challenge to the team."
That ... does not make much sense. Butterworth saying it was "an impropert replay assist," is as close as the NFL will likely ever get to saying they were wrong about a ruling. But he then goes on to defend replay assist by noting that teams can still challenge the play and, well, fix the wrong call made. The issue is that the Jaguars had to use one of their only challenges, and Coen doesn't just get that challenge back.
Head coaches are afforded two challenges each game. If they get both correct, then they get a third. Coen used all three during the game, winning the first two (including on a Malik Nabers catch in the first-half), before losing the Washington one. But what if there was a play worth challenging before the Washington catch? If Coen had challenged it, win or lose, he would not have been able to challenge the Washington play.
Even with the hindsight of Coen losing the Washington challenge, there is no coach in football who would not have thrown the red flag there. There are a number of scenarios where the Jaguars could have gotten burned by the league because of the replay assist challenge, and it never should have happened.
Will the NFL ever concede that? No, not likely. But that is the NFL's mode of operation when it comes to officiating. Right, wrong, or in between, they toe their company line and do not offer up accountability. This is not the first time a team has seen their games impacted by such mistakes, and the NFL's attitude means it also will not be the last.

title: 3 Things We Learned From the Jaguars' Loss to Giants: The Injuries Are Mounting
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- The Jacksonville Jaguars have a few key lessons they are going to have to learn after Week 11.
The Jaguars lost 23-18 to the New York Giants on the road Sunday, and it was a game that certainly saw the Jaguars not play their best when their best was required. And in that loss, there are plenty of lessons for the Jaguars to learn from.
So, what did we learn from the Jaguars' loss to the Giants? We break it down below.
The Jaguars entered Sunday with a few dings and bruises, such as center Robert Hainsey being ruled out and Bhayshul Tuten entering the game at less than 100%. Add in earlier injuries to Anton Harrison, Davon Hamilton, Caleb Ransaw, and Eric Murray and the injuries have really started to pile up. That was before left tackle Walker Little left the game in the second-half with a lower-body injury, and before Tuten left the game early as well after getting attended to during the second-half.
The Jaguars do not have all that much standing in their way of an AFC South title and a significant seed in the AFC as a whole. But injuries derail seasons every single year, and we certainly saw injuries play a big role in the Jaguars' loss on Sunday. Whether these injuries will impact the Jaguars moving forward as they play a few more tough teams remains to be seen, but it sure seems like they are starting to mount.
The Jaguars' injuries at present moment have impacted the offensive line the most, and the Jaguars clearly missed starting center Robert Hainsey especially. We saw this game as a chance for second-year center Jonah Monheim to stake his claim to a potential starting gig at center beyond the 2026 season, but it certainly seems like we should put that on ice at least for now. Monheim seemed to struggle against the Giants' front, especially against veteran defensive tackle D.J. Reader. That is not uncommon for a young offensive lineman, of course, but it does perhaps show the value of Hainsey.
Simply put, Hainsey has been there and done that in the NFL. He is in his sixth NFL season and has played more snaps in the league than Monheim by quite a bit, and that experience is likely a big reason why the Jaguars signed him last March to begin with. The trenches are a place where players get better as they get older, stronger, and more experienced, and those are a few boxes Hainsey certainly checks. It was a bad call to suggest him missing the game would not be a big deal, because it certainly felt like the Jaguars could have used him.
Two things can be, and ultimately are, true: Trevor Lawrence is a big reason the Jaguars lost the game on Sunday, and Trevor Lawrence is a big reason the Jaguars ever had a chance to win it at the end of the game. Lawrence had his worst game of the season Sunday, throwing two interceptions for the first time in a regular-season game since last year's battle against the Arizona Cardinals in Week 12 of the 2025 season. There were more than a few other times when Lawrence could have gotten picked off, too.
There seemed like some clear reasons why Lawrence played the way that he did. He was forced to play a frantic style of passer against the Giants' pass-rush, with Abdul Carter seemingly singlehandedly taking over the game for large stretches. Add in the injuries up front and the lack of a running game, and Lawrence was put in a rough spot throughout the course of the game. But even with that consideration, that doesn't change the fact that Lawrence was not at his best on Sunday.
This performance will likely deal a big blow to the Jaguars quarterback's MVP case since Brock Purdy is coming off a big-time game against the Minnesota Vikings, and Joe Burrow is clearly on a heater in terms of passing production. Lawrence has been elite for the majority of the season, and Sunday was likely a blip in the same way all top quarterbacks sustain blips over the course of 17-game seasons. But Lawrence is indeed human after all, something we have not seen for most of the year.

title: Game Balls From Jaguars' Loss to Giants: Parker Washington Shines Despite Controversial Call
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- The Jacksonville Jaguars are set to lick their wounds after a tough Week 11.
The Jaguars lost a very winnable game against the Giants in Week 11, slipping to 7-3 after a 23-18 loss at MetLife Stadium. But even with the poor outcome, the Jaguars still had several players come up big for them over the course of Sunday afternoon.
So, which Jaguars earned game balls after today's performance? We break down the three standout performers below.
While it certainly feels like Jaguars wide receiver Parker Washington got robbed of a touchdown (twice, somehow), he still had a stellar game all things considered. He was targeted a whopping 17 times, but more than anything he proved that when it is crunch time and the Jaguars need a big play, he is the first person they need to think of getting the ball to. His 3rd-and-20 catch and first down in the fourth quarter is a huge reason this was even a game at all.
Washington recorded 103 yards on eight receptions, surpassing 100 receiving yards in consecutive games for the second time in his career. His 13 receptions of 20-plus yards this season are tied for the most in the AFC, while his six receptions of 20-plus yards since Week 10 are the most in the NFL. There were not many players on offense who performed well, but it certainly felt like Washington was able to.
The Jaguars' defense had a few players put in standout performances on Sunday, including Antonio Johnson and Ventrell Miller. It was a quieter day for the Jaguars' two new additions to the defense in Jordan Davis and Jessie Bates III, but there was still one big-name defender for the Jaguars who was able to make plays when they needed it: defensive end Josh Hines-Allen, who recorded a sack, a forced fumble, and a pass deflection.
Hines-Allen is the only player in the NFL this year with two different games with a sack and forced fumble in the same four quarters, and he has been able to make big plays for the Jaguars in big spots this year. Perhaps the big plays do not always come in the form of sacks, but Hines-Allen made a massive difference to the Jaguars' defense on Sunday, and it was the kind of performance that should remind people how key he is to the Jaguars' defense as a whole.
What a run for Jaguars kicker Cam Little. Ever since the Week 5 game against the Philadelphia Eagles when he hit a walk-off, he has been a machine. Little went four-for-four on field goals against the Giants, becoming the ninth player in NFL history to make at least four field goals in three consecutive games. Little also became the first player in Jaguars history to make 12 field goals in a three-game span. He has scored 43 points over that stretch, the second-most points in a three-game span in franchise history. He has been terrific for Jacksonville this season, and is deserving of Pro Bowl and All-Pro honors if he keeps it up over the next two months.

title: 4 Winners, 4 Losers From Jaguars' Tough Loss to Giants: Trevor Lawrence's First Uneven Game
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- The Jacksonville Jaguars got punched in the mouth on Sunday night. Now, they will have to prove they can throw a punch right back.
Jacksonville lost to the New York Giants in a physical, intense, and controversial 23-18 battle that has been marred by some of the calls made throughout the game. But even without those calls, the Jaguars had plenty of self-inflicted mistakes.
"And with us as an offense as a whole, I thought we didn't come out with the aggressiveness and attacking that we normally have. I felt like they punched us in the mouth a little bit," Jaguars quarterback Trevor Lawrence said after the game. "It was nice to see the fight at the end of the game and that we were still able to have a shot, thanks to our defense. We let our defense down today."
So, who were the biggest winners and losers in Sunday's loss? We break it down below.
Parker Washington got robbed of a touchdown (more on that later), but he was still clearly the Jaguars' No. 1 wide receiver, and still clearly set to receive a big contract sooner rather than later. Washington was targeted 17 times (17!) on Sunday, and it was Washington who the Jaguars kept turning to in the red-zone, on third-down, and whenever they wanted to heave the ball downfield.
Washington has had better games in terms of pure efficiency, such as last week against the Titans, but this game just further proved that he is the undisputed top weapon in the passing game. The Jaguars had to throw the ball to get back into this game, and Washington was the first, second, and third guy they went to before they looked to anyone else. For someone in line for a big deal, that means something.
Jaguars fans have been begging for an impact from their pair of talented edge defenders from a box score perspective, and they got it on Sunday. Travon Walker played well by drawing a few holds and landing some key pressures, but it was Josh Hines-Allen who had the most productive night out of all of the Jaguars' defenders, which says something considering the Jaguars' defense had a pretty good game all things considered.
Hines-Allen recorded a first-half sack, had a pass-deflection, and recorded a punch-out fumble on Cam Skattebo that is a big reason the Jaguars hung in this game. Even though the Jaguars didn't score after the turnover, it felt like the Giants were about to put the game away in the third-quarter in Jaguars territory, and Hines-Allen prevented it from happening.
Cam Skattebo fumbles and the Jaguars carry it to the other side of the field pic.twitter.com/WbuSs1JpYd
Yes, you may still be wondering how Antonio Johnson didn't score on his recovered fumble from Josh Hines-Allen, but that should not get in the way of ignoring what Johnson did the rest of the game. He had two pass breakups, a tackle for loss, and consistently looked like one of the defense's most impactful players. Add in a near-interception, and it could ahve been an even bigger night for Johnson.
He did get beat for a red-zone touchdown by Malik Nabers, but ... let's be real. That was good scheming by the Giants to get Nabers in thes lot against Johnson instead of on the outside against Travis Hunter. Outside of that one play, though, the Jaguars got some really strong play out of their young, talented safety.
It was not an overly efficient night for any of the Jaguars' receivers, but this still felt like a solid performance from Jakobi Meyers. The veteran receiver only caught four of his 10 targets, but he turned them into 85 yards and several critical catches down the stretch. It feels like Meyers is making an important catch over the middle of the field at least once a week, and this week was no different for the Jaguars' reliable veteran.
Meyers was one of only two Jaguars players to get 10 targets or more, behind just Parker Washington. Josh Cameron and Brian Thomas Jr. combined for the same number of targets that Meyers got alone. There was never much of a debate of whether he was the Jaguars' No. 2 receiver, but it is clear this is the case.
The Jaguars did not outright lose this game because of the officials -- not by a long-shot. But the officials in this game were arguably the worst ceew the Jaguars have had all season, which says something considering some of the crews they have had on their games this season. Parker Washington's non-touchdown catch felt like an awful call in the moment, and the officials' explanation hasn't made things any better.
But it also went beyond that. Montaric Brown's early DPI ... looked weak. Jameis Winston looked short of the end-zone. And the Jaguars also had to waste a challenge on something the officials got clearly and plainly wrong on the replay assisted call on Chris Rodriguez's early third-down run. The NFL's officiating has perhaps never been as bad week-to-week as it has this year, and the Jaguars paid for it on Sunday.
That was pretty easily the worst game Trevor Lawrence has played all season. He got picked twice on two plays that, frankly, made no sense. He also put the ball in harms way several other times and forced the Jaguars' skill players to turn into defenders to ensure the ball was not intercepted. Context is required, and it is clear the Jaguars' protection issues led to Lawrence playing frantic at times, but this was his first bad game all season, and that is the only real truth to it.
"It was a rough day for us. Offensively, we just didn't play well at all. I felt like we just didn't come out sharp from the very beginning. I played really, really poorly today, and you're not going to win many games if I don't play better than that," Lawrence said. "So, I take a lot of it on myself. I did not make enough plays or enough of the routine plays, easy ones. I'm really frustrated with my performance."
Lawrence did have some good moments. He looked like a magician escaping pressure on probably a dozen different occasions, and he made some elite-level throws in the second-half. But the Jaguars will need Lawrence to be better moving forward than he was on Sunday.
The Bhayshul Tuten we watched over the first two months of the season looked like one of the best running backs in the NFL. Tuten was seemingly singlehandedly driving the Jaguars' rushing attack with yards after contact production that Liam Coen was coveting from his running game this season. But after getting injured in Week 8 against the Indianapolis Colts and playing three games since with a foot/ankle injury, it is clear that Tuten is far from 100%.
Tuten rushed 10 times for 33 yards, his third game in a row with a yards per carry average under 3.5 yards. He only had two such games in the first two months of the season, and it is clear the injury has just taken away the traits that make him such a special player. Add in the fact that he had to leave the game twice, and this felt like a lost Sunday for the Jaguars' star running back.
The Jaguars turned to second-year center Jonah Monheim at center in the place of injured starter Robert Hainsey, and it was ... not a great outing for the former seventh-round pick. Monheim has stepped up for the Jaguars plenty of times since he was drafted, making two starts in Hainsey's place last season and stepping in at other times, such as last week against the Tennessee Titans. But Sunday ... was different.
None of the Jaguars' offensive linemen played well sans perhaps Emmanuel Pregnon, but Monheim might have had the toughest performance of them all. He was beat several times in pass-protection, got little push in the running game, and ultimately did not have the kind of performance I think anyone was expecting.

title: 7 Instant Observations on Jaguars' Letdown vs. Giants: Parker Washington's Non-TD Looms Large
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- The Jacksonville Jaguars let one get away from them.
The Jaguars nearly had a frantic comeback to defeat the New York Giants in the final quarter of Week 11, but a few clear issues, and one big controversial call, led to a 23-18 loss and has dropped the Jaguars to 7-3.
So, what did we see from the Jaguars on Sunday? We break it down below.
The Giants had a brutal red-zone scoring defense entering the week, but that did not seem to matter for the Jaguars. Jacksonville has had a few weeks in a row where they have been unable to cash-in on red-zone trips a bit too often, going 3-of-5 against the Tennessee Titans last week and 2-of-4 against the Baltimore Ravens the week before. These were not breutal numbers, but it was clear the Jaguars' offense had left some meat on the bone.
This showed up in a big way against the Giants, and is likely what is the biggest reason the Jaguars lost. Jacksonville went 0-for-2 on red-zone trips in the first-half early and had to settle for two field goals instead, and then the Jaguars failed to convert a fourth-down in the red-zone after Antonio Johnson's recovered fumble. Had the Jaguars cashed in on at least two of these, this would have been a different day and not a tough loss when the Jaguars didn't really need one.
The Jaguars' offense under Liam Coen has always depended on balance. It is not a scheme set up to drop back and air it out all game, especially when facing as many 3rd-and-longs as the Jaguars faced Sunday. The best way for the Jaguars' offense to thrive is for the running game to do its part , but the Jaguars did not see the running game have much success Sunday. They had a few short-yardage situations early where they got the yards needed, but only two rushes of over 10 yards and countless runs (seemingly) getting stuffed was not the balance the Jaguars needed.
And when the Jaguars' run game is not a threat, that puts more pressure on the passing game and, more specifically, the offensive line. We saw how that worked out for the Jaguars against the Giants, who have the scheme and the athletes on defense to get after an offensive line that is not at their best. The Jaguars like to dictate things on their own terms, but they weren't able to do it much Sunday, and it led to one of the worst offensive days of the Coen era.
The Jaguars' offensive line has had better days, to say the least. The yards before contact numbers have not painted a very pretty picture for the offensive line all season, and it was clearly another issue in the running game on Sunday. But where the Jaguars' offensive line really struggled on Sunday was clearly in terms of their pass-protection, both on the edges and up front. Walker Little was beat for an early sack, Cole Van Lanen had perhaps his worst game as a starter, and both Jonah Monheim and Ezra Cleveland had some clear losses as well.
This felt a lot like the performance against the Denver Broncos in Week 2. The Jaguars' offensive line couldn't handle the pressure looks or wave of pass-rushers, and that is more or less what we saw happen against the Giants. Was it all a result of not having starting center Robert Hainsey? That likely played a role, but the more probable answer is that this is just who the Jaguars' offensive line is. They will be tested in bigger games than this one, and they will have to be better than they were in Week 11.
We spoke about the Jaguars needing to be able to play balanced on offense to give themselves a chance. That starts and stops with Bhayshul Tuten, who left the game twice after coming into the game at clearly not 100%. Tuten has been dealing with his injuries for a few weeks now, barely practicing during the span of the last few weeks. It showed over the last two weeks, with Tuten toughing it out but clearly lacking the juice he had earlier in the season.
Then Sunday happen. Tuten's heavy limp when he game off the field the second time late in the fourth-quarter after a carry said it all. Tuten is nowhere near 100%, and a Jaguars' offense that badly relied on him over the first two months of the season is missing him. The last time we saw Tuten healthy, he had the best game of his career and the offense looked unstoppable. The Jaguars need that Tuten back, even it means resting him for a few weeks.
Trevor Lawrence was certainly not playing with the best support system considering the pressure the Jaguars were seemingly allowing on every single play. But, just like in Week 2 against the Broncos, we did not see Lawrence react to the constant pressure with consistent stretches of quarterback play. That is not to say Lawrence didn't make some superhero-like plays, especially when it came to avoiding sacks, but Lawrence was also far too reckless as a result of the pressure making him press when it came to decision-making.
Neither of Lawrence's two interceptions can really be explained. They were bad plays from a quarterback who has otherwise been abble to avoid many of those types of plays over the last 12 months or so. This was the first multiple-interception game for Lawrence since that Arizona Cardinals interception-fest a year ago, and it certainly has not become the norm for him, but those takeaways were brutal.
To his credit, Lawrence turned things on after his second interception. He did some elite things on the final few drives of the game, but the earlier turnovers felt like they were a direct result of the pressure the Giants put on Lawrence.
Josh Hines-Allen has played his role well in the Jaguars' scheme over the last two seasons. It is not a scheme that is exactly asking its defensive ends to pin their ears back and get after the quarterback on down after down, and that has of course led to some, let's call it anxiety, about the Jaguars' sack numbers from many observers. Hines-Allen made a big impact Sunday though, showing that his role goes far beyond sacks, even if he did record one of those in the first-half.
Hines-Allen's forced fumble on Cam Skattebo in the second-half is the reason the Jaguars were able to hang around during the second-half of the day. It was a great punch-out, and Hines-Allen was probably the best individual performer for the Jaguars' defense on Sunday, which came at exactly the right time for the Jaguars.
I do not think the officials lost the Jaguars the game. The Jaguars did that themselves with too many missed chances, especially with the turnovers from Lawrence leading directly to six points. But that doesn't change the fact that the officials had a downright egregious showing during Sunday's game, with at least three big moments coming to mind.
First, it was Jameis Winston seemingly being short on the first touchdown of the game on a quarterback sneak. It looked like on the replay that Winston was clearly short unless he carries the football with the crown of his helmet. The Jaguars were offsides on the play so they would have had tostop them again, but this felt like a clear miss.
Jameis Winston inverts into the end zone "And no Baha Men callouts this time" - Jim Nantz pic.twitter.com/HYujuOV09c
Then there was a Chris Rodriguez Jr. third-down conversion on a rush in the first-half that the officials ruled a first-down. But then replay assistance overruled the ruling. Then the Jaguars had to challenge the play, which they won, and revert it back the original call. The issue is the Jaguars had to use one of their challenges on the play to get it back to the original call. What a rule!
Then there was the Parker Washington touchdown that wasn't. It sure seemed like Washington got three different feed, and a knee, down in the end zone while catching the ball. Despite this, it was ruled incomplete both on the field and then after the review. That was one of the worst missed calls of any NFL game this season, and the Jaguars had to suffer for it.
"I did not think he lost possession of the football... I think it's a touchdown, fellas." CBS rules analyst Gene Steratore disagreed with this…

title: Jaguars vs. Giants: Inactives Make Jordan Davis' Debut All the More Important
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- The Jacksonville Jaguars were always going to need Jordan Davis to make a big impact in Week 11. Their list of inactives has put even more pressure on his debut.
The Jaguars announced their Week 11 inactives for Sunday's contest with the New York Giants, and it includes a key piece of their defensive tackle rotation in backup defensive tackle Matt Dickerson. With Dickerson set to miss the game with a neck injury, the Jaguars will need Davis and fellow new defensive tackle Davon Godchaux to hold down the fort entirely at nose tackle.
No, Dickerson was not the lynchpin of the Jaguars' defensive tackle rotation, but he has started the last two games for the Jaguars at nose tackle as they prepared for the debut of Davis. The Jaguars had Davis and Jessie Bates III sit last week as they got their bye weeks after not having a bye with the Philadelphia Eagles or Atlanta Falcons, though the Jaguars have been able to see both of them practice for a full week now.
“I think you're always looking at what people do well, is probably the way I would say it. You're never going to wholesale change anything you do when you get new guys, but it's really where do they fit in, what do they do best, what positions can they help us and can you really give them the opportunity to excel?" Jaguars defensive coordinator Anthony Campanile said this week.
"That's what we've kind of spent the last week doing and just getting them acclimated. We have a better feel for that, better feel for them as well. So that's been good.”
Davis is set to play a big role for the Jaguars in his debut game, which was always going to be the case. But now with the defensive tackle room just a bit thinner, the Jaguars will need Davis to step up even more.
There will also be another debut for the Jaguars on Sunday, with fourth-round rookie defensive end Wesley Williams active for the first time this season . Williams will step in at the backup defensive end spot behind Travon Walker, Josh Hines-Allen, and Bryan Thomas Jr. with the Jaguars set to be missing veteran defensive ends Danny Striggow and B.J. Green II.

title: Jaguars-Giants Week 11 National Predictions Roundup: Jacksonville Battling More Than Expectations

JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- The wait is nearly over, and it is just about time to see how the Jacksonville Jaguars answer yet another tough road test.
This time, that test is set to come in the form of the 5-3-1 New York Giants at MetLife Stadium in a game that is set to consist of plenty of rain, and plenty of physical trench play. The Jaguars have answered almost every challenge that has come their way during the Liam Coen era, and this is another chance to meet the high expectations and standards that the Jaguars have created.
"But any given Sunday—the NFL is the NFL. I was with the Rams in ‘22 when you lost to the 0-13 Jets. It is any given Sunday, anything can happen. And I do think our group believes that. They know that," Coen said on Friday.

This is an opportunity as we move forward throughout these next few weeks to go and put it on tape with this team, our final football team of who we are for the rest of the season. title: 3 Reasons the Jaguars' Week 11 Battle With the Giants is a Critical Game
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- This is a big week for the Jacksonville Jaguars, and for more reasons than you may believe.
The Jaguars are set to play the New York Giants in Week 11, another road test against a team with some real strength to it on paper. Every week in the NFL is an important week, but this has certainly had a bit of a big-game feel to it throughout the week of preparation.
When looking deeper at the context of Week 11, though, it is clear that there are more than a few reasons why this is an important game for Liam Coen's squad. We break down a few of those reasons below.
The rest of the AFC has quite the easy schedule in Week 11, at least in terms of the other AFC teams who are set to battle the Jaguars for a spot at the top of the AFC playoff seeding in two months. The Kansas City Chiefs, Cincinnati Bengals, Buffalo Bills, and Denver Broncos are all set to play teams with losing records, while the Jaguars are playing a Giants team that is likely going to represent the NFC East in the playoffs this season. Several of these teams have easy schedules in general for the rest of the year, which means there is not much of a margin for error for the Jaguars entering the second-half of the season.
That is not to say surprises can't happen. They happen each week in the NFL, and any given Sunday isn't just a cliched saying. But chances are the Jaguars will need to beat the Giants to make sure they keep pace with the rest of the top teams in the AFC, putting even more pressure on them to find a way to win on the road this weekend. The Jaguars have won road games in back-to-back weeks, and this is a chance to make it a hat trick at a time where they badly need it.
For the Jaguars to keep things rolling toward another potential AFC South title , they will have to continue to pace well ahead of the Houston Texans. All signs point toward the Jaguars being able to considering the lead they have on the Texans, but a four-game lead with seven weeks left would sound a lot better than a three-game lead. The Texans won a game against the tanking Indianapolis Colts on Thursday Night Football, which puts the onus on the Jaguars moving into the week.
That is not to say the Jaguars wouldn’t be the clear favorites in the AFC South regardless of what happens in New Jersey on Sunday. But the Jaguars can take some of the air out of the Texans’ sails if they pick up a win, which would mean something considering how CJ Stroud has been playing as of late. The AFC South is unlikely to go down to the wire like it has in recent years, but that doesn’t take away the importance of keeping the lead in the division.
The Jaguars already have an impressive résumé over the last half of the season, but there is no denying that they have not exactly been challenged out of the bye week. Jacksonville has played three teams in a row who have losing records and who are in really bad spots in the Indianapolis Colts, the Baltimore Ravens, and the Tennessee Titans. While the Giants do not exactly have an impressive list of wins this season, they should at least pose more of a threat than any other team. The Jaguars have played since they have returned from the bye.
Jacksonville will get more chances down the stretch to prove that they are truly one of the best teams in the NFL, such as a road matchup with the Chicago Bears in a few weeks. But this is a game where the Jaguars can show that it doesn’t matter what kind of team you put in front of them, they are going to be ready to play on Sunday.

title: What the Jaguars' Cap Space Looks Like After Another James Gladstone Restructure
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- The Jacksonville Jaguars' roster looks different after the trade deadline, and now so does their cap situation.
The Jaguars have been able to give themselves a form of 2026 cap relief from contract restructures dating back to training camp, and they have done so again in the wake of the trade deadline now twice. First it was creating another void year for linebacker Foyesade Oluokun, and now the Jaguars have done the same with left tackle Walker Little.
The Jaguars' decision to add a void year to Little's deal to create cap space has reportedly helped clear up $3.66 million in cap space today. According to OverTheCap , the Jaguars' $10,003,345 in cap space ranks No. 13 among teams in 2026. The Jaguars are still set to be $22,111,585 over the 2027 salary cap as of today, ranking their current 2027 cap as No. 27.
The Jaguars made similar moves during training camp, with general manager James Gladstone saying on Sept. 1 that the primary purpose of such moves would be to give the Jaguars flexibility moving forward, and it can likely be assumed that is the same reason for recent decisions after the Jaguars added several new pieces at the trade deadline.
"We want to make sure we have the flexibility we need to keep things on the table as the season progresses. In the same breath, we're always going to do our part to consider all options, and through that lens not all those are going to come to the table or to the public's understanding," Gladstone said in September. "I think the understanding that we are always going to turn over every stone is certainly going to be the case."
The Jaguars have certainly done that under Gladstone, balancing the ability to keep cap space for key extensions, while also not being overly aggressive in free agency outside of a few floor-raising deals in 2025. While doing so, the Jaguars have also been able to add through trades with the additions of Jessie Bates III, Jordan Davis, Jakobi Meyers, Davon Godchaux and several others over the last two seasons.
As things stand today, the Jaguars have enough cap flexibility today for anything that could come up on the horizon in terms of needing money today. There are a few obvious extension candidates, such as eventually Bates and, even sooner than that, Parker Washington. If that is the path the Jaguars want to go down, they certainly seem equipped to do so today while also keeping an eye on 2027.
To get under the cap in 2027, chances are the Jaguars will have to move on from a few veteran contracts, while also having to stay out of the early waves of free agency for the second year in a row. The Jaguars also have several other starters in contract years outside of Bates and Washington who they will have to make decisions on, setting the stage for a potentially active 2027 for Jacksonville.
