title: 4 Instant Observations From Raiders Week 11 Loss to Broncos
full_text:
The Las Vegas Raiders' outing against the Denver Broncos will go down as a loss, but it could be argued that the Raiders won in many ways that may not matter until next season. Las Vegas overcame a slow start on offense to give the Broncos a run for their money.
It is more than clear that the Raiders are still a few players away from beating the league's best teams. However, the last two weeks have also confirmed that when they are clicking on all cylinders, they can at least compete against the league's best for a full four quarters.
That, in itself, is progress from their 3-14 campaign last season. Below are four instant reactions to Las Vegas' Week 11 loss to Denver.
It wasn't pretty, but maybe that is how the Raiders' defense needs to win games. Furthermore, it was pretty good compared to the weeks before Weeks 10 and 11. In Week 11, the Raiders' defense held the Broncos to 50 yards rushing in the first half.
This is after multiple weeks of allowing opposing teams to run for nearly or over 100 yards before halftime. Slowing down Denver's ground game early and making crucial stops through the air with their shaky defensive backfield helped keep the team in the game until Las Vegas' offense woke up.
The unit still has several roster issues that must be addressed this offseason. Still, the unit held Bo Nix to a 66.9 rating in the first half. Las Vegas' defensive backfield did its job on Sunday.
They have had more than a few forgettable moments this season, but given how long the unit has to go each game without the offense sustaining drives or scoring points, it is hard to deny the progress they have made this season, especially over the past two weeks.
Las Vegas entered Week 11 missing interior defensive lineman Tonka Hemingway, arguably the defensive line's best run stopper in the middle. The Raiders lost two more interior defensive linemen before halftime, as Tim Keenan and Adam Butler sustained injuries.
JJ Pegues also left the game early due to an injury.
The Raiders have suffered injuries to Thomas Booker and Foley Fatukasi this season, and they moved on from Jonah Laulu. Denver ran for 50 yards in the first half. They ran for 41 yards in the third quarter. Las Vegas is extremely thin along the interior defensive line.
The Raiders' front office must thoroughly address their interior defensive line this offseason. It will rank behind their cornerbacks and interior offensive line on their to-do list.
It took nearly the entire first half, but it looked like Fernando Mendoza's first two starts against stout defenses are already paying off. Initially, Week 11 looked like a continuation of the second half of Week 10 for Las Vegas' offense. Then, the play-calling and execution finally clicked for the Raiders.
In the second quarter, the Raiders' offense manufactured two scoring drives spanning at least 65 yards. Then, in the third quarter, Las Vegas' defense stopped the Broncos on fourth-and-short, giving the offense a short field to work with. Mendoza and the Raiders capitalized with a touchdown.
The touchdown featured a solid mix of plays that kept the Broncos off balance. For Las Vegas' offense to play as well as it did from the second quarter on, without the best tight end in the league, makes it fair to believe the Raiders really are just a few added players away.
Las Vegas' defense showed what it can do when its offense can sustain drives and score points. Mendoza showed what he could do without his best pass-catcher. With more time, practice, and game repetitions, it is fair to believe he will be the franchise quarterback they expect him to be.
Mendoza missed multiple passes that a more experienced Mendoza likely would have completed. It takes more than one game for quarterbacks and receivers to get their timing down. Sunday was another loss, but it was also more valuable game experience for the rookie quarterback.
Sunday's near-comeback win makes it fair to wonder what this season could have been like with Mendoza getting more experience earlier. Sunday's loss also makes it fair to wonder how good Mendoza and the offense will be under Klint Kubiak with an improved roster next season.
Ezekiel is a former Sports Editor from the Western Herald and former Atlanta Falcons beat writer.

title: Raiders Stock Report: Risers & Fallers After Narrow Loss to Broncos
full_text:
The Las Vegas Raiders entered Week 11 looking to establish consistency on either side of the ball. They did so in good ways and not-so-good ways against the Denver Broncos on Sunday. The Raiders are a work in progress; the Broncos are on the other side of a rebuild that started years ago.
Sunday's loss proved how slim the margin for error is on game days. It was also a reminder of how far the Raiders have come since last season and how much further they have to go.
In Week 11, Las Vegas quickly fell behind and was forced to play catch-up the rest of the way. The difference was seeing just how close they were to swinging momentum in their favor. The Raiders were legitimately a couple of plays away from potentially getting going earlier.
Then, as has happened so often this season, a play here, a play there, and the Raiders were down by double digits. The gap between the Raiders and the rest of the AFC West has closed somewhat but remains sizeable. Below are the risers and fallers from another yet loss for the rebuilding Raiders.
Week 11 was another week of cold spells for the Raiders' offense. Las Vegas struggled to sustain drives without Brock Bowers, leaving the Raiders' defense vulnerable to a potent Broncos offense. Las Vegas' defense held the fort as best it could in the first quarter.
Still, the Raiders' defense played a solid first quarter. Three of the Broncos' first 10 points were due to Las Vegas' special teams. A questionable pass interference call against Eric Stokes set up another seven. Leonard's unit was the best unit on the field for most of the game.
Las Vegas' defense handed their teammates on offense an opportunity to grab momentum early. The unit was rewarded with three plays off and a short field to defend. The rest was history, as Las Vegas' offense struggled to pass midfield for much of the first half.
The Raiders' defense has areas it can improve, but the first half of Week 11 was the perfect example of Las Vegas' defense being left out to dry by a largely ineffective offense until it was too late. The unit also had an impressive defensive stand against the Broncos' offense right before halftime.
That is the Jeanty we have all been waiting on, and it was just the tip of the iceberg. Jeanty had success through the air and on the ground in Week 11, notching a 46-yard run and a 68-yard touchdown catch.
McCoy had a solid play in the first quarter that saved four points. It was a play where Bo Nix and the Broncos teed the rookie up in one-on-one coverage, targeting him with veteran wide receiver Jaylen Waddle. McCoy showed the improvement Las Vegas' coaching staff recently mentioned he made.
On that play, his speed seemed to be coming back to him. There were times this season when that wasn't the case. Las Vegas needs to get McCoy on the field more, as it is clear how valuable game experience has been to his recovery.
Las Vegas' offense without Brock Bowers solidifies all the areas where they still need to improve the roster. The Raiders must overhaul their offensive line this offseason. Nothing short of an overhaul will do. Addressing their starting-caliber offensive linemen has to be the front office's top priority.
Then, they need at least one or two more dependable pass-catchers. They must do so even if they retain veteran receiver Tre Tucker. In Week 11, their lack of a pass-catcher is debilitating. Three of Las Vegas' first four drives resulted in punts.
Those three drives lasted 10 plays and gained 11 yards. They had nearly as many yards in penalties. This put them in a hole they could not work their way out of.
They came alive later in the game, but it was too late. The unit has to get out of its own way sooner. Week 11 makes it fair to believe they can do so.
The Broncos blocked a Raiders punt deep in their own territory that set up a field goal a few plays later. The three-play drive that lasted just over a minute and a half came after Las Vegas' defense forced a punt on Denver's opening drive, playing well in many areas they had struggled in.
The Raiders' defense was once again put in a bad situation after doing their job. Denver's 3-0 early lead had little to do with Las Vegas' defense. The blocked punt essentially handed the Broncos points despite the solid defense the Raiders played on the opening drive.
The unit also allowed for another punt by AJ Cole to be tipped shortly before halftime.
Ezekiel is a former Sports Editor from the Western Herald and former Atlanta Falcons beat writer.

title: Raiders Aim To Stack Solid Defensive Performances on the Road
full_text:
The Las Vegas Raiders Week 11 matchup against the Denver Broncos will be another uphill battle for a Raiders team with several roster holes on it. Those holes and roster shortcomings have been on display for most of the past two weeks, as the Raiders have lost six of their last seven games.
Las Vegas' defense is slated to face a potent Broncos offense on the road this Sunday. They say styles make fights. In this instance, that does not bode well for the Raiders.
After spending many years rising through the league's coaching ranks, Rob Leonard's first 10 games as a defensive coordinator have been unlike anything he had experienced entering this season. Leonard recently gave insight into what the regular season has taught him so far.
“Leadership is lonely. I’ve learned a lot. I’m drawing kind of a blank on where to start. But still, the same principles I believed in when I got it, of everybody on the same page as a staff, everybody on the same page for the players, and the more confidence that they’ll play with from all the details," Leonard said earlier this week.
"As the season goes on, the details of what you need to get better on with your core things, you have to beat the opponent to the punch on all those things.”
The season's first 10 games have been filled with lessons for Leonard and Las Vegas' entire defense, with most coming from the back end of the unit. It has been a long six weeks for the Raiders, but there have been bright spots during that span.
Progress for the Raiders' defense is relative to what they have displayed throughout this season. Their performances against teams with a winning record are littered with opposing offenses' explosive plays through the ground and through the air, sometimes at will.
Las Vegas' Week 10 loss to the Seattle Seahawks still featured explosives from arguably the best receiver in the league, but overall, the Raiders' defense played better than in weeks prior. Rob Leonard's unit forced a turnover on Seattle's first drive of the game, setting the tone for the first half.
In the first half of Week 10, Las Vegas' defense held Seattle to one touchdown, a fumble, and two punts. This helped the Raiders take a lead into halftime for the first time since Week 4.
"I just think of the objectives we tried to accomplish. Did we start fast? That was one of them. We did, and then to be honest with you, some of the others we did not. So, like I said, you’re striving for improvement, but we lost the game," Leonard said.
Regardless of Sunday's results in Denver, it is still possible for the Raiders to show improvement from last week and from the first half of the season. At this point in their rebuild, progress is nearly as critical, and potentially even more important, than wins.
"I want these guys, even after the losses, to build off the positives we did do. You’re just being honest with what we did well, and it was nice to have some positive feedback on certain areas," Leonard said.
The Raiders enter their Week 11 matchup against the Broncos looking for another step forward, no matter how it may look. The defensive backfield gambles Las Vegas took this offseason were discussed often heading into Week 1.
Those gambles happened at positions where mistakes are more glaring than others. Starting multiple first- and second-year players in their defensive backfield has been high-risk, high-reward for Las Vegas all season. It will be again this Sunday, when the Raiders face the Broncos.
Las Vegas desperately needs its defense to continue forcing turnovers at the rate it has this season. They also need the unit to improve performance-wise, especially early in games.
Week 11 against the Broncos will be a tough task for Leonard and his unit. The good news is that they have more to gain than to lose. The second half of this season is all about progress for the Raiders, especially on defense.
Ezekiel is a former Sports Editor from the Western Herald and former Atlanta Falcons beat writer.

title: Raiders Looking Inward for Hopeful Improved Results Going Forward
full_text:
The Las Vegas Raiders hope Week 11 will be kinder to them than the past two months have been. Although improved compared to last season, the Raiders are in the middle of their second losing streak of at least two games, with a third consecutive loss possible against the Denver Broncos.
On Monday, Raiders head coach Klint Kubiak shared his thoughts on a well-coached Broncos team.
"Coach [Sean] Payton has been winning for a long time. He’s one of the best in the business. His teams are ready to play, and they play their best at the end of the game,” Kubiak said earlier this week.
Kubiak elaborated, noting that it will take the Raiders' best efforts in the week leading up to Week 11 and the game itself on Sunday in Denver. Week 11 will mark the third time the Raiders will face a team on the road the week after that team's Bye Week.
This naturally gives those teams a competitive advantage, which will require even more preparation and effort on Las Vegas' part.
“That’s what’s expected every day. So, just continue to emphasize it. But this is the NFL. You finish every play, or else you’re going to get beat,” Kubiak said following the team’s final practice before Sunday’s matchup against the Broncos.
Several offensive linemen around the league have had their tendencies dissected and exposed in recent weeks. There have been multiple instances of players around the league unknowingly giving away clues to opponents about what is coming.
None of those players were Raiders, but they are not immune to it. Raiders offensive coordinator Andrew Janocko noted earlier this week that, like most other teams in the league, Las Vegas' coaching staff analyzes their own tendencies as much as their opponents'.
“We try to self-scout everything. And I think every team in the league does that. Every team’s trying to gain just that little bit of edge. So, everything that we’re doing, we’re trying to just make a little bit better, whether it’s self-scouting, whether it’s getting our plan ready to go. We try to dot every i, cross every t, and so does every other team,” Janocko said earlier this week.
Sunday, Las Vegas will face a Broncos team that has had its number in recent seasons. Denver has swept the series in each of the past two seasons. The two teams play each other twice in the next four weeks. Despite losing, Las Vegas played well at times in its previous two trips to Denver.
This time, the Raiders hope Kubiak and the other changes they made leading up to Week 11 are enough to keep things competitive as long as possible. Simply keeping the game close into the fourth quarter would be a win for the  Raiders. Scoring points in the third quarter would, too.
Las Vegas' schedule lightens up between and after those two games. They are only two weeks away from a much-needed Bye Week, which, paired with an upset win on Sunday, could be just the spark the Raiders need over the final few weeks of the season.
As the Raiders look to keep improving under Kubiak throughout the second half of the season, any advantage could help compensate for Las Vegas' lack of talent compared to their competition. Defensively, the Raiders need all the help they can get.
Raiders defensive coordinator Rob Leonard expressed his thoughts on how critical every detail is in preparing each week. Leonard noted that figuring out specific opponents' tendencies is usually up to individual players; it is a skill veterans often possess, which he appreciates.
“I think it’s all based on the player. First-year player, you’re just trying to get lined up, and what’s the call? But I am always impressed with veteran players, what they can process within a snap, from stances to what they’re communicating at the line of scrimmage. But I think that’s a player by-player basis of how much detail they can take in and process when the bullets are actually flying,” Leonard said after Thursday’s practice.
“We’re not playing well enough. We’re not playing up to the standard we need to be. So, effort covers up a lot. So, there’s definitely room for improvement there. And to say it’s division from the start, no, we’re not playing at a high enough or good enough level right now. So, there’s definitely room for improvement.”
Ezekiel is a former Sports Editor from the Western Herald and former Atlanta Falcons beat writer.

title: Raiders vs. Broncos: Players To Watch for AFC West Matchup
full_text:
Sunday is an opportunity for the 4-6 Las Vegas Raiders to create some chaos in the AFC West as they travel to Denver, Colorado, to face the 7-2 Denver Broncos.
All week, we have been digesting rookie quarterback Fernando Mendoza's debut and what the Broncos could bring to the table on Sunday. As the Raiders' defense may have found its groove against the Seattle Seahawks, their offense, play-called by head coach Klint Kubiak, must improve this week.
If the Raiders are to upset their division rival, here are some players who could help them achieve a culture-defining victory.
The Raiders may finally find some success in the run game this weekend against a Broncos defense that is allowing the ninth-most rushing yards per game. I think we finally see Ashton Jeanty break through for an ultra-productive game, reaching the century mark for the first time since Week 1 against the Miami Dolphins.
Jeanty has been terrific as a pass-catcher out of the backfield, but he truly unlocks his value when the run game gets going. He can be a special player in this league, and Sunday could be a chance to unlock some newfound confidence.
Earlier in the week, I wrote about how the Raiders could respond to a potential Brock Bowers absence and forgot to mention a key name: wide receiver Jack Bech, a true inside-out pass-catcher who has the size to handle blocking assignments on the perimeter and act as a big slot of sorts for Kubiak's offense.
Bech's ball skills and physicality make him an intriguing option, as we could see the Raiders deploy more 11 personnel if Bowers can't go, and even if he does play, Bech should still be a key player to watch.
The Broncos' offensive line is a sound unit with two great offensive tackles, but outside of Maxx Crosby, someone on the edge must make a play. I think that could be Malcolm Koonce, who is second on the team in pressures, according to Next Gen Stats .
A Koonce performance that could call for shades of 2023 would give the Raiders a great boost to their defense against a Broncos offense that has had its struggles but clear moments of strength, especially in the fourth quarter.
When Bo Nix last played football two weeks ago against the Carolina Panthers, he tested their defensive backs downfield consistently because they were ravaged by injuries on the back end. While the Raiders aren't hurt in the secondary, their rookies make them vulnerable targets for Nix to test them early and often.
This opens the door for Stukes, who has begun to settle in and play great football at free safety over the last few weeks. Stukes' range, football intelligence, and ball skills make him a legitimate threat to downfield shots for Nix.
Jared Feinberg, a native of western North Carolina, has written about NFL football for nearly a decade. He has contributed to several national outlets and is now part of our On SI team as an NFL team reporter. Jared graduated from UNC Asheville with a bachelor's degree in mass communications and later pursued his master's degree at UNC Charlotte. You can follow Jared Feinberg on Twitter at @JRodNFLDraft

title: Why Beating Broncos Would Be Huge Needle-Mover for Raiders
full_text:
The Las Vegas Raiders are preparing for a pivotal division matchup with the Denver Broncos this afternoon.
This game has become extra important for Klint Kubiak's team, as they are sitting at 4-6 but not out of contention for the No. 7 seed in the AFC Wild Card race. They haven't played well as of late, but other teams fighting for the same spot haven't distanced themselves.
All the Raiders have to do is go to Denver and take down the division-leading Broncos in a crucial November game. Easy enough, right?
What would a win mean for the Silver and Black, if they can win against a division rival?
Fernando Mendoza makes his second career start against a defense that hasn't had the statistical success, but is still one of the better units in the league. This won't be easy for the rookie, especially if his offensive line and weapons don't help him.
On the other side of the ball, the Broncos' offense has found a rhythm in the last three games, averaging 28 points per contest. The Raiders have been struggling on defense, allowing 30 or more points in six of their last seven games.
The Raiders are on the outside looking in for the seventh seed in the AFC playoff picture, which is currently held by the Cleveland Browns. They sit behind the New England Patriots and Houston Texans, and with a win, they increase their playoff chances to 18 percent, according to NFL.com.
While those chances are still quite low, fans should be excited that the Raiders will still be on "In the Hunt" graphics in November. They probably like that the team hasn't been eliminated from playoff contention before Thanksgiving.
The Raiders have work to do if they want to beat the Broncos and keep their playoff hopes alive.
They have to run the ball better. Their defense has to get more stops. Neither has happened in the last two months.
If the Raiders can't sustain drives on the ground or stop other teams from putting the ball in the end zone, nothing is going to improve in 2026. This year was always forward-thinking, but they're not out of it yet, so they should still focus on improving in these areas right now.
Las Vegas has the opportunity to pull off a big upset this afternoon, which would change the course of its season. The Raiders would be playing with a world of confidence if they can get this win.
Carter Landis studied journalism at Michigan State University where I graduated in May of 2022. He currently is a sports reporter for a local television station, and is a writer covering the Las Vegas Raiders

title: Four Losers And Four Winners From Miami's Week 11 Loss
full_text:
Chilly weather, broken tables, and the Miami Dolphins falling to the Buffalo Bills in Orchard Park. It's been a common theme since 2016, the last time the Dolphins won a game in Western New York. They didn't come close to breaking that streak Sunday.
While the Dolphins have lost as many games as they have, a good chunk of them had been by a touchdown or less. That wasn't the case against Buffalo, as after the Bills went up 13-0 with 13:23 to go in the second quarter, the deficit never went back down to less than eight points.
Against a team looking to compete for a spot in Super Bowl LXI, the youth and inexperience of the Dolphins reared their ugly head in a way that hasn't been seen since maybe the San Francisco loss. That said, you can find positives if you look hard enough, and there was especially some good from the defense.
As you'll probably come to find out, the entire offense looked shaky in this game. McCord got no help from his offensive line, and a lot of his wide receivers forgot to wear their extra-sticky gloves. He's playing the Bills in Buffalo, for crying out loud.
He looked like someone who hadn't played many games of professional football, with a generous number of passes that either sailed over receivers or were underthrown. He rarely went for the long ball, and when he was under pressure, he equally struggled with check-downs or anything that required him to scan the field. He only threw one interception, which in itself feels like a win.
At no point in this game did it look like he could take over by himself, which is justified because that was always going to be impossible given the circumstances.
Back-to-back weeks for Chop being one of the biggest winners on these lists. Numbers-wise, his performance doesn't stand out with three tackles, a pass deflection, and a QB hit. If it were any other quarterback, he probably would have also recorded at least two sacks, but Josh Allen did what he does best and escaped an impossible situation.
The one time he couldn't make magic happen, though, was on that Robinson pass deflection, leading to an errant throw that sailed right to Jacob Rodriguez for an interception. He's not a one-dimensional player, as he was also solid in managing the run game, helping the defense limit the Bills to 95 rushing yards, an astronomically low number for a team with Allen and James Cook III.
The rookie sensation had a hard time establishing himself. He was targeted 10 times, and while a fair number of the throws were off the mark, he was only able to haul in two receptions for 30 yards. More than anything, though, this will be the game that showcased perhaps his biggest issue — the drops.
There were four in this game for Douglas, with none bigger than the one on third-and-goal early in the third quarter. It forced their third field goal of the day, and it was the closest they ever got to a touchdown the rest of the game.
Filling in for Dante Trader Jr., Anderson made the most of an extended workload and recorded 12 tackles, a sack, three pass deflections, and an interception. It's easily his best performance of the season, considering how red-hot Buffalo's offense was entering this game. The sack was critical, as it forced a 54-yard field goal attempt from Tyler Bass that sailed wide left in the third quarter.
The interception, meanwhile, was the first of back-to-back picks thrown by Allen and McCord toward the end of the first half. It wasn't all perfect for Anderson, as DJ Moore's touchdown was assisted by both Anderson and Michael Taaffe blowing the coverage, and forcing us all to watch Moore pretend to be a seal for two full seconds.
Just when you thought maybe Jackson was improving after a clean stat sheet with no pressures, sacks or penalties against Indianapolis, things got ugly against Greg Rousseau and Buffalo. He was responsible for two sacks by Rousseau, and every time he didn't pressure McCord, it felt like a small victory.
Jonah Savaiinaea also had a rough game, but it seems clear that one of the positions where Miami needs a fresh face at is right tackle. Jackson's best attribute this season isn't blocking, but rather how he's stayed healthy, and that's not good enough. It doesn't matter who the quarterback is; the right side of the line of scrimmage is always a battleground that they'd better avoid being near.
It sure is great not to have a small panic attack every time a kicker is brought on the field. Carlson set the tone in the second quarter with back-to-back 52-yard field goals, then added a 27-yarder in the third quarter for good measure.
Yes, it's only one game for Carlson, but it's refreshing to see someone provide consistency to Miami's special teams, as it's been anything but that this season. No one will find long-term reasons to remember this game from a Dolphins perspective, but at least it looks like Miami has one less problem to worry about on their roster for the time being.
Here we go again. Wright can't catch a break; the jokes about him being a magnet for defenders in the backfield have unfortunately aged well. He recorded 10 yards on five carries, and this is somehow an improvement from his games against the New York Jets, New England and Indianapolis.
Wright actually was decent on kick returns with 79 yards on three returns. Once he gets a full head of steam, he tends to be hard to bring down, but he never gets that opportunity on offense. That's why it's puzzling that he's been given this many carries up to this point as opposed to anyone else.
In fairness, it would have been hard to beat what Washington was able to cook up against the Colts as a receiver, runner, and ... thrower. But even in a bad game for Miami's pass offense, he was serviceable enough for 30 yards on three receptions, with four fewer targets than Douglas.
Surprisingly, it's his ability to run the ball that might be something Bobby Slowik and the offense should look into moving forward. Any way to get him the ball more is welcome, especially when the rookies struggle in games like this against a tough defense, and teams like Denver and Chicago are still to come.
Jake Gibson is a writer for the Miami Dolphins on SI. He began his sports journalism career with PantherNOW, the student newspaper at his alma mater, Florida International University, where he began as a sportswriter before being promoted to Sports Director. Jake also works for the Five Reasons Sports Network and is the host of the Shula Bowl Podcast. A native of Homestead, Florida, Jake grew up a South Florida sports fan and has currently attended five Super Bowls in person.

title: Five Instant Overreactions to the Dolphins-Bills Matchup
full_text:
Miami's defense put up a valiant effort, but it wasn't enough, as the Dolphins ultimately fell to the Bills by a score of 26-9.
Let's overreact to some key developments, both positive and negative, from this Week 11 matchup.
The Miami Dolphins offense was abysmal, and many of the struggles came from underwhelming individual performances.
Caleb Douglas, who had previously dropped a pass in each of the last two games, dropped another three throws Sunday, and only caught two of his 11 targets. Fellow rookie Chris Bell also had a deep pass bounce off his fingertips.
Miami’s weapons couldn’t create separation on key downs, and the offensive line, particularly along the right side, struggled once again. Jonah Savaiinaea and Austin Jackson are difficult to ignore and easy for opposing defenses to key in on. Their consistent one-on-one losses and need for help not only hamstring the Dolphins from a game plan perspective, but also take away potential support for Patrick Paul and Kadyn Proctor, who gave up timely pressure.
The struggles from the Dolphins’ youth, while inevitable, are extremely difficult to overcome with this little to rely on in terms of veteran presence. Miami's offense badly needs an influx of talent in the 2027 offseason.
Chop Robinson's resurgence after an underwhelming second season is a very positive development for this Dolphins team, and he once again looked strong against Buffalo.
Robinson’s conversion rate of speed to power has vastly improved this season with his added weight, and when he attacks from the wide-nine alignment, he can eliminate the space between him and the tackle in a hurry. He did so multiple times in this game, pressuring Josh Allen and moving him off his spot.
There were also several instances of Robinson moving bodies in the run game, caving in offensive linemen and tight ends to make it easier for his teammates to make plays.  Robinson's play has become more consistent, and if he continues to develop, he could be a foundational piece of Miami's defense moving forward.
Outside of a long, game-clinching drive following a Miami turnover on downs, the Dolphins’ defense did more than enough to keep them in the game. More importantly, they did it with a drastic talent discrepancy.
Even with the late success, James Cook only averaged 4 yards per carry, and Josh Allen finished 27/45 with two interceptions.
The film will tell the full story, but for Josh Allen, a quarterback who has historically torched the Dolphins with his legs, to not record a carry is impressive work from Miami's defensive players and staff. Their pressure and back-end coverage appeared to frustrate him, and forced him into bad throws on multiple occasions. Once again, against a stellar offense, Hafley's group puts up a performance to be proud of.
The well-chronicled Miami Dolphins special teams struggles have been nothing short of embarrassing, and this game was yet another prominent example of that. Buffalo not only converted a fourth down with a fake punt but also lined up for an onside kick up two scores, only to take a delay-of-game before kicking off regularly.
Daniel Carlson looked solid, making three field goals, including two from 50+ yards. However, the kick return team was undisciplined, with Kaytron Allen committing a 15-yard unnecessary roughness penalty.
Chris Tabor's unit has been the worst on a team that is bereft of talent. While on offense and defense, there have been instances of the sum playing better than their individual parts; that hasn't happened in the kicking game.
Malik Washington's ability as a runner and receiver have been on display this year. A week after throwing a touchdown and making an impressive catch, Washington had a nice carry where he lined up as a running back, and in another instance, made a crucial one-handed snag on fourth down.
Washington should be Miami's solution for easy offense. For someone who consistently makes the first defender miss, the Dolphins haven't done nearly a good enough job getting him designed touches. He's easily their most explosive and consistent weapon right now (given Caleb Douglas' struggles catching the football) and should see his opportunities match his ability.
Tyler DeSena is currently a journalism student at the University of Central Florida. Prior to joining Dolphins On SI in 2026, DeSena worked with dolphinstalk.com, and created independent social media content on X, YouTube and TikTok.

title: Dolphins Sunday Mailbag: Douglas, Uche, Brewer, and More
full_text:
Part 2 of the pre-Bills game Miami Dolphins On SI mailbag:
Does Bell or Kevin Coleman get in the end zone against Buffalo? Put on your sports betting hat! (Assuming Bell plays)
Bell indeed will play, but I don’t bet and don’t make recommendations. Purely for enjoyment purposes, I certainly wouldn’t count on either player scoring a touchdown if I’m being honest.
Some talk of re-signing Uche has surfaced in recent weeks. What would a fair contract for both parties look like and if the Dolphins do re-sign him, should they envision him in his current role or should their sights be on adding someone else and having him serve more as a rotational/backup piece?
Hey Dana, Uche is making about $1.3 million this season, which is a very low salary for a starter and I don’t know if you could bring him back for less than something like $4 million. In an ideal world, Uche would be part of a rotation on the edge with Chop Robinson and maybe one or two other players.
Another recent position group that got hit really hard was offensive tackle in 2022. Austin Jackson was supposed to be the starter at RT, but he missed a bunch of the season, came back, and got hurt again. Armstead only played 65% of the snaps. Shell and Little played a lot, and Kendall Lamm came in late in the season and was almost immediately injured and missed the rest of the year. Another fun part of this is the salary cap. The Dolphins are well known at this point for paying a lot to players who are no longer on the team. But now they also are top heavy in injuries. The five highest cap hits (per OTC) this year that are actually with the Dolphins are Sieler, Jackson, Brooks, Willis and Brewer. So three of their top five cap hits that are on the team are not playing right now. So their top 8 cap hits are either dead money or on IR (Sieler is the 6th highest). We know all the big ones, but how scary is it that only six players on the active roster have a higher cap hit than Zach Wilson?
Editor’s note: This message came before it appears as though Brewer would play against the Bills, but the point remains. And, yes, the Zach Wilson cap money from 2026 is just not good.
If you end up with the No. 1 pick, do you take the wide receiver Smith or do you look for a decent haul in a trade? And then you can pick an edge in the top 10.
Hey Frank, I’ve said time and time again on the All Dolphins Podcast and the Dolphins Collective and have written that I never would take a wide receiver with the first overall pick unless the gap between that player and everybody else in the draft was insane — and, I’m sorry, that’s not the case with Jeremiah Smith, as good as he is. I’m a big proponent of positional value and I think a quarterback, pass rusher or cornerback can have a bigger and more immediate impact than a wide receiver. So if the Dolphins get the No. 1 pick, the move should be taking Drew Mestemaker if they have a conviction he can be an elite QB or try to trade down to pick up additional assets.
Hey Poup! I know it's only 9 games, but what trade is looking better 9 games in? Caleb Downs for Proctor, Coleman and Traore? Or Waddle (including subsequent 49ers trade) for Johnson, Chris Bell, Trey Moore and Kyle Louis?
Hey Luis, this is a very interesting question and there are two factors not mentioned here, first the fact that Downs was a prospect with no NFL experience and then there’s the cap hit taken with the Waddle trade in 2026 but the money/cap saved in future years. All that said, I like the Waddle package better, but those look like great trades right now.
Hi Alain, it seems there are several groin injuries plaguing the Dolphins. Do you think this could have anything to do with their extended stretching protocols?
Hey Luke, I’m not a medical expert, but I think more stretching actually would help prevent groin injuries, not create them. I also think the data would support that notion. Sometimes there’s just bad luck involved that we have to accept.
Alain, will we see a fade route in the end zone to Douglas in the future when we get into the red zone with his high-point catch ability? I know opportunities have been limited but seems like he would do well with that as well in other situations before the red zone.
Hey Jeff, I like your thinking and the only question I would have is whether Douglas’ high-pointing ability would translate into the end zone where it’s more quick jumping as opposed to have a lot of time to judge a pass downfield, which is what we’ve seen so far. But I would like to see them try (as long as they don’t overdo it). It’s certainly preferable to calling it on a regular basis with Tyreek Hill.
I have not seen an update on Trey Moore since September, he was listed as a starter had a good camp and then the Dolphins had us think he was just nicked up. Any word on his return and what his injury is?
Hey Marc, no, this has been well documented, Moore sustained a not-insignificant ankle injury in the preseason opener against Washington. Head coach Jeff Hafley said in the aftermath of the injury he was “hopeful” that Moore could be back at some point in the 2026 season. I’ve thought along that it’s 50-50 at best we’ll see Moore at all this season.
Alain Poupart is the publisher/editor of Miami Dolphins On SI, host of the All Dolphins Podcast, and co-host of the Dolphins Collective. Alain has covered the Miami Dolphins on a full-time basis since 1989 for various publications and media outlets, including Dolphin Digest, The Associated Press and the Dolphins team website. In addition to being a credentialed member of the Miami Dolphins press corps, Alain has covered three Super Bowls (for NFL.com, Football News and the Montreal Gazette), the annual NFL draft, the Senior Bowl, and the NFL Scouting Combine. During his almost 40 years in journalism, which began at the now-defunct Miami News, Alain has covered practically every sport at one time or another, from tennis to golf, baseball, basketball and everything in between. The career also included time as a copy editor, including work on several books, such as "Still Perfect," an inside look at the Miami Dolphins' 1972 perfect season. A native of Montreal, Canada, whose first language is French, Alain grew up a huge hockey fan but soon developed a love for all sports, including NFL football. He has lived in South Florida since the 1980s.

title: To Win or Not To Win? That Seems To Be a Question for Miami Dolphins Fans?
full_text:
The Miami Dolphins will look to pull off a gigantic upset and win a game at Buffalo on Sunday for the first time since 2016, and sadly a question that some — maybe even many — fans will be asking is: Would that even be a good thing?
This is the reality of a team still in the early stages of a rebuilding project that's gotten off to a promising start but still has some steps to go. One of those is continuing to acquire high-end talent, and what better way than to be picking at the very top of the draft?
And this is where wins can become losses.
The Dolphins, who will be eliminated from the race for the AFC East title if they lose at Buffalo on Sunday, currently hold the third overall position in the 2027 draft order — though they're tied with the Tennessee Titans and Los Angeles Chargers for the worst record in the league at 1-8.
After the injuries that had defensive tackles Zach Sieler, Jordan Phillilps and Zeek Biggers and quarterback Malik Willis join De'Von Achane on injured reserve — with only Willis having a chance to return this season — the idea that the Dolphins might finish with something like a 2-15 or even 1-16 record isn't necessarily farfetched.
In an ideal world, the Dolphins would experience some success in the second half of the season with some wins mixed in here and there and still land the top pick in the 2027 draft.
Except it doesn't work that way.
Each win could cost the Dolphins the shot at the No. 1 overall pick and the chance to take quarterback Drew Mestemaker or wide receiver Jeremiah Smith or try to parlay that pick into additional draft capital with a team looking to make the move up for the top selection.
So, again, the question becomes whether a gigantic Dolphins upset win over the Bills on Sunday would be preferable to another loss if it gets them closer to that No. 1 overall pick.
The Dolphins, of course, were in this situation seven years ago in Brian Flores' first year as head coach after they started 0-7 and were outscored by an average of 40-6 over the first four games.
The Dolphins, though, never once held the top spot in the 2020 draft at any point during that 2019 season because Cincinnati started the season 0-11 before finally getting a win. The popular story goes that the Dolphins lost their shot at the No. 1 overall pick when they defeated the Bengals in overtime in Week 15 that year, but that's fiction and even had they lost that game and wound up tied with 13-3 records, Washington then would have had the top pick, not Miami.
So the notion that the Dolphins lost Joe Burrow because they defeated the Bengals in late December 2019 is simply not true. That chance was lost basically when the Dolphins defeated the playoff-bound Philadelphia Eagles earlier in the month in a game that featured the famous "Mountaineer Shot."
As it was, the Dolphins ended with the fifth pick as fans know too well and selected QB Tua Tagovailoa with their first of three first-round picks that year.
The Dolphins then went 10-6  in 2020 to start a string of four consecutive winning seasons. So did it work out better for the Dolphins that they enjoyed some success toward the end of Flores' first year with the wins against the Eagles and at New England in the season finale or would it have been better had they gone, say, 1-15 and ensured getting Joe Burrow?
Given the season Burrow is having, it's easy to look back and, say, sure the Dolphins would have been better off losing all those games in 2019, but didn't the Dolphins establish a mentality, a mind-set during the second half of that 2020 season instead of tanking?
The argument for tanking in 2019 also seemed stronger than it does this year because Burrow was such a great prospect coming out of LSU, though that didn't become apparent until maybe midway through that season.
We've already seen comparisons made of Mestemaker to the QB the Dolphins will face Sunday, Josh Allen, and if the Dolphins scouts see it, then it becomes a lot easier to cheer for losses because he would become an absolute no-brainer at the top of the 2027 draft.
But there are no guarantees.
The other question is whether Dolphins fans would feel better about head coach Jeff Hafley and the whole organization if the team ended up winning, say, two or three more games this season as opposed to finishing 1-16, which would become the worst record in franchise history.
It's a tough balance to strike because fans should want the team to do well every time out, but looking out for the long-term benefits of the franchise also makes sense.
The Dolphins have had either the first or second pick in the draft twice in their history, but they didn't take a quarterback either time.
In 2005, the Dolphins selected Auburn running back Ronnie Brown at number 2 in Nick Saban's first year as head coach and went with veteran journeyman Gus Frerotte as their starting QB. Looking back, it's pretty obvious they messed and should have taken Aaron Rodgers, though he wasn't selected until pick 24.
In 2008, the Dolphins had the top pick and bypassed the chance to take Matt Ryan by selecting tackle Jake Long, a decision that's easy to criticize after the fact because Ryan had a long and successful (though maybe not great) career with Atlanta that included one Super Bowl trip and Long   basically had six good years before injuries derailed his career.
The Dolphins did need a quarterback that year, but they waited until the second round to select Chad Henne, who had a long career in the NFL but almost exclusively as a backup.
So in hindsight, sure, the Dolphins probably should have taken Ryan.
But it says here that Long was on a Hall of Fame track before his injuries and we also need to point out that Ryan wasn't a slam dunk because it wasn't just the Dolphins who passed on him but also the St. Louis Rams picking second overall and taking defensive end Chris Long despite also having a need at quarterback.
For historical reference, three quarterbacks taken first overall went on to win the Super Bowl with the team that drafted them — Peyton Manning, Troy Aikman and Terry Bradshaw. John Elway, Eli Manning and Matthew Stafford also won the Super Bowl as first overall picks, but each with their second team.
This all brings us back to the original question of whether it's better for the Dolphins to get some wins down the stretch this season or whether the more losses, the better.
The reality is there might not be a correct answer because either choice isn't ideal.
But it's where the Dolphins find themselves in 2026.
And the hope is they're not in that position again anytime soon. However that gets accomplished.

title: Dolphins Saturday Mailbag: How to Make the Run Defense Work
full_text:
Part 1 of a pre-Bills game Miami Dolphins On SI mailbag:
Would another team signing Daniel Jones have to pick up his contract? Would JES do that?
Only if Jones is claimed off waivers, which all players now are subject to after being released because the trade deadline has passed. If no team claims Jones in the first 24 hours, then he becomes a free agent, Indy is totally responsible for what’s left on his contract and he negotiates an entirely new contract with a new team. And I would be shocked if Jon-Eric Sullivan even gave the idea of adding Jones any consideration considering he's been in the league for a long time and it's pretty clear by now his ceiling is solid backup.
From Jorge Francisco boyd:
Hi Alain, how do you think the Dolphins are going to be able to stop the run without Sieler, Biggers and Jordan; how is the new QB going to have a chance with that OL play we have been seen lately?
Hey Jorge, how to stop the run without those three players is going to be a huge challenge and this is where head coach Jeff Hafley is going to have to come up with something creative because you can’t ask the D-tackle replacements to be able to do what Sieler, Biggers and Phillips. Whether that means moving the safeties closer to the line of scrimmage or maybe using more big bodies up front, I’m not sure, but something will have to be done. Protecting the QB has been a problem all season, and I think the best way to protect Kyle McCord is calling more short passes.
While he had a fairly good game (against the Colts), what's going on with Patrick Paul this season? He seems universally ranked in bottom third of OTs. This was not the ceiling we expected.
I’m not sure what rankings you’re using, though Pro Football Focus does have Paul 50th among 72 graded tackles, which indeed is bottom third. I’m also not sure whose expectations you’re referencing, though it was fair to hope he could take another step in 2026 after his obvious jump from his rookie to his second season. As it stands right now, Paul looks like a solid left tackle, but there’s probably another level he can reach.
Hey Poup, beyond current players improving by next season, which 5-6 positions do you think Sully will need to find upgrades for either in the draft or FA to get this team to .500 next year? (Have gone to games since 1967.)
Hey Richard, yeah, there’s no shortage of positions where the Dolphins could use upgrades and my list would include quarterback, wide receiver, tight end, right guard, right tackle, edge defender, cornerback and safety.
Greetings Alain! One comment on Colts game before questions. First time in a post-game press conference that Hafley looked PO'd. Love to see it. I give Dolphins winning at Buffalo about 5% .You have one league's top rushing offenses vs. a seriously depleted D-Line. 2nd start QB in a hostile environment, leaky O-Line, etc. How does Miami cope with a stacked box? Wondering why Miami doesn't use more play action against the stacked box. Showing my age, they should hire Steve DeBerg to teach it. Best-play action QB ever IMHO. Of course it would help to have WRs that could get open . Even if defense gets pressure, we all know Josh Allen senses it and takes off for 10 or so yards . Defense has its hands full. Thoughts? As always, appreciate all the great written content on Miami Dolphins on SI.Com plus the best two podcasts out there with All Dolphins and Dolphins Collective!
Hey Dave, thanks as always for the kind words. Think you partly answered your own question about not calling more play-action passes, that being the lack of wide receivers getting open on a regular basis. The pass protection also has been leaky most of the season and play action creates an ever-so-slight delay in the quarterback dropping back. And, yes, Steve DeBerg was the master at ball handling. The defense most definitely will have its hands full and it may be that their best hope is to make Allen uncomfortable and watching him force things.
How do you see the Buffalo game shaking out? Or maybe a gut reaction is a better tool?
Hey Ed, this obviously is a tough matchup for the Dolphins because of the talent gap, though the possibility of the Bills looking past Miami to their Thanksgiving night showdown against Kansas City certainly exists. My gut tells me the Bills come out sluggish, the Dolphins are feisty as always, it’s a close game at halftime, but then Buffalo pulls away in the second half.
Hola, Alain. It was good to see Tim Graham talking with you, but his beard made me feel ancient. At least you look tanned, rested and ready to serve. How long before the Dolphins plug you into the D-line?
LOL … for those not aware, Tim Graham covers the Bills for The Athletic (used to cover the Dolphins for the Palm Beach Post) and we had a great conversation on the All Dolphins Podcast earlier this week. And the Dolphins probably would sign right now anybody and everybody who could help them on the defensive line, first hoping that new additions Keith Cooper Jr. and Jordan Jefferson can deliver and that Kenneth Grant can take a big step forward.
Why don't Dolphins throw more deep passes to loosen 8 man boxes?
It’s all fine and dandy to want to throw deep passes on a regular basis, but that requires good pass protection and receivers who can get open deep, and the Dolphins aren’t necessarily gifted in either area.

title: How Dolphins Edge Chop Robinson Took His Game to Another Level
full_text:
In a season that's overall disappointing for the Miami Dolphins, there might not be a more pleasant development that the performance of 2024 first-round pick Chop Robinson.
The edge defender from Penn State is playing the best football of his career, particularly in the past month or so, looking very much like the disruptive force on the defensive line the Dolphins were hoping they got with the 21st overall pick two years ago.
This is significant for the Dolphins because Robinson entered the season as a question mark in terms of being a future building block after a highly disappointing 2025 season.
While sacks aren't the end-all, be-all numbers by which to judge pass rushers, they are significant and Robinson has been on a tear in that regard over the past month with four in the past four games.
He's now got five on the season, which leads the team and has him on a pace to reach double figures for the first time in his NFL career.
Better yet, Robinson is becoming more of a factor as a run defender, the latest example coming against the Indianapolis Colts last Sunday when he fought off a blocker to meet Jonathan Taylor in the open field and then tackled him short of the first-down marker on a second-down play.
We had seen flashes from Robinson before, particularly in the second half of his rookie year when he had five of his sacks that season and 11 of his 14 quarterback hits.
What was missing was consistency and more production.
This year also started very quietly, though it didn't help that Robinson had to miss the Week 2 game against the Kansas City Chiefs because of a concussion he sustained in practice.
Robinson has just gotten better every week, though, and it might be tough to find many more impressive pass rushers around the NFL over the past month.
Head coach Jeff Hafley explained Friday before practice how Robinson has been able to take that major, and very much welcome, step forward.
"I think it's his preparation," Hafley said. "One, he's getting in the groove. You know, he didn't play consecutively early in the season. It's his preparation, and I think, like, there's nothing magical about playing well when you get a good player who starts to really learn how to practice, and I mean practice hard, like game like, and take every individual individual drill as if it's going to show up on the field, and then the jog through, and then the walk through, and then the practice.
"He's just starting to show up and understand how to practice like a very high-level player. So when it starts to happen in the game, it's no surprise. And I think he's starting to see that and feel that. And in turn, his confidence is up, right? Because he's doing it over and over and over again. So it's been a very cool process to watch him grow. And I think there's still a lot more in him as he really becomes a complete player."
With his performance these days, the big question with him just might have turned from whether he'd be part of the team's future as to when to address his contract as he becomes extension-eligible after the season along with the team's decision on his fifth-year option due by May 1.
At this point, that fifth-year option decision seems like a slam dunk, which is probably not what we would have said at the start of this season.

title: Grand Theft Contract: The 10 Worst Dolphins Deals of the GTA Era
full_text:
Since the release of Grand Theft Auto VI apparently is a very big deal, we decided to have some fun with it with Grand Theft Contract with a countdown of the top 10 worst deals the Miami Dolphins have signed since the video game's initial release in November 1997.
So, without further do, here it is.
That the Dolphins are carrying a $3.8 million cap charge for a backup quarterback who was beaten out by a rookie seventh-round pick (Quinn Ewers) is all you need to know about this flushing money down the drain.
Spoiler alert, this won't be the last QB contract we dump on. There really hadn't been anything in the first three seasons to suggest that Tannehill was a difference-maker at quarterback, so giving him a four-year, $77 million extension was silly and the Dolphins ended up eating $18.4 million of cap space in 2019 after finally giving up on him.
The Dolphins made the playoffs in that 2016 season, but it wasn't thanks to the player who had been the first overall pick 10 years earlier because Williams contributed basically nothing after signing a two-year, $17 million deal.
The one saving grade here is that the Dolphins structured Daniels' three-year, $24 million contract in such a way they're only eating $4.8 million of cap space this year, but getting just four snaps out of Daniels still is rough.
While Suh actually played pretty well for the Dolphins during his three seasons with the team, the Dolphins just gave crazy money (six years, $114 million, $60 million guaranteed) for an interior defensive lineman with good, not great pass-rushing ability.
What made this three-year, $90 million extension so bad is the Dolphins simply didn't need to do it because Hill still had two years left on his previous extension. Then again, this was the summer of "You get a contract, you get a contract, you get ..."
Byron Jones actually was a very good cornerback, but he also wasn't a difference-maker and giving him $82.5 million over five years was just a bit much.
The Dolphins ended up paying Fuller $10 million for three games and 65 offensive snaps. And this was a deal signed by a player who hadn't played more than 11 games in any of the previous four seasons, so the lack of durability maybe could have been foreseen.
Bill Parcells wanted the Dolphins to become more physical after they got pushed around by the Baltimore Ravens in the 2008 playoffs, so in came Grove on a five-year, $29 million contract. But like Fuller, Grove had battled injuries and it happened again in Miami, and he was gone before the start of his second season with Miami.
Come on, was there really a doubt about this one? The Dolphins eating $99 million of cap space between this year and next says everything that needs to be said here.

title: Examining the Dolphins Drought at Buffalo And Ranking the Close Calls
full_text:
Stop us if you've heard this one before, but the Miami Dolphins are going to be heavy underdogs when they travel to face the Buffalo Bills on Sunday, and of course they should be.
Beyond the polar opposite records of the two teams — 1-8 for the Dolphins and 8-1 for the Bills — there's also the matter of Miami not having won in Buffalo in 10 years.
December 24, 2016 is the exact date of the Dolphins' last victory in Buffalo, a 34-31 overtime decision that got Miami to the playoffs after Denver lost later that afternoon.
Since then, the Dolphins have dropped 10 straight, including a playoff game in the 2022 season.
But there have been some close calls, including three games decided by three points, one by eight points, and two more where the outcome remained in doubt until the fourth quarter.
And some of those close calls have come in games where the Dolphins were prohibitive underdogs, like they will be Sunday.
So while all logic suggests a comfortable Buffalo victory Sunday, maybe even a blowout, what's happened during the streak should give us pause — yes, even with the Dolphins down three defensive linemen.
Here then is a ranking of the Dolphins' 10 straight losses at Buffalo in terms of their performance and how closely they came to winning.
The Dolphins entered the game as 13.5-point underdogs with rookie seventh-round pick Skylar Thompson at quarterback because Tua Tagovailoa was out with a concussion and Teddy Bridgewater was out with a hand injury. Big plays on defense and a long punt return by Cedrick Wilson Jr. put the Dolphins in position to go win the game down three near midfield before the final drive stalled.
This may have been Tagovailoa's best post-extension performance and a late touchdown pass to Jaylen Waddle tied the score 27-27 before Jordan Poyer's roughness penalty on a third-and-9 penalty kept alive a game-winning drive that ended with Tyler Bass' 61-yard field goal.
On a snowy Saturday night after rough losses against the 49ers and Chargers, the Dolphins found themselves with a great opportunity tied at 29-29 when they had a first-and-10 at the Buffalo 41. But after the drive stalled, the Bills got out of a second-and-18 jam and put themselves in position for a chip-shot game-winning field goal with a DPI against cornerback Kader Kohou.
Coming in as 12-point underdogs after starting off 0-2, the Dolphins were ready to get the ball back in a 21-21 game in the fourth quarter when Zach Sieler was flagged for roughing the kicker, the first of two gigantic plays that cost Miami the game along with Tagovailoa's later interception on a first-and-10 from the Bills 21.
The Dolphins were 17-point underdogs when they went to Buffalo with an 0-5 record to face the 4-1 Bills, yet led 14-9 heading into the fourth quarter before a late collapsing that included a Preston Williams fumble inside the Miami 30. That game ended with Micah Hyde returning the Dolphins' onside kick attempt for a touchdown.
There was nothing particularly noteworthy about this game, other than it featured three interceptions by Dolphins QB Jay Cutler.
This was the week after the Dolphins hung 70 points on the Denver Broncos to get to 3-0 on the season, and the teams traded touchdowns on the first five possessions before the Bills scored 10 points in the final 3:12 of the first half to go ahead 31-14.
This was a rough day for the Miami offense, and it was encapsulated by a dreadful play near the end of the first half when the Dolphins were in position to break a 3-3 tie. This was when on a third-and-5 from the Buffalo 12 with 24 second left a shotgun snap from center Austin Reiter hit Mike Gesicki while he was in motion and the Bills recovered the fumble to end the scoring threat.
The Dolphins actually were favored in this game because the Bills already had clinched the AFC East title and they were expected to play their starters little or not at all and Miami would clinch a playoff spot with a win. The Dolphins actually led 3-0 after the first quarter, but then Josh Allen threw three touchdown passes that combined with a punt return for another score made it 28-6 at halftime. Allen was done after that, and so were the Dolphins' playoff hopes.
In what became Adam Gase's final game as Dolphins head coach, Josh Allen got his first win against Miami by passing for three touchdowns and rushing for two more as a 14-14 halftime game got out of hand.

title: Dolphins First Week 11 Injury Report: Brewer Status Quo, Punter Problem, and More
full_text:
Center Aaron Brewer missing another practice as he remains in the concussion protocol clearly was the biggest headline of the Miami Dolphins' first injury report for Week 11, but there are several other issues worth monitoring.
The most glaring ones would be at wide receiver, where injuries continue to happen, and at punter.
The situation with punter Bradley Pinion missing practice because a right groin injury maybe shouldn't have been easy to predict after the Dolphins signed punter Jack Browning to the practice squad earlier Wednesday.
As a general rule, NFL teams don't have two punters or two kickers on the team (active roster and practice squad) unless there's an injury, so the Browning move should have been a sign.
As we indicated earlier, Browning has appeared in five NFL games but none since the 2024 season and hasn't even punted in a preseason since then.
The issue at wide receiver is that rookie Caleb Douglas joined the list of injured players at that position as he was limited with a shoulder injury. There was good news there, though, with Chris Bell back at practice (albeit on a limited basis) after both he and Jared Wayne missed the game against the Indianapolis Colts on Sunday.
Wayne was among the five players who didn't practice, a group that included safety Dante Trader Jr. (shoulder/groin) and cornerback Jaylin Simpson (knee).
Trader has been battling injuries for a few weeks now and one wonders whether he'll need to be shut down at some point to allow him to get back to 100 percent.
While it's early in the week, the best projection if Trader can't play against Buffalo would be for Zayne Anderson to get the start alongside rookie Michael Taaffe even if Kyle Louis has been getting regular snaps on defense since coming off IR. Louis has been used as a type of nickel linebacker as opposed to a true safety.
Simpson is primarily a special teams contributor, and if Wayne can't play again, then it would mean another game for veteran Jalen Tolbert.
Along with the five players who didn't practice, the Dolphins had five others who were limited. Besides Bell and Douglas, there was LS Tucker Addington again (shoulder), CB JuJu Brents (neck) and C Andrew Meyer (neck).
In the event that both Brewer and Meyer wound up sidelined for the Buffalo game, then we'd be looking at Jarrett Kingston, who played center for two snaps against the Colts when Meyer briefly left the game.
The Bills also had five players sit out practice Wednesday, with guard O'Cyrus Torrence's absence related to a personal issue.
The focus for Buffalo should be in the secondary, which was missing Wednesday cornerbacks Dee Alford (concussion) and Christian Benford (groin).
Furthermore, three safeties were limited in practice, including recent acquisition Amani Hooker (knee) along with Damar Hamlin (toe) and Cole Bishop (shoulder).

title: How the Dolphins (AKA Vice City Manatees) Have Embraced GTA VI
full_text:
It's officially the day before one of the most anticipated video games of all time releases on the PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X/S: Grand Theft Auto VI. Developed by Rockstar Games, the newest entry in the series will take players back to Leonida and Vice City for the first time since 2002.
The city of Miami has embraced the game's release in a way that hasn't been seen since Los Angeles hyped up GTA V all the way back in 2013. That includes the Miami Dolphins, who have partnered with Rockstar to ensure all of Miami-Dade County is ready when the game goes live.
Something you'll find in the game is a parody of the Dolphins that has appeared on real-life signs, billboards, and art. What we know about the in-game equivalent of the Dolphins is limited, but some clues could indicate they'll be a big presence in the latest story to come out of Vice City.
Just like the Miami Heat and Miami Marlins, the Dolphins have an in-game counterpart with a similar name, but not the same because of licensing and copyright issues. The Heat are known as the Narcos (yikes), the Marlins are the Flamingos, and the Dolphins are the Manatees.
The resemblance is undeniable, with the Manatees adopting an aqua and pink color scheme, and the logo featuring a manatee rocking a VC football helmet in front of a pink and black sunbeam. They compete in the American Football Federation (AFF). If you're one of the fans who miss the era of Dolphins logos that feature the dolphin wearing the M helmet, GTA VI has you covered.
Rockstar Games has prioritized advertising fictional in-game brands out in Miami, and the Manatees are no exception. Digital signage for the team has been spotted at Bayfront Park, Miami International Airport, and the Clevelander. Manatees merchandise, including jerseys and footballs, is being sold online.
Two people can be seen wearing Manatees jerseys in the game's trailers and box art. The first is Dre'Quan Priest, who appears to be friends with the game's playable protagonists, Jason Duval and Lucia Caminos. The second is the unnamed cover girl featured on the game's box art, wearing a cropped Manatees jersey over a bikini.
We don't know much about the Manatees, including whether or not they're also in a rebuild. We don't even know where they play, as Hard Rock Stadium might not be featured in the game, unlike the Kaseya Center (Sahara Arena) and loanDepot Park (Fleeca Field).
You would think the Flamingos would play at Flecca Field, but instead, it appears to be home to a second football team, the Mambas, according to banners hanging around the stadium. There's much less information about this team aside from a mention during a heist in GTA V, in which you steal a football signed by a former player, BJ Smith.
The Miami Dolphins have partnered with Rockstar Games, featuring GTA VI advertising at Hard Rock Stadium in the form of signage around the seats, video boards, and walkways leading into the stadium. It's equally hard to miss the Vice City-themed Goodyear Blimp flying over Hard Rock Stadium on game day.
From the Dolphins' perspective, the Vice City Manatees provide an opportunity for players around the world to want to become fans of the real-life team, just like the Narcos and Flamingos. Consdering GTA V sold 235 million copies worldwide and generated over $10 billion in revenue,  that's a lot of reasons to be all aboard the latest installment.
A popular trend on social media is seeing what people and teams looked like back in 2013, when GTA V was originally released on the Xbox 360 and PlayStation 3. That includes the Dolphins, who debuted their new-era logo and uniforms at Sun Life Stadium that year.
This was the second season for head coach Joe Philbin in what would be known as a mediocre era for the Dolphins, as he never got the team to the playoffs or even a winning record before being fired in 2015.
Miami ended up with an 8-8 record, with their most memorable win in 2013 coming on Halloween night over Cincinnati when Cameron Wake sacked Andy Dalton in the end zone in overtime for a game-winning safety.
Quarterback Ryan Tannehill led the Dolphins to three straight wins to begin the season with an offense that featured running back Lamar Miller and wide receivers Brian Hartline and Mike Wallace. On defense, Wake and Brent Grimes were the stars, allowing only one game in which the opposing offense scored 30+ points.
Turnovers killed the Dolphins, with Tannehill throwing 17 interceptions that season. They lost six of their next eight games before a late-season run, winning three straight (including a marquee win over New England) before dropping their final two games to Buffalo and the New York Jets.
They didn't do themselves any favors in the 2013 NFL draft, trading up to take defensive end Dion Jordan with the third overall pick. They passed on offensive tackle Lane Johnson, who was selected by Philadelphia right after. He would go on to play for the Eagles for 14 seasons, becoming a six-time Pro Bowl selection and winning two Super Bowls.

title: Vikings Week 11 Report Card: Grading Every Position After Brutal 35-10 Loss to the 49ers
full_text:
Breathe, Vikings fans. Sunday night's 35-10 beatdown came against the best team in the league , with a quarterback who's been with Minnesota for less than two weeks. Still, the Vikings looked overwhelmed from the start, and this loss is certainly a speed bump on the way to a Super Bowl.
Just a week after dominating the Packers, the Vikings got a taste of their own medicine from the 49ers. Let's get into some (mostly terrible) positional grades.
Kirk Cousins was mostly fine in his second game in purple this season, but the pick-six in the second quarter put the contest out of hand really early.
Outside of that big mistake, the Vikings can take some comfort knowing Cousins orchestrated long drives, completed 68% of his passes, and overall, just looked like a quarterback in control. That's certainly a consolation prize after the bad loss, but the long-term prospects of this offense aren't as dreary as they were a few weeks ago.
Aaron Jones Sr. turned back the clock on his 11-yard touchdown run, but otherwise the Minnesota run game was a complete non-factor for about the seventh time this season. Even before the night turned into a game of catch-up, the backs for the Vikings were getting bottled up after short gains—mainly by Fred Warner—and finished the night with just 56 yards on 19 carries.
If Cousins's pick-six didn't end the game, Justin Jefferson's fumble did. The Vikings star receiver coughed up the rock on the opening drive of the third quarter, effectively cutting down any chance at a comeback.
FUMBLE ‼️ 49ers recover! MINvsSF on NBC/Peacock Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/qRIoGFuZWE
Without Jordan Addison, the other receivers just didn't elevate the offense enough, and Jauan Jennings finished with three catches for 20 yards despite his quest for revenge on his former team.
T.J. Hockenson returned from injury and showed that his connection with Cousins is still alive and well, with six catches for 55 yards. It was just his second game all season with more than five catches, and the Vikings will need him down the stretch.
Cousins's flak jacket earned an 'A' grade after the Vikings' offensive line was a sieve all night. The 49ers sacked Cousins once, but he was hit seven times and had to pick himself up off the ground after almost every play. The quarterback-center exchange looked off early, and there wasn't any push in the run game, either.
If the Vikings have the most ferocious front seven in football, Brock Purdy never got the message. Minnesota took down Mr. Irrelevant just once, and he looked cool, calm and collected in the face of defensive coordinator Brian Flores's attacks. Jalen Redmond displayed his typical dominance , even drawing a huge intentional grounding call, but the Vikings' front just wasn't collapsing the pocket at all in this one.
The NFL's leading sack duo was stonewalled as neither Dallas Turner or Andrew Van Ginkel got to the quarterback for the first time all season. The Niners didn't have tons of success on the ground against Minnesota's backers, averaging just 4.1 yards per carry, but they didn't really need to. The splash plays that usually follow this group around simply weren't there.
Purdy got pretty much whatever he wanted, and the Vikings' secondary just had no answers without the pressure up front. Safety remains a problem, and both Theo Jackson and Harrison Smith were beaten for touchdowns. Is it time for the Thomas rookies to get a closer look?
Will Reichard had a chance at history but came up about a yard short on his 71-yard field goal attempt. Despite the lopsided loss, Brett Thorson only punted twice due to a pair of turnovers and the missed kicks.

title: 3 Most Important Vikings Takeaways After Week 11's 35-10 Beatdown Loss Against the 49ers in Mexico City
full_text:
Sunday night’s matchup between the Vikings and 49ers in Mexico City seemed to be an easy candidate for the NFL’s game of the year. With massive playoff seeding implications on the line , a top-level San Francisco offense against Minnesota’s elite defense, all on an international primetime stage, the stakes were certainly high . Unfortunately for the Vikings, the lights may have been too bright.
The good news? The differing methods of altitude prep didn’t seem to be a deciding factor. The bad news? The Vikings were simply outmatched by what seemed to be a far superior NFC opponent. Here's what stands out from Minnesota's blowout loss.
The Vikings defense certainly didn’t get off to the start they were hoping for, giving up a touchdown to tight end George Kittle on the 49ers' opening drive. Quarterback Brock Purdy would connect with Kittle for another TD to start the second quarter as San Francisco’s offense operated with a level of surgical precision we’ve yet to see against Brian Flores’ vaunted defense. Mike Evans would also get on the board with a back-corner TD to give the Niners three first-half passing scores.
That's TWO touchdowns now for George Kittle 🔥 MINvsSF on NBC/Peacock Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/Cr7tUdtRoN
San Francisco would continue to move the ball well in the second half, tacking on a Christian McCaffrey TD in the fourth. The Vikings won the time-of-possession battle, but with the efficiency of the 49ers offense, it didn’t matter. While sacks and turnovers have been a staple of the Vikings defense, they finished with only one sack and zero turnovers. The Vikings defense's season-long dominance should not be ignored, but I'm not sure anyone could have foreseen this kind of outcome .
Kirk Cousins took the field for his second start since returning to the Vikings via trade at the Nov. 10 deadline against a 49ers squad that picked him off three times in his last game as a Raider. The 38-year-old veteran made some solid plays early, helping to set up an Aaron Jones rushing score late in the first. Then, after a few unspectacular drives, Cousins threw a brutal pick-six to safety Ji'Ayir Brown, giving San Francisco an 18-point lead heading into the half.
49ers PICK-6 ‼️ MINvsSF on NBC/Peacock Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/qEKqUbC7fV
Cousins showed significant frustration in the first half after multiple questionable hits and even more questionable pass protection from his offensive line. He started off the second half with a massive completion to Justin Jefferson, but the star receiver fumbled to kill the drive. Even when Cousins made the right throws, it wasn’t enough. He finished the night 26-of-38 for 235 yards and the aforementioned pick-six before Carson Wentz stepped in late in the fourth.
It’s not hyperbole to say that the last four games may have been a season-defining stretch for the Minnesota Vikings. The Cousins acquisition sparked hope against the Packers, but it seemed to lose its shine on Sunday night. No matter how they got there, Minnesota’s 1-3 record against four of the NFL's best teams is a blow to their championship aspirations.
Flores is getting cooked tonight but 10 points on offense is RARELY going to win you anything.
The Vikings defense has been too great this season for the team to be called “frauds,” but the lack of preparedness in many of the team's biggest games under Kevin O’Connell should raise serious concerns. He will have a chance to get his squad right against an easier upcoming slate, but the entire team and staff will need to seriously step up if they hope to be a serious playoff threat.
With O’Connell still searching for his first playoff win in year five, performances like Sunday’s will continue to raise more questions than answers.
