title: Saints vs. Bears: Staff Picks and Score Predictions for Sunday
full_text:
The New Orleans Saints (3-6) face another difficult challenge Sunday when they travel to Soldier Field to take on the Chicago Bears (7-2).
Coming off a disappointing loss to the Carolina Panthers , the Saints continue to struggle with offensive consistency and finishing games under head coach Kellen Moore.
Those problems could prove costly against a well-rounded Chicago team that boasts one of the NFL's most productive offenses and a top-10 defense.
Can the Saints pull off an unlikely upset, or will their struggles continue against one of the NFC's top contenders?
Here's how our staff predicts Sunday's matchup will unfold.
This is a game that doesn’t favor the Saints.
The Bears are by far the best team the Saints have faced since the Detroit Lions , who beat New Orleans in overtime. They have one of the league’s best offenses , led by quarterback Caleb Williams , and one of the league's most balanced teams.
Defensively, the Bears have a top-10 defense.
Chicago boasts a top-10 defense, ranking eighth in scoring (20.4 PPG) and seventh in total defense (310.9 YPG). Their strength lies against the run, allowing 91.1 yards per game (seventh-fewest), while placing 15th against the pass (219.8 YPG).
Crucially, the Bears lead the NFL in third-down defense (22.8% conversion rate allowed) and rank 12th in red-zone touchdown efficiency (53.8%). They maintain consistent pass pressure with 26 sacks (ninth) and seven interceptions (tied for 11th).
Also, this will be the first cold-weather game for the Saints as the temperature will be in the 50s throughout the game.
I don’t think the Saints will pull off the upset, but what I do know is that the Saints have played better on the road as both of their wins came on the road against the Baltimore Ravens and New York Giants . I do think its defense will do enough to make this game tight before Chicago pulls away near the end.
This is a Saints team that seems to be searching, searching for an identity, a consistent offense, people on the same page.
The New Orleans offense sputters and coughs more than my old 1969 VW Beetle. No matter what I would do to that little air-cooled engine, it never could quite get started, and when it did, it usually took a few minutes of driving before it would get going smoothly. Once it was warmed up, that little thing was a joy to drive. Unfortunately, it took a while to even get to that point.
The Saints O reminds me of that Beetle.
They can't seem to get going in the beginning. Once they get warmed up and going, they are fun to watch. Until then, it's almost torturous to be a part of.
Eventually, I had to get rid of that little car. Keeping the valves aligned properly on that rapidly expanding air-cooled engine proved to be one of those "I'll be doing this forever" kind of projects, so I just gave up and moved on.
The New Orleans offense is at that point, in my opinion. A squad that cannot consistently move the ball, stopping and starting itself with poor run blocking, or wide receivers and a quarterback who aren't on the same page, or play calling that comes across as vanilla as can be (think runs in the middle).
Now, Brandon Staley's group is another story, another car if you will. They remind me of a Tesla. The Saints defense can really get going with the first acceleration, but fade at the end.
A battery-powered Tesla is a lot like that. They can fly right out the gate and tear the street up, but don't expect that to last, as those batteries won't go 300-plus miles (no matter what they say) like a gas-power engine will, losing energy much sooner than their gas counterparts.
This Saints defense has produced through the first three quarters, especially for the last few games. Although getting turnovers has been a notable absence for this group, it has played well, up until the final quarter. To wit, the Panthers' game.
I say all that to say this: you cannot do any of what the offense and defense has been doing against a quality team. The Panthers, Browns, and Steelers were not quality teams. This Bears team is.
It will take a complete game, start to finish, for this Saints team to have a chance to beat Chicago. The local boys haven't done that all year long.

title: Saints vs. Bears: Scouting Chicago's Dangerous Defense and 4 Key Playmakers
full_text:
The New Orleans Saints (3-6) face another difficult challenge Sunday when they travel to Soldier Field to take on the Chicago Bears (7-2), whose defense has played a key role in the team's success this season.
While head coach Ben Johnson's offense has attracted considerable attention, Chicago's defense presents its own challenges for a New Orleans team that continues to struggle with offensive consistency under Kellen Moore .
Chicago's defense has been a driving force behind the Bears' impressive 7-2 start in Johnson’s second season at the helm, establishing itself as one of the NFL's toughest units to move the football against.
The Bears rank eighth in scoring defense (20.4 points allowed per game) and seventh in total defense (310.9 yards per game), with their greatest strength coming against the run. Chicago is surrendering just 91.1 rushing yards per game, the seventh-fewest in the league, while ranking 15th against the pass (219.8 yards per game).
However, what makes this defense particularly dangerous is its ability to get off the field. The Bears lead the NFL in third-down defense, allowing opponents to convert just 22.8% of their opportunities, and rank 12th in red-zone touchdown percentage allowed (53.8%). Chicago has also pressured opposing quarterbacks consistently, recording 26 sacks (ninth) while collecting seven interceptions (tied for 11th).
With injuries along the offensive line and an inconsistent rushing attack, the Saints must find ways to protect quarterback Tyler Shough, establish offensive balance and avoid costly turnovers.
Here's a statistical breakdown of Chicago's defense and three players the Saints must account for Sunday.
Through Week 10 of the 2026 NFL season; NFL rankings in parentheses.
Booker has emerged as one of Chicago's most productive pass rushers this season, leading the Bears with five sacks while recording 27 tackles and two forced fumbles.
Containing Booker is crucial for New Orleans given its offensive line injuries.
With center Erik McCoy (biceps) and tackle Taliese Fuaga (knee) injured, the Saints' line faces a stern test.
New Orleans has struggled to protect quarterback Tyler Shough, and Booker's pressure could disrupt Kellen Moore's offensive rhythm.
Thieneman has quickly established himself as one of Chicago's most productive defensive players, leading the Bears with 57 tackles, including 31 solo stops, while adding 1.5 sacks, an interception and a team-high five pass deflections
The rookie safety's versatility has been a significant asset to Chicago's defense, allowing him to contribute against the run, provide coverage support and make plays near the line of scrimmage.
Bush has emerged as a cornerstone of Chicago's defense this year, holding the team's second-highest tackle count at 53 (including 29 solo tackles) along with two sacks.
Bringing speed, physicality, and veteran leadership to the center of the field, he plays a key role in anchoring a unit that surrenders just 91.1 rushing yards per game—the seventh-best mark in the league.
Johnson remains one of the most important pieces of Chicago's secondary, providing the Bears with an experienced cornerback capable of matching up against opposing teams' top receiving threats.
Through nine games, the two-time Pro Bowler has recorded 27 tackles, one interception that resulted in a touchdown and a forced fumble.

title: Saints vs. Bears: Scouting Caleb Williams and Chicago's Dangerous Offense
full_text:
The New Orleans Saints (3-6) face one of their toughest defensive tests of the season Sunday when they travel to Soldier Field to take on the Chicago Bears (7-2).
In his second season as Chicago's head coach, Ben Johnson has established one of the NFL's most productive and balanced offenses, ranking seventh in scoring and total offense and fourth in rushing offense.
Between quarterback Caleb Williams ' playmaking ability, a talented backfield tandem featuring D'Andre Swift and Kyle Monangai , and an emerging star in wide receiver Luther Burden III, the Bears have no shortage of offensive weapons.
Considering New Orleans' offensive struggles, Brandon Staley 's defense will have little margin for error if the Saints hope to pull off an upset.
Here is a statistical breakdown of Chicago's offense and three players the Saints must account for Sunday.
Through Week 10 of the 2026 NFL season; NFL rankings in parentheses.
QB Caleb Williams (1,546 passing yards, eight touchdowns, five interceptions)
RB D'Andre Swift (576 rushing yards, 10 touchdowns)
RB Kyle Monanagai: 60 carries for 324 yards (5.4 yards per carry) and three touchdowns
WR Luther Burden III: 644 receiving yards, four touchdowns
WR Rome Odunze: 32 catches for 328 yards and a touchdown
TE Colston Loveland: 37 catches for 363 yards and two touchdowns
Despite missing three games earlier in the season with a hamstring injury, Williams has completed 68.7% of his passes for 1,546 yards, eight touchdowns and five interceptions in six games. He has also rushed for 145 yards and two touchdowns.
The former No. 1 overall pick's arm talent, mobility and ability to extend plays outside the pocket present a significant challenge for New Orleans.
While Chase Young, Carl Granderson and the Saints' defensive front must consistently generate pressure, maintaining disciplined rush lanes to contain Williams will be just as important to keep Williams from escaping the pocket and creating explosive plays downfield.
Swift serves as one of Chicago's primary offensive engines, driving both the ground attack and contributing significantly through the air.
Through Week 10, Swift has rushed for 576 yards and 10 touchdowns on 155 carries, alongside 24 receptions for 162 yards. Despite averaging 3.7 yards per carry, his high-volume scoring efficiency makes him critical to Chicago's offensive consistency.
Paired with Kyle Monangai, Swift forms a versatile backfield rotation designed to control game tempo and keep down-and-distance manageable.
To stay competitive, the Saints defense must disrupt this backfield early and prevent Chicago from establishing a sustained rushing rhythm.
In his second NFL season, the former Missouri standout has established himself as Chicago's top receiving threat, securing 49 catches for 644 yards (13.1 yards per reception) and four touchdowns.
Clearing concussion protocol on Tuesday, Burden delivers a major boost to the Bears' receiving group ahead of Sunday's game. His downfield separation, run-after-catch dynamic, and adaptability in Johnson's offensive system present a tough defensive assignment.
With cornerback Martin Emerson Jr . dealing with a concussion and the Saints releasing safety Justin Reid this week , New Orleans' secondary will face a considerable test against Burden and Chicago's talented receiving corps.

title: Saints Stock Down Report: Moore Running Out of Excuses Ahead of Bears Matchup
full_text:
Coming off their bye week with a chance to win consecutive games for the first time this season, the New Orleans Saints got the same old, same old .
While a handful of individual performances were encouraging during their loss to the Carolina Panthers last Sunday, the defeat exposed recurring issues that have plagued New Orleans all season, from questionable coaching and poor offensive execution to costly mistakes in critical moments.
With a challenging three-game stretch looming, it's becoming increasingly difficult to overlook the Saints' lack of progress in Year 2 under Kellen Moore .
Here are three whose stock has fallen after Sunday's loss to Carolina.
At what point does the rebuilding excuse run out?
The Saints have scored nine first-quarter points through nine games and have been held scoreless in the opening quarter seven times. Coming off a bye week, New Orleans failed to score in the entire first half against Carolina.
After the Carolina loss, it is the 25th time that the Saints have trailed in a game … out of the 26 games Moore has coached in. That’s worst in the NFL since the start of the 2025 season.
Recurring offensive struggles and an inability to win winnable games have made it increasingly difficult to identify tangible progress under Moore .
Even worse, New Orleans has to play the Chicago Bears (7-2), Cincinnati Bengals (7-2) and the Green Bay Packers (6-4) over its next three games, and the chances of winning at least one of those games are low considering not only are they better personnel-wise, but they have better coaching staffs.
Playing without Erik McCoy and Taliese Fuaga certainly didn't help, but Sunday's performance exposed the Saints ' lack of quality offensive line depth.
New Orleans rushed for 49 yards on 25 carries, averaging 2.1 yards per carry, but without Tyler Shough ’s 25 yards off of scrambling out of the pocket, the Saints averaged 1.4 yards per carry. On top of the poor run blocking, the unit could not protect Shough, surrendering three sacks. Pro Football Focus gave starting right guard Jeremiah Wright an abysmal 25 overall grade.
The offensive line remains one of the franchise's biggest roster construction failures.
McKinstry 's costly pass interference penalty in the closing seconds helped Carolina move into field-goal range, setting up Ryan Fitzgerald 's game-winning kick.
Although one play doesn't define an entire performance, the former second-round pick must show more consistency as the Saints evaluate their long-term future in the secondary, especially after releasing safety Justin Reid on Thursday.

title: Saints Stock Report: Rookie WR Steps Up, Two Defensive Players Continue to Shine and the Luck of the Irish
full_text:
The New Orleans Saints suffered another frustrating loss Sunday, falling 20-17 to the Carolina Panthers at the Caesars Superdome and dropping to 3-6 on the season.
While the Saints continue to struggle to put together a complete performance under head coach Kellen Moore , several players stood out despite the disappointing result.
From a rookie wide receiver's breakout to another dominant showing by a veteran pass rusher, here are four Saints whose stock is rising after Sunday's loss to Carolina.
After a rough debut last week against the Cleveland Browns, the rookie wide receiver rebounded in a huge way.
Tyson caught 11 of 13 passes for 80 yards, the most receptions by a Saints rookie since Pierre Thomas in 2007. He emerged as Tyler Shough 's most reliable target, with Carolina limiting Chris Olave to three receptions for 30 yards and Devaughn Vele to just two catches for 14 yards.
It's an encouraging sign after he missed the first two months of the season due to a hamstring injury he suffered midway through training camp and it shows that he is now a little more up to speed.
With Tyson and Olave, the Saints have a promising receiving duo to build around.
Elliss delivered arguably his best performance of the season, recording a career-high 15 tackles, two tackles for loss, a sack and a pass breakup.
The veteran linebacker continues to justify his offseason acquisition and has established himself as one of the most important pieces of the Saints' defense.
Granderson recorded seven pressures and a sack against Carolina, extending his streak of consecutive games with a sack to six.
The veteran edge rusher already has matched his career high with 8.5 sacks through nine games, emerging as one of the few consistent bright spots for New Orleans this season.
Smyth delivered under pressure, connecting on a 55-yard field goal with 41 seconds remaining to tie the game at 17.
Although his kick will be forgotten because the Saints gave up the game-winning field goal just moments later, Smyth continues to demonstrate why he deserves to be the franchise's long-term answer at kicker as he is 4-for-5 on field goal attempts this season.

title: The Good, Bad and Ugly: Can the Saints Do Anything Right?
full_text:
The New Orleans Saints had an opportunity to take control of the NFC South on Sunday, but instead delivered another frustrating performance that raised more questions about the direction of the franchise.
New Orleans (3-6) suffered a heartbreaking 20-17 loss to the Carolina Panthers at the Caesars Superdome, surrendering a game-winning 54-yard field goal by Ryan Fitzgerald as time expired.
Despite Carolina committing 17 penalties for 152 yards, the Saints couldn't capitalize, finishing with just 49 rushing yards, two turnovers and another disappointing offensive performance under head coach Kellen Moore .
The loss dropped New Orleans to 1-4 at home and 0-2 against NFC South opponents, leaving the Saints searching for answers as their season continues to unravel.
Here is the good, bad and ugly from Sunday's loss.
Rookie wide receiver Jordyn Tyson led the Saints with 11 receptions, the most since Pierre Thomas caught 12 passes against the Chicago Bears in December 2007.
After missing the first seven games of the season, the rookie wideout has wasted little time demonstrating why New Orleans selected him eighth overall in April's NFL Draft.
His separation, contested catches, and reliability complement Chris Olave and should make this passing attack even deadlier.
However, the offense has become too predictable.
After a strong performance last week, the Saints' rushing attack went back to its old ways, gaining just 49 yards on 23 carries (2.1 yards per carry) against Carolina.
Quarterback Shough led New Orleans with 25 rushing yards, while Travis Etienne Jr. (14 yards), Audric Estime (6 yards), and Alvin Kamara (4 yards, 3-yard touchdown) combined for minimal output.
Although the absence of right tackle Taliese Fuaga and center Erik McCoy provides important context, the struggles within the ground attack were already present prior to their injuries.
Moore was hired because of his success as the offensive coordinator of the Philadelphia Eagles , one that had the NFL’s top rushing offense in 2024 and propelled them to a Super Bowl victory. He must fix the run game for New Orleans to sustain drives and score consistently.
Through nine games this season, the answer has been a firm no.
Carolina repeatedly handed the Saints chances by committing 17 penalties and struggling offensively, but New Orleans failed to capitalize.
The Saints were shut out in the first half, committed two turnovers, and generated insufficient offense against a sub-.500 Panthers squad. Even after Charlie Smyth tied the game with a 55-yard field goal with 41 seconds remaining, a pass interference penalty on Kool-Aid McKinstry set up Fitzgerald's game-winning kick.
More concerning is the lack of progress under head coach Kellen Moore.
Over nine games, the Saints have struggled with offensive inconsistency, poor execution and an inability to close games. Their 3-6 record inspires little confidence, and individual flashes from Tyson, Shough, and the defense cannot mask overall failure. To make matters worse, the Saints have trailed in all but one of the 26 games that Moore has coached in as the head coach of the Saints.
With upcoming road trips to Chicago and Cincinnati followed by a home game against the Green Bay Packers , the schedule provides no relief. Instead of making a statement in the NFC South, New Orleans showed just how far it remains from contention.

title: Winners and Losers From Giants' 23-18 Win Over Jaguars
full_text:
Defense, defense, and more defense. The New York Giants solidified their identity in Sunday's 23-18 home win over the Jacksonville Jaguars, built on relentless pressure and clutch secondary play.
The offense requires significant adjustments, and the Jags certainly did their part to help Big Blue secure this outcome, but NFL fans should have newfound respect for this team.
While a controversial no-touchdown call will understandably generate a ton of headlines, New York rattled an MVP candidate and made a title contender look pedestrian for much of the game.
Dennard Wilson crafted a brilliant blueprint, and a Carter-led defense executed it excellently. We are giving the unit its due in this edition of winners and losers.
When Abdul Carter underwhelms at the line of scrimmage, criticism tends to get quite loud. That is bound to happen when a player is outspoken and asks to wear Lawrence Taylor's jersey number as a rookie. But when the noise turns up, he usually responds.
The conversations surrounding the stellar second-year outside linebacker will carry a much different tune heading into Week 12. Carter has left a sizable imprint on almost every game he's played this season, but his sack numbers have been lacking. On Sunday, he recorded two sacks on Trevor Lawrence and was a constant pest.
The 23-year-old expertly evaded offensive linemen, using subtle movement and eye-opening explosiveness to smash through Jacksonville's wall of protection. He recorded 12 quarterback pressures , and frequently disrupted the Jaguars' timing.
Carter's value transcends the box score. He draws holding penalties and forces play-callers to abandon their game plan. Carter ascended to his best form on Sunday.
Redemption has defined the 2026 Giants, especially their cornerback room. Greg Newsome and Deonte Banks have dramatically boosted their standing, but as they rose, Paulson Adebo fell. The much-maligned 2025 free-agent signing reminded everyone why he was once trusted as the team's No. 1 cornerback.
Adebo performed at an elite level in the fourth quarter, recording an interception that led to a crucial field goal and making several other positive plays. He finished with one pick and four passes defended, while allowing just one reception for 23 yards .
It is good to know that Adebo can lock down wide receivers on a given day, because Newsome exited early with an ankle issue. Following an injury-marred and largely unproductive first couple of months, Adebo, a former third-round draft pick, could be poised for a memorable conclusion to 2026.
Amid concerns that he was backsliding, Deonte Banks returned to being a game-changer. He stayed ready and punished Lawrence for an ill-advised pass, snagging a first-quarter interception that set up a 53-yard Dominic Zvada field goal.
The No. 24 overall pick in the 2023 NFL Draft added three passes defended and posted six total tackles. How a CB responds after a humbling two-game stretch says a lot about his growth.
Message received, loud and clear.
Giants fans were not just worried about run defense when Dexter Lawrence forced his way off the team. They understood the invaluable versatility that Lawrence brought to the defensive line. Well, his replacement is doing a pretty good job of filling that dual role in the trenches.
D.J. Reader thrived as a pass rusher, registering a thunderous sack that ultimately kept the Jaguars out of the end zone on their opening drive. He got another QB hit later on and finished with four tackles.
Reader is the free-agent heist that keeps on giving.
The veteran safety who went undrafted in 2021 always seems to be in the thick of the action. Ar'Darius Washington makes tackles, records multiple pass breakups, and moves with infectious energy.
He epitomizes what this team has become. Those who run a high motor and avoid needless mistakes will thrive on this defense. It is no mystery why his snap count has increased so sharply in just a month.
Defense is the theme of this edition, so it is only right to wrap up our winners with the Giants' defensive coordinator.
Dennard Wilson disarmed one of the NFL's top offenses in the first half, and he pressed the right buttons when things got tight late. His diverse packages , which utilize players in a variety of ways, perfectly encapsulate where the league is going.
Wilson is what organizations want in a modern-day DC, and if Big Blue keeps producing these results, he will be a sought-after head coaching candidate.
The Giants have found a clear upgrade at center in Bryan Hudson, but the third-year undrafted offensive lineman still has his flaws. They showed up in Week 11.
Hudson surrendered five pressures (four hurries and one hit) in 70 snaps . He also drew an unsportsmanlike penalty after a late hit. He cannot make such mistakes moving forward, as several challenging matchups await.
Although the 23-year-old quarterback faced plenty of pressure throughout the day, he left points and yards on the board with several missed throws.
McCarthy, who made a touchdown-saving play when he chased down Jaguars safety Antonio Johnson after Johnson recovered a late third-quarter Cam Skattebo fumble, completed 18 of 38 passes for 173 yards and a touchdown pass to Malik Nabers.
He showed off his legs a few times, but it was an overall uneven showing.
Give the man credit. Micah McFadden moved with high intensity and positioned himself to make big plays against Jacksonville. But he could not finish.
The fifth-year linebacker couldn't bring down Trevor Lawrence and posted a whopping six missed tackles .
Hustle is important, but so is fundamental soundness.
Yes, Cam Skattebo helped to clinch the victory with two five-yard runs, joining Malachi Fields in lighting a much-needed offensive spark at the most critical juncture. But one heroic moment doesn't let him off the hook for his earlier missteps.
The perennially amped-up running back mustered only 34 yards on 14 carries and committed what should have been a game-changing fumble with about four minutes remaining in the third quarter.
If not for the Giants' defense, the Jaguars would have gained crucial momentum and possibly stolen the win.
Skattebo also gets docked for breaking his no more backflips pledge just days after saying he would. Even on a day with brutal lows, though, he still shined in the end, and did so like only he knows how.
The scouting report on the Craig Wrolstad-led officiating crew wasn't very encouraging, as they were one of the most flag-happy crews in the league this season. True to form, they didn't disappoint in this one, tossing 14 flags that went for 107 yards (one flag was declined), t he most flags thrown in any Week 11 game.
But it wasn't so much the number of flags they threw as it was the three flags that were thrown and then later picked up.
Then there was the matter of a couple of controversial calls, including the Parker Washington no-touchdown call that went in the Giants' favor. We wouldn't be shocked if Wrolstad's crew gets low grades from the league when they're evaluated this week.

title: Four Takeaways From the Giants' 23-18 Win Over the Jaguars
full_text:
Ten days after being chastised for not finishing the game against the Commanders in Week 10, the New York Giants made sure the story was different, narrowly defeating the Jacksonville Jaguars 23-18 at a raucous MetLife Stadium on Sunday.
By all accounts, it was another game with sloppy moments for John Harbaugh's crew, who ultimately found a way to ice the contest in the waning minutes of the fourth quarter as the Jaguars repeatedly tried to mount a last-ditch comeback.
Learning from their past faults, the Giants' defense shut the door on their opponent's attempted rally and notched the team's sixth win of the season, pushing their hopes of winning the NFC East one step closer.
Football is a game of talent and winning in the margins, and thanks to these four components of their showing, New York displayed both as they upset one of the best teams on their remaining schedule.
Where would the Giants have gone without Abdul Carter's incredible afternoon? The answer: nowhere near the level of success they had in stifling the Jaguars' productive offense.
As soon as Brian Burns went down for the season, the bulk of the team's pass-rushing responsibilities was placed on Carter's shoulders. Many have been waiting to see him show the flashes he displayed at Penn State, and he did, putting on a pass-rush clinic off the edge.
Carter finished with the Giants' best pass-rush grade (91.6) by producing a season-high 12 pressures, the second-most by any player in a single game this year, along with two sacks, two hits, and a 23.7% win rate . The next-closest player to him in pressures was D.J. Reader, who finished with five, including a sack.
On nearly every Jaguars possession, it was nearly impossible for quarterback Trevor Lawrence to operate in the pocket without feeling Carter breathing down his neck.
In fact, one could argue the former No. 3 pick might have gotten home to Lawrence a couple more times had officials not missed a few potential penalties, on top of the many they did call on Jacksonville (more on that later).
Either way, Carter responded to the critics waiting to witness the dominant shades that got him drafted as arguably the best prospect in the class. He was instrumental in keeping the Jaguars offense, which ranked fourth in scoring before Week 11, at bay, with just six points in the first 30 minutes.
No one on the Giants roster exemplified the chip-on-their-shoulder mentality against a 7-2 Jaguars team that few gave them a chance to beat. They did just that, and Carter deserves all the kudos for being the real MVP of another impressive defensive outing for Dennard Wilson's unit.
It doesn't matter how good a team's record looks on paper. It's harder to win football games in the NFL when a team commits a bunch of penalties, and the Jaguars took the cake.
Jacksonville committed 13 penalties for a whopping 107 yards on Sunday, most of them on the offensive line.
The impact was that the Jaguars had to play behind the sticks on a ton of late downs, and the Giants capitalized, holding them to 5-of-15 on third-down conversions.
Meanwhile, the Giants committed only six penalties, costing them 46 yards, against a Jaguars team that entered Sunday much sharper at avoiding the yellow flags and had the third-best offense in converting third downs (46.8%).
Much could be attributed to how dominant the Giants and Dennard Wilson were in sending different blitz packages at a banged-up front for Jacksonville and testing the durability of their depth as the game wore on. Carter's solo production certainly helped draw a few flags.
With all their miscues, Lawrence and the Jaguars didn't make it any easier on themselves to sniff out the end zone. Instead, they finished the day with an ugly 1-6 efficiency inside the Giants' 20-yard line, and their lone score came via an 18-yard pass connection to receiver Brian Thomas Jr. midway through the fourth quarter.
That was also a key improvement for New York's unit, which ranked dead last in the same category before shutting down the Jaguars in the red zone for nearly an entire game and showing them that playing the field-goal game is far from a feasible approach to winning in this league.
After two weeks of missed opportunities and off-field drama, it was nice to see Malik Nabers back as the Giants' No. 1 receiving threat as he sparred with Jaguars cornerback Travis Hunter for most of the afternoon.
Nabers' game looked off in the previous two contests, as he collected 10 catches for 87 yards and infamously dropped what looked like a surefire touchdown against the Eagles in Week 9.
However, he returned to form against Hunter and the Jaguars, reeling in seven of 12 targets for a team-high 77 yards and a touchdown that put the Giants up 17-6 in the second quarter. It was the third game this year in which Nabers was targeted 10+ times, and he took advantage of Hunter's inexperience at cornerback.
Last season, Hunter leaned more on the offensive side of the ball, but the Jaguars have been focused on crafting his defensive game in 2026. He was one of their best man-coverage defenders entering Week 11, but he was ultimately responsible for five receptions on seven targets for 41 yards in his primary assignment.
The more surprising part of Nabers' touchdown was that he and quarterback J.J. McCarthy made the long-ball connection to cap the drive. McCarthy and the Giants tried slinging it downfield numerous times to test the Jaguars' secondary, only to come up short pretty much every time.
Still, with the big games that Harbaugh and company have left to face on their slate, players need to step up, and Nabers, who wants the ball in bunches, is certainly one of them. When those bunches come, he needs to produce, and he did for a premium score on Sunday.
Playing quarterback is one of the toughest positions in the NFL, and it often comes with more criticism than praise when mistakes happen.
J.J. McCarthy didn't have the shiniest stat sheet against the Jaguars, completing 18 of 38 pass attempts for 173 yards and one touchdown pass as Jacksonville's talented pass rush pressured him all day.
Perhaps the biggest play that the gunslinger made all day wasn't on the offensive side of the ball. In fact, it was a rare tackle by the fearless McCarthy, one that might have spared the Giants from another humiliating collapse down the stretch.
With a 20-6 lead growing in the third quarter, the Giants started to find a groove on their second possession of the frame, running 10 plays for 46 yards and seeking one extra end-zone visit to punctuate what had been an impressive showing to that point.
On the 10th play, Cam Skattebo's fumbling woes came back to haunt him as defensive end Josh Hines-Allen nailed the "Peanut Punch" and knocked the football loose. Safety Antonio Johnson picked up the ball and saw open grass ahead as the Jaguars looked to get back into the game.
After Johnson took it 42 yards the other way for what appeared to be a touchdown, the last man standing was McCarthy, who brought him down with a functional tackle to cut off the Jaguars' six-point lifeline.
Normally, teams might cringe at the sight of their quarterback laying his body on the line, but had McCarthy not done it, the Jaguars would have trimmed the deficit to a single score. Later in the fourth frame, they would put up nine more points that would have meant a late loss for Big Blue.
Instead, the Jaguars eventually settled for a field goal on that drive as the Giants' defense stiffened up inside the red zone and found the spark they needed to put the rest of the organization on their backs until the final whistle.

title: Abdul Carter Answers Critics With Two Sacks, 12 Pressures in Giants' Win Over Jaguars
full_text:
EAST RUTHERFORD, N.J. — New York Giants outside linebacker Abdul Carter knows what he has inside of him.
And after hearing the criticisms about his play all week long, to which he responded with a simple post on his X account vowing to "show y'all," and after undoubtedly hearing that the Giants shouldn't even bother to take the field against the Jacksonville Jaguars (7-2 before their humbling 23-18 loss to Big Blue), Carter was even more certain of what was to come.
"As a defense, we showed what we're really about," Carter told CBS' Tracy Wolfson once the game had ended. "And for me, I'm the best in the world."
Carter certainly delivered a performance, one of many the Giants hope to see from him for however long his NFL career might last, that can serve as a building block toward his quest to be "the best in the world."
The second-year defender registered a career-high-tying five quarterback hits, along with four total tackles, 2.0 sacks and two tackles for loss.
His two sacks were the first of what the Giants hope will be many multi-sack games in his career, and he had 12 quarterback pressures in all.
"Twelve pressures, did he?" said a delighted head coach John Harbaugh after the game. "Twelve pressures. Should have given him two game balls, I guess."
Turning serious, Harbaugh said he wasn't surprised to see Carter have the kind of game he did.
"Reading the quotes, you know, I mean that he gave you guys. He's been saying the same thing to me," he said.
"But more than that, he's been practicing that way. So to see him break out and get the sack and the quarterback hits, it was great."
It certainly was, as the Giants not only took another step forward in their quest to win the NFC East, but also showed they can stand toe-to-toe with, and outslug, a team with a winning record that many had deemed an AFC powerhouse.
"I really just told myself, I'm just going to take the over and win this game for us," Carter said, also giving a shoutout to the rest of his teammates on defense for helping make it a team effort.
"God put me in this position. He gave me these abilities, and I'm just taking advantage of them."
Beyond the numbers on the stat sheet, Carter drew at least two holding penalties in what was a flag-filled game, with the Jaguars taking the brunt of the yellow flags.
The former Penn State defender also helped some of his teammates get into position to make plays, a welcome sight for the young man who said the Giants were disrespected coming into the game.
"Yeah, we heard, you know, everybody pretty much counted us out, saying we pretty much had no chance," he said.
"We couldn't stick with their offense, but we just took that as disrespect. We came out with a chip on our shoulder."
And for Carter, it was one of many performances that will hopefully help him achieve his "best in the world" goal.

title: Giants WR Malik Nabers Touts Team Effort in Win Over Jaguars
full_text:
New York Giants receiver Malik Nabers is no stranger to playing an integral role in his team's offensive success.
The Giants' sixth overall selection in the 2024 NFL Draft caught seven passes for 55 yards, including quarterback J.J. McCarthy's sole touchdown toss, in New York's 23-18 Week 11 victory over the Jacksonville Jaguars at MetLife Stadium.
While earning their sixth win of the season was fulfilling enough for Nabers and his teammates, the Giants took extra satisfaction in holding their fourth-quarter lead over one of the NFL's top-performing teams.
"It was good. We have been in these types of games over the last few weeks, and we weren't able to put it away [in previous games to seal victories], but I'm glad we were able to do it today," Nabers said.
"We kind of flipped over from weeks prior, having a slow start [offensively] in the first half and then having a fast start [today] in the second half."
After a disappointing Week 10 loss to the Washington Commanders, New York ground out a five-point win by making timely plays in the game's closing moments.
Rookie receiver Malachi Fields caught a 19-yard pass to move the Giants into Jaguars territory, while running back Cam Skattebo secured the win with a 5-yard run for a first down on the final drive.
Though Nabers was Big Blue's leading receiver in Week 11, it was rewarding to watch his teammates put the exclamation point on their hard-fought victory over the Jaguars.
"I think Malachi [Fields] does not get enough praise for what he does," Nabers said. "He gets open really well; he catches the ball really well. He put the game away when we needed to. Giving him the opportunity to do that shows how good of a player he is."
Through 29 career games, Nabers has become New York's top perimeter pass-catcher. The LSU product has caught 192 passes, the third-most through that many games in NFL history behind only Odell Beckham Jr. (199) and Puka Nacua (194). He has also amassed 2,178 career receiving yards and 12 touchdowns.
Still, Nabers proved on Sunday that he can win his matchups from multiple alignments. Despite drawing multiple Jaguars defenders for much of the game, Nabers broke free for his touchdown while aligned in the slot.
For Nabers, it was simply a matter of solid coaching becoming reality.
"Our coaches just schemed it up to get plays like that [offensively], just seeing a lot of different kinds of [defensive] coverages," Nabers recounted. "By watching film, it played out just how we practiced."

title: NFL Replay Office Clarifies Controversial Call in Giants Win Over Jaguars
full_text:
EAST RUTHERFORD, NJ — The New York Giants ' sixth win of the 2026 NFL season came with its share of controversy.
Big Blue's defense sacked Jacksonville Jaguars QB Trevor Lawrence three times and intercepted him twice, while running back Cam Skattebo earned a game-sealing first down late in the second half to secure the 23-18 victory for the Giants over the Jags at MetLife Stadium on Sunday.
While both teams made enough mistakes to snatch defeat from the jaws of victory, a controversial call from the game's officiating crew continues to cast a dark cloud over New York's Week 11 win.
Trailing 20-6 early in the fourth quarter, Lawrence seemed to give the Jaguars their first six-point score of the day by connecting with receiver Parker Washington in the back left corner of the end zone.
Washington appeared to make a remarkable contested catch, securing the football while getting both feet down at the edge of the end zone.
"I did not think he lost possession of the football... I think it's a touchdown, fellas." CBS rules analyst Gene Steratore disagreed with this being ruled incomplete after review on a potential Parker Washington TD for the Jaguars. 🏈🦓🎙️ pic.twitter.com/4RdlPYAYXQ
Still, officials initially ruled the pass incomplete. Although Jaguars head coach Liam Coen challenged the ruling on the field, referee Craig Wrolstad and the replay official upheld the incomplete call. Jacksonville used its final timeout and was forced to settle for a 31-yard field goal from kicker Cam Little.
"He Needs to Maintain Control of the Ball Throughout the Process of the Catch."
After their Week 11 showdown, both the Jaguars and the Giants were eager for clarification on the polarizing call.
"The ruling on the field was an incomplete pass," Vice President of Instant Replay Mark Butterworth told PFWA pool reporter Pat Leonard. "First, to overturn a call, we need clear video evidence to overturn the on-field ruling. It was determined that the receiver did not gain full control of the ball until he was out of bounds."
To his credit, Leonard followed up by asking Butterworth to confirm that both the ball's movement in Washington's hands and the placement of his feet prevented a conclusive overturn of the in-game call.
"Even though he has it initially when the right foot touches, you are saying that as his left foot comes down and as the rest of his body contacts out of bounds, the movement of the ball determines that there is no clear and obvious evidence that a catch was made?" Leonard asked.
"Yes. That is correct," Butterworth answered. "He needs to maintain control of the ball throughout the process of the catch."
Wrolstad's officiating crew has earned a reputation for having a quick draw when it comes to penalty flags. As New York Giants On SI reported earlier this week , the 13-year veteran referee and his team entered this Week 11 matchup between the Giants and Jaguars having issued 138 total penalties (third most) for 1,214 yards (second most) in the league.
"Through eight games this season, Wrolstad's crew is averaging 19.7 flags per game, with 9.13 coming against the home team and 8.13 against the visiting team," the report continued.
In total, the Jaguars were whistled for 13 penalties, losing 107 yards. New York, in turn, was penalized six times for a loss of 46 yards.

title: Giants Grade Out: Carter and Defense Shine in 23-18 Win Over Jaguars
full_text:
East Rutherford, NJ — Grading the New York Giants' 23-18 win over the Jacksonville Jaguars.
J.J. McCarthy was a little too streaky for our tastes, finishing 18-of-38 for 173 yards and one touchdown.
Meanwhile, the Giants' running game, predictably, couldn't get much going against the tough Jaguars run defense. New York finished with 77 yards on 25 carries, averaging 3.1 yards per carry, and one touchdown, scored by quarterback Jameis Winston on a tush push.
Cam Skattebo had yet another fumble (he currently leads the league with five), and after that, the Giants only ran the ball once until the last two minutes of the game, when they were looking to chew up what was left of the clock.
The Giants' defense had Jaguars quarterback Trevor Lawrence skittish all evening, with Lawrence finishing 25-of-47 for 301 yards, two interceptions, and only one touchdown.
The Giants also sacked Lawrence three times, twice by Abdul Carter, who declared himself the "best in the world" after the game. He delivered the goods, racking up eight total pressures, including two tackles for loss and two sacks.
What the stat sheet didn't show is that Carter also drew multiple holding penalties from the flag-happy crew led by referee Craig Wrolstad.
The bottom line is that it is NFC Defensive Player of the Week-worthy production. Overall, the defense rose to the occasion, with four tackles for loss, 11 quarterback hits, two interceptions, and 14 pass breakups. That's about as solid a night as you'll see.
Another week, another miss from the right hash by Dominic Zvada, who this time missed a chip-shot 32-yarder wide left. While he did make his other three attempts, from 53, 43, and 54 yards, we're not sure how much longer the Giants can keep taking these chances with an inconsistent kicker.
Elijah Campbell had a big penalty on a huge opening kickoff, but after that, the special teams settled down. Jordan Stout averaged 54.5 net yards and pinned the Jaguars inside the 20 on one of his four punts. Xavier Gipson handled the punt returns (one) and kickoffs, and there wasn't a single muff.
Solid effort by defensive coordinator Dennard Wilson, who sent the dogs after Trevor Lawrence and never allowed him to get fully comfortable in the pocket.
We're still not enamored with the running offense, as we don't really see it as having an identity in terms of the blocking scheme, which, we wonder, might be creating the inconsistencies the Giants have struggled with.
And speaking of the running game, we get it that Skattebo's fumble might have created some doubt about having him touch the ball again, at least until later in the fourth quarter, when the clock was winding down.
But why they didn't at least turn to the more sure-handed Devin Singletary to chew precious seconds off the clock is a mystery.
Still, credit to John Harbaugh for using the gut punch they suffered against Washington as added motivation to wake the sleeping Giants in time to earn their sixth win of the season.

title: Giants Tame Jaguars 23-18 on Strong Day for Defense
full_text:
EAST RUTHERFORD, NJ — For the second time in as many weeks, the New York Giants struggled to hold a fourth-quarter lead at MetLife Stadium.
Unlike their disappointing Week 10 loss to the Washington Commanders in prime time, New York shined in the 4:25 p.m. ET slot, grinding out a 23-18 Week 11 win over the Jacksonville Jaguars.
Giants quarterback J.J. McCarthy completed 18 passes for 173 yards and one touchdown. Jaguars quarterback Trevor Lawrence went 25-for-47 for 301 passing yards, one touchdown, and two interceptions in the losing effort.
Yet the story of the day was New York's defense, with cornerbacks Deonte Banks and Paulson Adebo each intercepting Lawrence. Safety Jevon Holland led all Giants with nine tackles, while linebacker Abdul Carter had his first multiple-sack game of the season with two.
With the win, the Giants improve to 6-3-1, further strengthening their lead in the NFC East and taking a sizable step toward their first playoff berth since 2022.
The Jaguars struck first in Week 11 behind a 47-yard return by Ameer Abdullah on the game's opening kickoff. Jacksonville running back Chris Rodriguez, Jr. advanced his team into field goal range with an additional 21-yard run. Despite a 10-yard loss on a sack of Lawrence by New York defensive lineman D.J. Reader, the Jags added three points on a 42-yard field goal by kicker Cam Little.
New York shifted the momentum back in their favor as Jacksonville faced 3rd-and-6 from their own 39. With the Giants defense bringing the blitz, cornerback Deonte Banks positioned himself perfectly to intercept Lawrence's pass intended for receiver Parker Washington. The Giants, who had difficulty moving the ball, tied the game at 3 when rookie kicker Dominic Zvada hit a 53-yard field goal from the right hash.
On their ensuing offensive drive, the Giants earned the game's first touchdown on a seven-play, 53-yard drive. McCarthy's drive-opening 8-yard pass to receiver Malik Nabers was ruled incomplete upon review. However, Big Blue's starter found Nabers for an 11-yard pass on his next throw.
The Giants advanced deep into Jacksonville territory after a 37-yard defensive pass interference penalty on cornerback Montaric Brown.
New York finally found the end zone on their fourth attempt from the Jags' 2. Quarterback Jameis Winston earned the 1-yard touchdown, giving the Giants a 10-3 lead with just over two minutes remaining in the first quarter.
Although the Jaguars cut the lead to 10-6 with a 35-yard field goal from Little, Big Blue was ready to answer. New York's second touchdown drive came on a nine-play, 66-yard march that drained 5:19 from the clock in the second quarter.
McCarthy helped move the team past midfield with a 22-yard run to Jacksonville's 34. Following a 14-yard completion to tight end Chris Manhertz, McCarthy found Nabers for the eight-yard touchdown strike. With the Zvada extra point, the Giants claimed a 17-6 lead.
After traveling 28 yards on seven plays, the Giants added three more points to extend their lead before halftime. Zvada connected on his second field goal attempt of the day, from 54 yards.
Malik wide open in the end zone 😮‍💨 📺: CBS pic.twitter.com/ujVwSiO8Na
End of First Half: Giants 20 Jaguars 6
Despite a missed 32-yard field goal by Zvada and a fumble by Cam Skattebo on 1st-and-10 at the Jacksonville 32-yard line, the Giants held the Jaguars to zero points in the third quarter.
The highlight of the quarter for New York came with the Jaguars facing 4th-and-1 at the Giants' 11-yard line with 1:06 remaining. Cornerback Dru Phillips broke up Lawrence's pass intended for receiver Jakobi Meyers, forcing the Jags to turn the ball over on downs.
Unfortunately, the Giants couldn't capitalize, failing to score in the period as well.
Jacksonville wasted little time in getting back on the board, settling for a field goal on their opening drive of the fourth quarter. Lawrence began the series with a 23-yard completion to Meyers and appeared poised for their first touchdown drive of the game.
However, the Jags' starter couldn't cap the nine-play, 49-yard drive with a scoring strike. Lawrence's would-be touchdown pass to receiver Parker Washington was ruled incomplete, forcing the Jaguars to settle for a 31-yard field goal from Little. Jacksonville had cut New York's lead to 20-9.
After cornerback Paulson Adebo intercepted Lawrence on 2nd-and-10 from the Jags' 18, the Giants needed only three yards on four plays to extend their lead to 14 points. Zvada redeemed his earlier miss by connecting on a 43-yard field goal, giving New York a 23-9 advantage.
The Jaguars finally reached the end zone on a 10-play, 75-yard drive that lasted just 3:24. Lawrence completed consecutive 15-yard and 16-yard passes to receiver Josh Cameron before connecting with Meyers on a 26-yard bomb.
He capped the drive with an 18-yard scoring strike to receiver Brian Thomas, Jr. Though their two-point attempt was thwarted by linebacker Kayvon Thibodeaux, the Jaguars once again cut into New York's lead at 23-15.
Jacksonville added to the rising anxiety throughout MetLife Stadium by once again moving the ball on a 10-play, 60-yard series.
Surprisingly, coach Liam Coen opted for the field goal instead of trying for a crunch-time touchdown. Little added three to the Jaguars' total by making a 26-yard field goal, further reducing Big Blue's lead to 23-18 with 3:40 remaining.
Fortunately for the hometown crowd, New York exorcised its late-game demons by grinding out a seven-play, 29-yard drive.
Skattebo essentially gave New York the win by securing a first down on a five-yard run with just over two minutes remaining. McCarthy and the offense settled into victory formation, giving the club its sixth win of the season.
FINAL: Giants 23, Jaguars 18.
On 2nd down of the game's opening drive, cornerback Greg Newsome suffered an ankle injury. He was briefly evaluated on the sideline before heading back to the locker room.
His status was quickly set to questionable, and he was eventually ruled out for the remainder of the game. Paulson Adebo replaced him in the lineup.
Giants linebacker Abdul Carter entered Week 11 with two sacks on the season. During the first half, he matched that total, logging two.
Carter finished the game with four total tackles, two tackles for loss, and the aforementioned pair of sacks. The third-overall pick in the 2025 NFL Draft was also credited with 12 pressures, the second-most of any player this season.
The Dallas Cowboys improved to 5-6 as quarterback Dak Prescott threw four touchdown passes and ran for a score. The Cowboys earned a 51-30 victory over the Tennessee Titans at AT&T Stadium.
Former Giant Saquon Barkley ran for a touchdown, helping the Philadelphia Eagles snap a seven-game losing streak. The Eagles (3-7) defeated the Pittsburgh Steelers 19-16 at Lincoln Financial Field.
The Washington Commanders (3-5-1) will host the Cincinnati Bengals at Northwest Stadium for a Monday Night Football showdown on Nov. 23. Kickoff is set for 8:15 p.m. ET.
The Giants will travel to Lucas Oil Stadium to face the Indianapolis Colts (3-8) in a Week 12 showdown. Kickoff is set for 1:00 p.m. ET on Sunday, Nov. 29, in Indianapolis.

title: Giants vs. Jaguars Live Blog: Updates, Highlights and Analysis From Week 11
full_text:
The New York Giants don't want to hear about how good the Jaguars have been.
Who could blame them? How the Jaguars, who are 7-2, are ahead of the Giants doesn't matter in this nationally televised Week 11 clash between two opponents who see each other once every four years.
What matters is the roster the Jaguars are bringing to MetLife Stadium, what challenges the Giants need to mitigate and what areas of weakness they can potentially exploit.
"All you do is look at the team they are right now, the opponent that we're facing," head coach John Harbaugh said.
But make no mistake about it: The Giants have heard the praise that has been heaped on the Jaguars, which has grown louder now that they are the next team up on Big Blue's schedule.
And while every game is important for the Giants to win, the Jaguars represent the kind of team Big Blue would conceivably face if it completes its quest to win the NFC East and earn a postseason berth. Let's say no one would blame the Giants if there is a little extra juice flowing through their veins.
They're seeking to show their critics that their 5-3-1 start is not the result of a fairly simple schedule, but the mark of a team that is trying to get better every single week. It has also made resiliency a calling card, considering the injuries and setbacks Harbaugh's first Giants roster has had to face.
It all boils down to seeing just what this team is made of with the opportunity that's before them, as Harbaugh noted.
"What are we going to do with this opportunity? What are we going to do over the next few weeks? Where are we going to go? It's up to us to determine who we are," he said.
"So, there's a lot at stake, and we'll find out how we're going to handle it. I mean, you don't know. You can talk all you want, you can say all you want, until you get out there and you start doing it and you find out really where you're at. And we're going to learn a lot."

title: Giants Week 11 Inactive List: Pinnock, Desrosiers Among Those Out vs. Jaguars
full_text:
Armed with a relatively healthy squad ahead of their nationally televised home game against the Jacksonville Jaguars, the New York Giants ’ Week 11 inactive list consists mainly of excess numbers at certain positions.
Safety Jason Pinnock headlines the inactive list. Pinnock has been part of the rotation at safety since Week 3 and started in Weeks 6 and 7. However, Ar'Darius Washington appears to have moved into a position where he's earned a bigger slice of the pie.
In addition, the Giants signed Tavierre Thomas, who can plug in at safety or cornerback, and they have Elijah Campbell and Tyler Nubin at safety, meaning that they can afford to deactivate one this week.
Running back Greg Desrosiers is also inactive this week. That became apparent when the Giants elevated Phil Mafah off the practice squad on Saturday.
Desrosiers, whom the Giants poached off the Chargers practice squad three weeks ago, could lose his roster spot this week as the Giants need to clear an opening for defensive lineman Dawaune Smoot, who is now out of standard practice squad elevations.
Tight end Thomas Fidone II, offensive linemen J.C. Davis and Josh Sills, defensive lineman Darius Alexander, and cornerback Nic Jones are the other inactive players for the Giants this week.
Fidone's inactivity is a mild surprise, considering Theo Johnson had another drop last week. Johnson now has 11 drops in two and a half seasons.
He has also seen his pass targets drastically reduced thanks to the addition of Isaiah Likely at the position. Johnson has been targeted in the passing game just 12 times and has caught only five balls.
Jones was the only player who didn't practice for part of the week (he sat out Wednesday and Thursday and was limited on Friday). With Thomas now on the roster and Paulson Adebo in reserve, the Giants can afford to spare a cornerback this week.
Defensive end Danny Striggow (concussion) was downgraded from questionable to out on Saturday after not clearing the protocol in time. He joins center Robert Hainsey (knee) as the two Jaguars who won't play due to injury.
The rest of the Jaguars' inactive plaqyers are receiver C.J. Williams, defensive tackle Matt Dickerson, defensive tackle Albert Regis, and safety Jalen Huskey.

title: Giants vs. Jaguars Week 11: Time, Channel and What to Watch
full_text:
The New York Giants might be building a case for the most resilient team through their first nine games of the 2026 season, but in a league as fast-paced as the NFL, every game is precious.
Sadly, New York had to be reminded of that harsh truth a little over a week ago when they were defeated 24-21 by the Washington Commanders on the back half of their biannual division series and four days after they earned an enormous road win against the Philadelphia Eagles to help broaden their lead in the NFC East standings.
Similar to their first meeting in Week 5, a 27-27 overtime tie, John Harbaugh and the Giants had chances to close out the game and unofficially knock the Commanders out of the race for the division crown.
Despite a pair of fourth-quarter Washington turnovers, the Giants couldn't deal the knockout punch. As they move on to Week 11, one of the league's heavyweights, the Jacksonville Jaguars, is next to pay them a visit in a game that has been flexed into the late-afternoon window.
Part of the NFL's decision was definitely a well-awaited sign of respect for Big Blue, who have been doubted in most of their games, yet, under the influence of their head coach, have found thrilling ways to win in the margins to steal a number of their five victories.
The Jaguars, who come in tied for the second-best record in the sport, want everyone to see what the franchise is really made of as they hope to contend for the Lombardi Trophy later this season.
Sparked by the leadership of head coach Liam Coen and a more capable offense led by quarterback Trevor Lawrence, Jacksonville has been bludgeoning opponents on the scoreboard.
On defense, the Jaguars are another team that can frustrate the hell out of the Giants offense, with a bevy of pass rushers that give them the third-best pass-rush win rate and have helped them force 16 turnovers, while New York has given up 14 this season.
In recent weeks, the Jaguars have doubled down on their quest to win their first-ever Super Bowl title by trading for a few veteran playmakers to strengthen their unit, including defensive tackle Jordan Davis, who is quite familiar with facing the Giants after seeing them only two games ago with the Philadelphia Eagles.
From top to bottom, the Jaguars are ready to test the Giants' ability to bounce back from a brutal defeat and see whether they have what it takes to play with the big dogs in the postseason in Harbaugh's first year.
Another storyline to watch is how this matchup affects the vibes around the Giants' chances of holding onto the lead in the NFC East, as the Jaguars are just the first of four playoff-caliber teams they will face in the coming weeks.
They were lucky to get some outside help last Sunday, but another bad loss mixed with wins by the Dallas Cowboys and Commanders, who still have life in the division, could begin to make things a little uncomfortable as we hit the latter stretch of the schedule.
The Giants have already proven numerous times that they can rally from tough outcomes and put their best foot forward when least expected. If they want to shock the rest of the league as they welcome the Jaguars to MetLife Stadium, they'll need another overall team performance with no room for fourth-quarter mistakes.

This Sunday's matchup will mark just the ninth all-time meeting between the Giants and Jaguars, dating back to the 1997 season when the latter was added to the NFL as an expansion team.
The series is tied 4-4 as the two franchises take the gridiron in Week 11, including a clean split in the previous four meetings dating back to 2010.
New York has taken three of the last four contests at home, but lost the most recent game in East Rutherford, 20-15, in the 2018 season opener at MetLife Stadium.
Both squads last met in Week 7 of the 2022 season in Jacksonville, where then-quarterback Daniel Jones led the Giants to a 23-17 win on the road, improving their record to 6-1 at the time.
The game will be aired on CBS. Jim Nantz will serve as the play-by-play announcer, with former NFL defensive end J.J. Watt joining him as the analyst and Tracy Wolfson as the sideline reporter.

Craig Wrolstad is the designated official for Sunday's game. Wrolstad is one of the longest-tenured active referees in the NFL, joining the league in 2003 as a field judge before earning the promotion to referee in 2014. He has worked in three Super Bowls in various roles.

title: Jets Week 11 Report Card: Grading Every Position After Snapping 5-Game Losing Streak
full_text:
It has not been smooth sailing lately for the Jets, but a trip out west appeared to be just what they needed in a 27-24 win over the Chargers to snap their five-game losing streak.
Considering the Chargers came in with a 1-8 record and the lowest-scoring offense in the league, this was certainly a favorable matchup for Gang Green amid a season that has been full of poor coaching and execution on the field.
Despite those obvious concerns entering Week 11, the Jets finally did all the little things well by going 9-of-11 on third down, 3-of-4 in the red zone and only committing four penalties for 18 yards, all while outgaining the Chargers in total yards, 341-261.
To the chagrin of many fans, there was simply no sign of the Jets tanking in this game as they put everything together on the field by not punting a single time and scoring points on every offensive possession until they ran the clock out to seal the win on their final drive. The defense may have given up four drives of at least 10 plays from the Chargers, but the offense's ability to finish its own drives in the end zone made up for it and gave the team what had been missing all season.
Before the Jets head south to face the Dolphins in a rematch of a 28-25 Week 7 loss at MetLife Stadium, let's hand out some grades for each unit after Sunday's win over the Chargers.
Although QB Geno Smith suffered a left ankle injury against the Bills, it was clear on this week's injury report that he was going to be good to go for Sunday's game.
The Jets were glad he was available after completing 17 of his 21 passes for 176 yards, three touchdowns and zero interceptions. He also marched the Jets back down the field after an opening-drive field goal and found running back Breece Hall for a seven-yard score in the corner of the end zone (h/t NFL), giving New York its first TD in 10 quarters.
Geno to Breece Hall for a Jets TD! NYJvsLAC on FOX/FOX One Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/00cok49kom
Not only did Smith get sacked only once and not turn the ball over, but he was efficient in converting third downs and helping the Jets move down the field. Keeping pace throughout a game and finishing drives has been an issue for Gang Green this season, but Smith led the Jets on three TD drives and carved this Chargers defense up.
When the leading receiver on a team only has three catches and 39 yards like WR1 Garrett Wilson did on Sunday, you would assume the offense was nonexistent. While the low-volume passing day from this banged-up receiving group was not ideal, Sterling Shepard shined after being called up from the practice squad with two catches for 24 yards and two TDs.
The former Giant scored both of his TDs in the red zone, but his second of the game— a 16-yard score to extend the lead to 10 in the fourth quarter (h/t NFL)—gave him the first multi-TD game of his 11-year career.
Two TDs for Sterling Shepard! NYJvsLAC on FOX/FOX One Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/1unKNT1rMh
Injuries to Omar Cooper Jr. (ankle, hip) and Isaiah Williams (rib) tested the depth of the WR room coming in, and a total of five catches, eight targets, and 69 yards from Wilson and Adonai Mitchell were not the most eye-popping. Still, the red-zone success from Shepard sparked this group and gave it something it has not consistently had this season.
The TEs were instrumental in opening up lanes for a ground game that averaged 4.5 yards per carry and helping move the chains, but their production in the passing attack was nothing to brag about. Even though rookie Kenyon Sadiq was viewed as someone who shouldn't be an afterthought following the grim injury report , he only had three catches on as many targets for 30 yards.
Mason Taylor, meanwhile, was held to just two receptions for 25 yards. This unit provided complementary production to the rest of the receivers and an offense that was clicking from the opening kick, but the lack of explosiveness continues to be an issue.
The game plan was clear offensively as Hall and Braelon Allen split the workload in the backfield and showed what they are capable of when they both get touches. Hall went for 20 carries, 86 yards and a long of 26, while Allen had 16 carries for 75 yards and a long rush of 15 yards. Neither scored a rushing TD, but the balance on the ground was key to sustaining drives and controlling the clock for more than 32 minutes.
It was a physical rushing attack, and it was even more impressive coming against a Chargers defense that held the Ravens to just 16 rush yards on 15 carries in Week 10. A TD would have been nice and needs to be something this group strives for going forward, but the balance from both backs is a good recipe for success regardless.
This unit has received its fair share of criticism this season, but it responded in a big way against the Chargers. From keeping the lanes open for 165 rushing yards to allowing one sack on Smith's 22 dropbacks and helping the offense convert the majority of its third downs without punting a single time, it was a solid display of situational football up front.
The inconsistency continues to be an issue, though, with 33 sacks allowed this season, so it's not like one dominant performance against a one-win team is going to immediately change the narrative. That said, it was a much more encouraging showing from a group that has been one of the weakest links at times.
This was the difference-making bunch in Sunday's game by a mile. Going up against a weak Chargers O-line with five players on injured reserve, the Jets took full advantage of that matchup with six sacks and constantly disrupting QB Justin Herbert (131 passing yards).
Darrell Jackson Jr. (0.5), Jack Heflin (0.5), Harrison Phillips (one) and Jowon Briggs (1.5) were key parts of that success, but the most impactful player was none other than rookie David Bailey, who had two sacks, five tackles (two solo), two tackles for loss, one pass defended, two QB hits and a forced fumble. This sack early in the third quarter was Bailey's second of the game (h/t NFL) and gave him 9.5 for the season.
2 sacks today, 9.5 this season for David Bailey 😤 NYJvsLAC on FOX/FOX One Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/CPQkr1Mrc3
Sure, Bailey was flagged for a costly roughing the passer penalty on the Chargers' TD drive to close out the first half and RB Omarion Hampton produced 89 yards on just 14 carries, but there was a lot to like after a punishing effort from the D-line.
While not as good as the unit up front, the LBs had some bright spots from this game. Jamien Sherwood led the entire team with 11 tackles (eight solo) and one forced fumble, while Demario Davis was not far behind with six tackles (four solo) and one tackle for loss.
There were a lot of impact plays and some active moments from this unit throughout the game, but it still had no answers for the Chargers' run game (158 total yards, one TD) and even allowed Hampton to break free for a 36-yard run on a TD drive late in the game. The league's third-worst run defense (137.4 ypg) is still a work in progress, but it was not all bad for a group that has certainly played worse this season.
Minkah Fitzpatrick was the leader of this group with six tackles (two solo), 0.5 sacks and one QB hit, while Dane Belton added six tackles (one solo) and Azareye'h Thomas had four solo tackles and one pass defended. They played well enough to win and did most of the little things well, aside from an illegal use of hands penalty on Thomas in the fourth quarter.
The Jets' secondary also kept Herbert in check for most of the game and did a solid job eliminating explosive plays. But the late breakdowns in the fourth quarter helped keep the game close as WR Ladd McConkey came down with both TD catches. That, along with the lack of turnovers, prevented them from putting the game out of reach sooner.

title: The Most Important Quotes from Jets After Chargers Win (and Why They Matter)
full_text:
Depending on who you ask, the New York Jets' 27-24 victory over the Los Angeles Chargers was either a nice win to end a losing streak, or the worst victory in franchise history that sank their chances of getting the top overall pick.
But if you ask Jets players and coaches, the win was an important one for the team as they try to improve down the stretch to end the year.
"Happy about a number of things," Jets head coach Aaron Glenn said. "I'm proud of the guys, they worked their ass off all week."
New York is clearly not tanking, and the players remain competitive for their head coach . Glenn wasn't the only person who spoke after the team's third win, either. Let's go through some of the most important sounds from the Jets locker room after a Week 11 victory.
David Bailey's performance this season has been special. What is even more special, though, is the impact his play has had on the rest of the team. The second-overall pick recorded another two sacks and a fumble forced on Sunday. He's now up to 9.5 sacks and six forced fumbles - just the third player to accomplish that feat since 2000.
But the joy Bailey plays with is what stands out the most to his teammates.
"I love him," Jets receiver Garrett Wilson said. "Every time I see him make a play I get so happy.”
New York's coaching staff remains impressed with Bailey's performance as well. It's not just as a mature player, or one that is clearly producing at a high level, but as someone who is looking to alter a game on one play.
"That's what he do," Glenn said. "We expect that from him. He's close to 10 sacks but the thing that sticks out to me is he's doing everything possible to get us the ball back. Anytime he's on the field, he gives us a chance for something big to happen."
New York's rookie class will be judged by more than just what Bailey does. But the fact the second overall pick is so good already shows this class could be a special one going forward.
You may have missed it on Sunday, but Jets offensive coordinator and play-caller Frank Reich came down from the booth to the field to call plays on Sunday. It's the first time this season he did that.
Perhaps the team not punting and having their most efficient outing since 2004 is a good indicator that this could be permanent. New York controlled the line of scrimmage and continued to get the ball in the hands of their best players throughout the game.
More importantly, having Reich on the sidelines was helpful for the quarterback room.
"It was pretty good to have him down there and we'll see how it goes from there," Jets quarterback Geno Smith said.
For what it's worth, it seems like having Reich on the sidelines could be permanent.
"I've always said that I'm going to do whatever it takes for us to improve and win games," Glenn said. "I'm not afraid of trying things. I thought it would be a good idea, so who knows. He had a chance to speak with the guys and I thought it was good for us."
New York's offensive output on Sunday was historic. Their running game led the way with 165 yards on the ground and 4.5 yards per carry. They were even better at protecting Smith - giving up just three pressures all game. Dylan Parham, Josh Myers, and Armand Membou did not give up a pressure on Sunday.
The starting five continues to get better with each game they play together. So long as the core remains, this will be a group that can dominate on Sundays for years to come. And no one was happier about the performance than Smith.
"I thought the offensive line did a tremendous job in not only the run game, but the pass game as well," Smith said.
It's worth noting that the Chargers had all three timeouts with under two minutes to play and they needed to stop the Jets rushing attack for a chance to tie the game. They simply couldn't do it, though - a sign of how good the entire offensive line was in Los Angeles.
It's been a long road for Sterling Shepard. The former second-round pick by the New York Giants was once a very serviceable starting receiver. Two injuries - a torn Achilles and ACL in back-to-back years - had derailed his career, though.
This season, Shepard has been on the Jets practice squad, but his impact on the team has remained as important as any other player on the roster. On Sunday, Shepard caught two passes for two touchdowns to help the Jets win a football game.
That alone makes Sunday something special for the veteran.
"The energizer bunny. That's who he is," Glenn said. "He has so much juice and he loves playing the game. He really does. I'm glad we have him."
Going from a league starter to a practice squad player is never easy for any veteran. But after the game, Shepard highlighted exactly why he has remained in the league - a positive attitude and a willingness to do whatever his team needs.
"This game will humble you," he said afterward. "I go out there every week and try to give our defense the best look possible."
Shepard is not going to be considered part of New York's top assets going into 2027. There's no guarantee he'll be on a roster at all either. But for one day at least, the 33-year-old got a chance to show he can still be a productive player when given a chance.
